findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-117-004: T4 establishes two key relational findings: (1) Peace's scope expands progressively — covenant-primary (to Israel, Num 6:26) → covenant-expansive (to nations in the prophets, Isa 57:19) → universally …
findings.finding_value: T4 establishes two key relational findings: (1) Peace's scope expands progressively — covenant-primary (to Israel, Num 6:26) → covenant-expansive (to nations in the prophets, Isa 57:19) → universally offered through Christ (Eph 2:14, Col 1:20) — with the only sustained exclusion being moral ("no peace for the wicked"). The covenantal boundaries are overcome in Christ; the moral boundary remains. (2) Peace is a site of cosmic contest: angelic mediation of peace is effective (Dan 10:19), elemental disruption of peace is real (Mar 4:39), and eschatological removal of peace is documented (Rev 6:4). Peace is not only a private inner condition but a publicly contested reality across the cosmic order.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-003: T1 names peace as integrative wholeness; T4 shows its relational structure is not incidental but constitutive. The peace-wholeness of T1 is not achievable in isolation — it is given by God (T4.1), ori…
findings.finding_value: T1 names peace as integrative wholeness; T4 shows its relational structure is not incidental but constitutive. The peace-wholeness of T1 is not achievable in isolation — it is given by God (T4.1), oriented toward God (T4.2), extended toward others (T4.3), and contested cosmically (T4.6). The interiority (T1) and the relationality (T4) are co-constitutive (confirmed from T3.11.3): the person at peace is the person in right relation — with God, with others, and with themselves. T4's expanding scope (covenant → universal) maps onto T1's eschatological dimension (the peace that has no end, Isa 9:7): the scope expands toward the same fullness that the essence reaches toward.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-008: T2 establishes the constitutional location of peace; T4 establishes the relational directions through which peace moves into and out of those locations. The synthesis: God gives peace (T4.1 → T2) by a…
findings.finding_value: T2 establishes the constitutional location of peace; T4 establishes the relational directions through which peace moves into and out of those locations. The synthesis: God gives peace (T4.1 → T2) by addressing the constitutional locations directly — the Aaronic blessing (Num 6:26) addresses the whole person; Joh 14:27 ("let not your hearts be troubled") addresses the heart specifically; Phili 4:7 ("peace will guard your hearts and minds") names both heart and mind as the guarded locations. The human receives peace (T4.4) through the same constitutional locations — the receptive soul (Psa 131:2, T2.2) and the directed mind (Isa 26:3, T2.4) are the reception points. The relational and constitutional analyses converge: peace moves through relational channels (T4) into constitutional locations (T2).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-016: T4's God-to-human direction (peace given through covenant, word, cross, Spirit) maps onto T5's mechanisms (proclamation, covenant-ground, cross-accomplishment, Spirit-formation) and sequences (gift re…
findings.finding_value: T4's God-to-human direction (peace given through covenant, word, cross, Spirit) maps onto T5's mechanisms (proclamation, covenant-ground, cross-accomplishment, Spirit-formation) and sequences (gift received → heart/mind guarded → somatic rest → expressed in community). The developing scope of T4 (covenant → universal) maps onto T5's eschatological trajectory: the expanding relational scope and the deepening eschatological fullness are the same movement outward from its source in God's identity as peace. The T4 finding that peace refused worsens peacelessness (Q&A-114) connects to T5's reversibility finding (T5.1.2) — the experiential peace is reversible in both directions: given and received, or offered and refused.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-017: T4's God-to-human direction and T6's causal sequences describe the same reality at different levels of abstraction. T4.1 (God gives peace through covenant/Christ/Spirit) is the relational description …
findings.finding_value: T4's God-to-human direction and T6's causal sequences describe the same reality at different levels of abstraction. T4.1 (God gives peace through covenant/Christ/Spirit) is the relational description of what T6.3.2 catalogues as causal inputs (trust, righteousness, discipline, Spirit, confession, love of law all produce peace). The covenant-of-peace (T4.1 — Isa 54:10) is the relational framework for what T6.4.2 names as the SHA.L root shared between peace and covenant at the structural level. The two analyses are not parallel but nested: T4 names the relational direction; T6 names the structural mechanism through which that direction operates.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-018: T4's relational scope findings (peace given to Israel → expanding to nations → universal in Christ) are lexically grounded in T7's vocabulary arc. The greeting-blessing (H7965K, T4.3 — human giving of…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational scope findings (peace given to Israel → expanding to nations → universal in Christ) are lexically grounded in T7's vocabulary arc. The greeting-blessing (H7965K, T4.3 — human giving of peace) has its person-type lexical ground in T7.1.6 (ish sha.lom — the man of peace as person-type). The absence of a dedicated antonym term (T7.1.5) confirms T4's finding that peace is primarily defined by its presence and relational giving, not by its absence — the vocabulary is positive-directional, matching the God-to-human direction of peace's primary flow (T4.1). The NT coinage eirēnopoieō (T7.1.9) names what T4.1.2 describes as the basis of God's peace-giving through Christ — the cross-accomplishment has its own unique verbal form precisely because it is a unique relational act.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — extensively and across five of seven groups. God gives covenantally toward Israel (872-001: land, promise, blessing — Gen 12:7, Gen 15:18); compassionately toward those in need (872-002: responsive giving to suffering — Gen 29:33, Hos 11:8 withheld giving-over); formatively toward the inner life (872-003: Spirit, wisdom, understanding — Neh 9:20, Job 38:36); judicially toward the faithless (872-004: giving-over as moral consequence — Hos 13:11, Jer 12:7); and transformatively toward the mourning (872-007: ashes → beauty, faint spirit → praise — Isa 61:3, Hos 2:15). Every mode of God-to-human giving is evidenced in the anchor verses. The God-to-human direction is the dominant directional structure of the registry (6 of 7 groups, OBS-060-017).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-004: T4 as a whole reveals that the relational architecture of this characteristic is directionally structured and asymmetrical. The dominant direction is God-to-human (6 of 7 groups, confirmed across T4.1…
findings.finding_value: T4 as a whole reveals that the relational architecture of this characteristic is directionally structured and asymmetrical. The dominant direction is God-to-human (6 of 7 groups, confirmed across T4.1); the human direction is responsive (T4.2: human gives back what was first given). The basis of divine giving is plural — covenantal, responsive, formative, moral-consequential, eschatological-grace (Q&A-102) — revealing that faithfulness is not a single relational mode but a relational orientation that differentiates itself across relational conditions while remaining unified in character. The human-to-God direction reveals responsive correspondence as the relational structure (Q&A-107): the proper relational form is one in which the human gives back to God what is his (glory, praise, self), having first received. The human-to-human direction is thinner in the data (Q&A-109) — reflecting the registry's God-subject dominance. T4.6 is substantially silent on spiritual beings. What T4 reveals as a whole: faithfulness-as-giving is constitutively a divine-initiative relational reality that the human enters through responsive participation. The human's giving is always downstream of divine giving; the correspondence is the proper form of the relationship.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-003: The five operational modes of giving (T1.4) map onto the four relational interfaces (T4) in a specific structural way. Performative and covenantal giving (modes 1) operate through the God-to-human int…
findings.finding_value: The five operational modes of giving (T1.4) map onto the four relational interfaces (T4) in a specific structural way. Performative and covenantal giving (modes 1) operate through the God-to-human interface (T4.1) with a covenantal basis. Responsive giving (mode 2) operates through the God-to-human interface with a responsive basis. Endowing giving (mode 3) operates through God-to-human with a formative basis. Judicial giving (mode 4) operates through God-to-human with a moral-consequential basis. Relinquishing self-giving (human mode) operates through the human-to-God interface. Glory-giving operates through the human-to-God interface. The relational interface is not external to the definition — it is a structural element of each operational mode. What this pair reveals: the characteristic cannot be defined without specifying its relational direction. The same act-concept (giving) becomes a different operational mode depending on which interface it operates through.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-008: The constitutional locations where the characteristic operates (T2 — heart, soul/nephesh, spirit, body) and the relational interfaces through which it operates (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal…
findings.finding_value: The constitutional locations where the characteristic operates (T2 — heart, soul/nephesh, spirit, body) and the relational interfaces through which it operates (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal a mirroring structure. God's giving proceeds from his leb (heart, Hos 11:8) and his nafshi (soul, Jer 12:7) — the deepest divine inner-being locations are engaged in the God-to-human direction. The human's giving toward God is expressed through the body (back, cheeks, face — Isa 50:6) and from the deepest inner orientation (Job 1:21 — recognition of divine sovereignty). The constitutional depths engaged in both directions are commensurate: God gives from his heart and soul; the human gives from the whole self, expressed bodily. What this pair reveals: the divine-human relational correspondence (DHC dimension, group 872-006) has a constitutional depth structure — the correspondence is not merely behavioural but engages the deepest constitutional levels of both parties. The giving that constitutes the correspondence is heart-to-body deep.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-012: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — perception, affect, volition, relational capacity all engaged) and the relational interface structure (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal a faculty-interface …
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — perception, affect, volition, relational capacity all engaged) and the relational interface structure (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal a faculty-interface correspondence. In the God-to-human direction: divine hearing (T3.1 — perception) precedes compassionate giving (T4.1 — responsive basis); divine affect (T3.4 — rahamim, leb) determines the direction of giving (T4.1 — basis of extension); divine relational capacity (T3.11) is the prior orientation that makes the giving possible. In the human-to-God direction: human perception (Q2 — recognising divine sovereignty), human affect (blessing under loss), human volition (choosing to give glory), and human relational capacity (genuine correspondence) are all required for the giving to be genuine (T4.2 — inner posture). What this pair reveals: the relational interfaces are not external channels through which giving flows; they are relational events in which the inner faculties of both parties are engaged simultaneously and correspondingly. The correspondence is not mechanical but genuinely personal.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-017: The relational interfaces (T4 — God-to-human primary, human-to-God responsive, covenantal scope) and the structural landscape (T6 — hub position, causal sequences, shared anchors) reveal that R060's h…
findings.finding_value: The relational interfaces (T4 — God-to-human primary, human-to-God responsive, covenantal scope) and the structural landscape (T6 — hub position, causal sequences, shared anchors) reveal that R060's hub position is constituted by its position at the centre of the divine-human relational network. The sequential patterns (T6.2 — giving→worship, suffering→giving, faithlessness→giving-over) are relational sequences: each involves God and the human in the roles described by T4. The shared anchors (T6.6) are high-density precisely because they are relational nodes — Hos 11:8 anchors five registries because it holds the divine inner-being and the human relational situation simultaneously. What this pair reveals: the structural hub position of R060 in the inner-being landscape is a direct consequence of its occupation of the divine-human relational centre. It is a hub because it is where the primary divine-human dynamic (God gives, human receives and responds) is most directly expressed and most extensively connected.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-018: The relational interface analysis (T4 — six of seven groups are God-to-human; the divine disposition ranges from covenantal to compassionate to formative to moral-consequential) and the primary anchor…
findings.finding_value: The relational interface analysis (T4 — six of seven groups are God-to-human; the divine disposition ranges from covenantal to compassionate to formative to moral-consequential) and the primary anchor identification (T7 — Hos 11:8 as the verse that uniquely reveals the divine inner-being decision structure) converge. Hos 11:8 is the primary anchor precisely because it holds the full complexity of T4 in a single verse: it shows the God-to-human relational direction (the giving is addressed at Ephraim/Israel), the multiple bases of divine giving (deserved-judgement vs. compassionate restraint), and the divine disposition (heart recoiling, compassion warming). The full vocabulary arc (T7.1.10 — enacted + constituted poles) maps onto the two directions of T4: the enacted pole (na.tan) is the God-to-human and human-to-God relational act; the constituted pole (emunah/hesed/pistis) is the dispositional quality that makes the relational giving faithful rather than merely generous. What this pair reveals: the relational architecture and the vocabulary architecture are the same structure described at two levels of abstraction.

Psa 5:5: "you hate all evildoers." Psa 11:5: "his soul hates the wicked." Deu 7:10: "repays to their face those who hate him, by destroying them." (2) The divine-to-human movement is consistently a response to what the human has done or become. Hos 9:15: "there I began to hate them. Because of the wickedness of their deeds" — the divine hatred is responsive to human choices.

Minimally and only in reactive/judicial form. Deu 32:19: "the Lord saw it and spurned them (na.ats), because of the provocation of his sons and his daughters." Lam 2:6: "the Lord has...spurned (na.ats) king and priest." These are judicial responses to Israel's prior contempt of him. God's movement toward the human in M06-B is not the extension of contempt as a disposition but the execution of a judicial response.

Yes, extensively. Group 252-003 (9 verses): Psa 106:40: "he abhorred his heritage." Amo 6:8: "I abhor the pride of Jacob." Psa 5:6: "the Lord abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man." God's abhorrence is sustained and serious — a real inner-being response to persistent covenant violation and corruption. The basis is always the accumulation of moral failure, never arbitrary.

Only in the descriptive sense of Isa 13:9 (the severity of divine judgment described using the cruelty term). The divine movement toward the human in M06-D is consistently the removal and judgment of the ruthless (Isa 29:20, 13:11) and the deliverance of those who suffer under them (Isa 49:25, Jer 15:21, 20:11). God is the answer to cruelty, not its practitioner toward the human person.

God acts to remove reproach from the human person (the dominant divine movement), and also imposes it as covenantal judgment (secondary, judicial). Removal: Gen 30:23 — "God has taken away my reproach." Jos 5:9 — "today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you." Isa 25:8 — "the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth." Imposition: Eze 5:14 — "I will make you a desolation and an object of reproach among the nations." Even the imposition is reversible (Eze 36:15).

Yes — Exo 23:22: "I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries." God takes up the adversary posture on the human person's behalf. This is not God extending enmity toward the human but God positioning himself as adversary to those who threaten the human. God's movement toward the person is as advocate and contender.

God acts as the judge of malice, not as its subject or practitioner. Eze 25:6-7: "because you have clapped your hands and stamped your feet and rejoiced with all the malice within your soul against the land of Israel, therefore, behold, I will stretch out my hand against you." God's movement toward the human person who exercises malice is judicial response.

The God-to-human direction is the most extensively evidenced directional axis across all seven sub-groups. This is the primary relational interface in M05. The cluster's characteristics are all first and most fully evidenced as divine dispositions toward the human person — before they are human dispositions toward others.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Yes — God's righteousness reaches the human person through: (1) proclamation (the declared standard that confronts the conscience, A1-005/006); (2) the Messiah (A1-007: God's righteousness incarnated and extended to humanity through Christ); (3) covenant faithfulness (A1-003: God's righteousness expressed toward his covenant people as reliability, keeping promises, betrothing in righteousness); (4) saving acts (A1-004: deliverance, vindication, restoration — all flowing from God's righteousness toward the person in need).

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — righteousness is given to the person by God: "born of him" (1Jo 2:29, VSG M26-A2-014); "the righteousness of God" in the person (2Cor 5:21, VSG M26-A2-008); credited to Abraham (Gen 15:6, VSG 3410-001). God extends righteousness to the human person as a gift received by faith — this is the primary mode of the God-to-human interface in M26.

**[C — Justification]** Yes — justification is definitionally a God-to-human act. "God who justifies" (Rom 4:5, VSG 3194-001); "justified by his grace" (Tit 3:7). Justification flows exclusively from God toward the person — the human person cannot justify themselves.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Yes — God executes avenging justice toward wrongdoers: "he has judged the great prostitute... and has avenged on her the blood of his servants" (Rev 19:2, VSG 944-002). God also executes justice toward the wronged through response to their cry (Luk 18:7–8, VSG 945-001: "he will give justice to them speedily").

**[E — Condemnation]** Yes — God condemns: "he condemned sin in the flesh" (Rom 8:3, VSG 4846-002); condemnation falls on those who disobey the gospel (2Th 1:9, VSG 949-001). God's condemnation is directed toward sin and toward those who reject righteousness.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Yes — God reckons: "it was counted to him as righteousness" (Rom 4:3–11, VSG 3410-001). The divine reckoning of faith as righteousness is the most explicitly God-to-human operation in F.

**[CLUSTER — T4.1]** E. God's righteousness operates toward the human person in every mode: as gift (A2, C), as proclamation (A1-005), as incarnation through the Messiah (A1-007), as saving deliverance (A1-004), as reckoning of faith (F), as avenging justice (D), and as condemnation of sin and unrighteousness (E). The God-to-human interface in M26 is comprehensive and operates in multiple directional modes.

findings.finding_value: Two modes of divine engagement with M46-A. First, divine commission of inner closure as judicial act: Isa 6:10 (God commands the making-fat of the heart as judgment on a people already resistant). Second, divine address to the inner-closed: Rev 3:17-18 (Christ addresses the Laodicean church with diagnosis and counsel — "I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire"). God both produces inner closure as judgment and addresses it with redemptive counsel.

findings.finding_value: M46-C has rich evidence of God toward the human person. God makes rich (1Sa 2:7), God's blessing makes rich without sorrow (Pro 10:22), God gives wealth and the power to enjoy it (Ecc 5:19), God provides richly (plousiōs) all things for enjoyment (1Ti 6:17). The divine provision of material goods is a recurring theme in M46-C — God is active in the material domain as the giver of wealth.

findings.finding_value: M01-A shows God operating toward the human person by: (1) **commanding** fear — Deu 6:13; 10:20; Ecc 12:13 (God directly requiring the reverential posture); (2) **implanting** it — Jer 32:40 (God pledging to place fear directly in the hearts of his people as a permanent disposition); (3) **forming** it through encounter — Deu 4:10 (God intending the Horeb encounter to produce lasting fear); (4) **rewarding** it — Exo 1:21 (God rewarding the midwives' fear-of-God-based disobedience with families).

M01-B shows God operating toward the human person through: (1) **angelic appearances** producing fear (Luk 1:12-13; Luk 2:9-10); (2) **Jesus's acts** producing fear (Mar 4:41; Act 5:5-11); (3) **divine commands to release fear** (Isa 43:1 anchor B-VCG-06; "do not fear" as God speaking directly to the person's fear-state); (4) **theophanic encounters** (Exo 19:16 — God's descent at Sinai producing involuntary trembling).

ya.re (H3372G) groups add the divine 'Fear not' command (298-001) as a structuring element — showing the divine address to inner fear as a distinct inner-being category. The reassurance pattern (divine declaration of presence + commanded displacement of fear) is significant for understanding how the inner-being state of fear is meant to be transformed.

M01-C shows God deploying terror toward enemy peoples: Exo 23:27 (anchor C-VCG-01: "God's terror is sent as an advance weapon" — God actively deploying terror into enemy inner lives); Jer 32:40 / Deu 11:25 (God placing dread of Israel in surrounding nations).

M01-D shows God producing dismay as judicial action: Psa 2:5 (God's wrath producing dismay in rebel kings); Jer 49:37 (anchor D-VCG-02: "God will terrify Elam before their enemies, making dismay the inner condition through which he breaks their will — his fierce anger is the divine source").

M01-F-VCG-03 shows God imposing covenantal-curse dread: Deu 28:66-67 (anchor: "continual dread without assurance of life is a covenantal curse" — God imposing the chronic dread as a covenant consequence of unfaithfulness).

God operates toward the human person across M01 in at least five distinct ways: commanding fear (M01-A), implanting it (M01-A, Jer 32:40), deploying it as weapon against enemies (M01-C), imposing it as judicial instrument against rebels (M01-D), and imposing covenantal-curse dread on the unfaithful (M01-F). God is uniquely active across the entire cluster — more so than in most other programme clusters examined to date.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, explicitly and repeatedly. God exults over his people with gladness and loud singing (Zep 3:17 — su.s and gil_verb); rejoices in doing Israel good with all his heart and soul (Jer 32:41 — su.s); will rejoice over restored Zion as a bridegroom over a bride (Isa 62:5 — su.s); will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in his people (Isa 65:19 — gil_verb and su.s); takes delight in prospering the restored (Deu 30:9 — su.s). The God-to-human direction is one of the most strongly evidenced directions in the corpus.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, extensively and across multiple registers: (1) **God produces joy in the heart** — Psa 4:7 ("you have put more joy in my heart"); Ezr 6:22 ("the Lord had made them joyful"); Ecc 5:20 ("God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart"); 2Ch 20:27 ("the Lord had made them rejoice over their enemies"); (2) **God gives joy as a gift** — Ecc 2:26 ("God has given wisdom and knowledge and joy" to the one who pleases him); Psa 126:3 ("the Lord has done great things for us; we are glad"); (3) **God fills with joy** — Rom 15:13 ("may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing"); Act 13:52 ("filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit"); (4) **God's own joy over his people** — Luk 15:7, 10 (joy in heaven and before the angels over the repentant sinner); Zep 3:17 (God rejoicing over his people with gladness); Jer 32:41 (God rejoicing over Israel in doing good); (5) **Jesus' joy given to disciples** — Joh 15:11 ("my joy may be in you"); Joh 17:13 ("that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves"); Mat 25:21, 23 ("enter into the joy of your master").

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes, in two registers: (1) **Spirit-produced agalliao** — the Holy Spirit is the primary agent producing Suffering-Joy in the human person: Luk 10:21 (Jesus' agalliao is "in the Holy Spirit"); 1Th 1:6 (adjacent — "joy of the Holy Spirit" received amid affliction); Act 13:52 (adjacent — "filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit"). The Spirit is God-toward-the-human-person in the constitutional dimension; (2) **Eschatological promise as the ground** — the "joy set before him" (Heb 12:2), "your reward is great in heaven" (Mat 5:12), and "when his glory is revealed" (1Pe 4:13) are God's word-of-promise operating as the cognitive-eschatological ground that the Spirit works through to produce Suffering-Joy. God-toward-the-human-person operates through both Spirit and word.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, extensively and at the most fundamental level. (1) **M04-L-VCG-01 — divine character goodness**: God is the originating subject of the evaluative-goodness faculty — Gen 1:4–31 (God sees and declares good); Gen 2:18 (God identifies the not-good and remedies it); Psa 25:8 ("good and upright is the Lord"); Psa 86:5 ("you are good and forgiving"); Psa 100:5; 106:1; 107:1; 118:1, 29; 135:3; 136:1 (the ki-tov formulas — God's goodness declared as the ground for praise); Nah 1:7 ("The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble"); Lam 3:25 ("The Lord is good to those who wait for him"); Psa 145:9 ("The Lord is good to all"); (2) **M04-O-VCG-04 — covenantal promise and good hand**: God's good hand enabling Ezra's journey (Ezr 7:9; 8:18); God's good hand enabling Nehemiah's petition (Neh 2:8); God's good hand as the testimony motivating communal action (Neh 2:18); God's good promises fulfilled (Jos 21:45; Jer 29:10; 33:14; Num 10:29); (3) **M04-O-VCG-03 — God producing wellbeing**: Ezr 6:22 ("the Lord had made them joyful"); 2Ch 20:27 ("the Lord had made them rejoice" — adjacent); Psa 112:5 ("it is well with the man who deals generously" — God's moral order producing wellbeing for the righteous).

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes — God's Delight directed toward the human person is the most extensively documented God-to-human inner-being movement in M04. Six modes: (1) **Rescue and exaltation from Delight** — Psa 18:19 / 2Sa 22:20 ("he rescued me, because he delighted in me"); Psa 37:23 ("the steps of a man are established by the Lord, when he delights in his way"); 1Ki 10:9; 2Ch 9:8 ("delighted in you and set you on the throne"); Num 14:8 ("if the Lord delights in us, he will bring us into this land"); (2) **Relational naming from Delight** — Isa 62:4 ("you shall be called My Delight Is in Her, for the Lord delights in you, and your land shall be married") — God's Delight toward Zion producing a new covenantal identity; (3) **Parental cherishing** — Jer 31:20 ("Ephraim my darling child" — sha.a.shu.im persisting through rebuke, God's heart yearning) — God-to-human Delight as the most tender relational form; (4) **Restoration from Delight** — Deu 30:9 ("the Lord will again take delight in prospering you") — divine Delight as the engine of national restoration; (5) **Wisdom as God's delight** — Pro 8:30–31 — God's daily sha.a.shu.im in Wisdom, and through Wisdom in the children of man — the creative-relational Delight that constitutes the human-divine relationship from the beginning; (6) **Trinitarian Delight** — Mat 3:17; 12:18; 17:5; Mar 1:11; Luk 3:22; Col 1:19; 2Pe 1:17 — the Father's eudokeo directed toward the Son, which is the archetype of all divine-to-human Delight.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes, in three primary God-to-human registers: (1) **God's pleasant character extended toward the community** — Psa 90:17 ("let the favor/pleasantness [no.am] of the Lord our God be upon us") — divine pleasantness as a character-quality that God extends toward his people; (2) **Divine beauty received by the worshiper** — Psa 27:4 ("to gaze upon the beauty [no.am] of the Lord") — God's own beauty as the object that the worshiper receives as Pleasure; God extends his beauty toward the seeking person; (3) **Divine river of delights** — Psa 36:8 ("you give them drink from the river of your delights [ed.nah]") — God lavishly supplying delight from his own inexhaustible source toward those who feast in his house; (4) **Eschatological acceptance as pleasing aroma** — Eze 20:41 ("as a pleasing aroma I will accept you") — God extending his receptive Pleasure toward restored Israel as a future-oriented covenantal gift; (5) **Pleasures forevermore** — Psa 16:11 ("at your right hand are pleasures forevermore") — God as the permanent source of pleasure in his own presence.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes, in two primary God-to-human directions: (1) **God performing wonders toward Israel** — the dominant VCG-01 pattern throughout: God's marvellous deeds are the divine acts directed toward the human community that produce Wonder as the response; Exo 3:20 (wonders done in Egypt); Exo 34:10 (marvels "before all your people"); Psa 31:21 ("he has wondrously shown his steadfast love to me when I was in a besieged city") — divine wonders extended as saving acts toward the person in distress; Joe 2:26 ("the Lord your God, who has dealt wondrously with you") — wonder-acts as the mode of divine engagement with the covenant community; (2) **God opening the eyes to behold wonders** — Psa 119:18 ("open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law") — the petition implies God extends the capacity for Wonder as a gift; the ability to perceive the wondrous in Scripture is itself a God-to-human act.

**[CLUSTER]** E — God-to-human operation is evidenced for all seven characteristics, but with a clear hierarchy of breadth: (1) **Delight (Char 4)** is the most extensively documented God-to-human characteristic in the cluster — six distinct divine registers (rescue from Delight, relational naming from Delight, parental cherishing as Delight, restoration from Delight, trinitarian Delight, and creative-Delight in Wisdom before creation). No other characteristic in M04 has as many distinct divine-to-human registers; (2) **Joy (Char 2)** is the second most extensively evidenced — God produces Joy in the heart (Psa 4:7), makes them joyful (Ezr 6:22), fills with Joy through the Spirit (Gal 5:22), and sends Christ's own Joy into the disciples (Joh 15:11); (3) **Gladness (Char 3)** operates from God primarily through his character (M04-L-VCG-01 — divine goodness as the archetype of all evaluative gladness) and through his providential acts (good hand, fulfilled promises); (4) **Wonder (Char 6)** — the entire VCG-01 corpus (61 verses) is God performing wonders toward Israel; God also opens the eyes to perceive wonders (Psa 119:18); (5) **Suffering-Joy (Char 7)** operates from God primarily through the Holy Spirit (Luk 10:21; 1Th 1:6) — the most constitutionally immediate divine-to-human Suffering-Joy; (6) **Pleasure (Char 5)** and **Exultation (Char 1)** are less God-to-human in primary orientation (they are more human-toward-God), but God's exultation over his people (Zep 3:17; Jer 32:41) and God's pleasant beauty (Psa 27:4's no.am) confirm God-to-human operation in both.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, in a specific and distinctive way. God deploys shame as a judicial verdict and as a moral instrument directed at human persons. The M07-B evidence documents God "putting enemies to shame" (Psa 44:7; 53:5; 86:17; Zec 10:5), exposing idol-makers to shame (Isa 44:9-11; 45:16), and placing shame on those who opposed his servant (Isa 41:11; 42:17). This is God using shame as a tool of judgment — it moves from God toward the person as a consequence of their action against God or his people. More remarkably, God also deploys shame as a restorative instrument toward his own people: the commands in Eze 16:52; Eze 36:32; Eze 43:10 — "be ashamed and confounded for your ways, O house of Israel" — are divine invocations of shame directed at his covenant people as the gateway to renewal. God extends shame toward the human person both as judgment (on enemies) and as corrective mercy (on his own people).

**[CHAR-2]** E — Extensively evidenced in VCG-03. God extends CHAR-2 to the proud as a judicial act: "your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down" (2Sa 22:28); "the Lord God of hosts will lop the boughs with terrifying power" (Isa 10:33); "I will change their glory into shame" (Hos 4:7). God also extends CHAR-2 redemptively through the mortal body's state (1Cor 15:43) — the dishonored mortal condition is God-ordained as the seed-state for the glorified body. The judicial basis is moral cause (pride, idolatry, opposition to God's servant); the redemptive basis is eschatological purpose.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — God extends CHAR-3 in the structural-assignment mode (VCG-02): the potter's sovereign assignment of vessels for dishonorable use (Rom 9:21) is God's prerogative in the creation and governance of persons. The basis is God's authority over his own creation; the content is the objective assignment of standing according to God's sovereign purpose.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — God is the standard against which CHAR-4's evaluative operation works ("in the sight of God," 2Cor 4:2). God's giving over of persons to dishonorable passions (Rom 1:24; 1:26) — "God gave them up" — shows God as the agent who permits the VCG-02 moral disorder as a consequence of idolatry. This is not God extending shamefulness but God releasing the person into the shamefulness their own choices have generated.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — God acts against CHAR-5 rather than extending it: 1Cor 1:28 — God choosing the despised to nullify things that are — is God's counter-movement against the world's contempt-verdicts. God's sovereign reversal of CHAR-5 is the theological foundation for why the recipient of contempt need not be defined by the contempt-verdict. God does not extend contempt-producing-shame toward persons; he extends the reversal of contempt and the vindication of the despised.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — God confirms and validates CHAR-6: Gen 20:6 (contextually) — God's response to Abimelech's appeal to innocence is to confirm it and grant protection. God is the authoritative validator of the innocence-claim: whether CHAR-6 is present is not merely a self-assessment but a reality confirmed or denied by God. God also reveals the incapacity for innocence (Hos 8:5) — the divine question "how long will they be incapable of innocence?" reveals that God tracks the moral condition of CHAR-6 and names its loss.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — God's movement toward the human person across M07 is the most theologically differentiated dimension in the cluster. Five distinct modes are evidenced. (1) God as shame-bearer's guardian — protecting those who trust him from being put to shame: the repeated Psalm formula "let me not be put to shame" (Psa 25:2; 31:1; 119:31) presupposes this guardianship; 1Cor 1:28 shows God choosing the despised to nullify the world's contempt-assessments (Chars 1, 5). (2) God as sovereign abaser — bringing the proud low as a judicial act: the sha.phel VCG-03 corpus (1Sa 2:7; Psa 75:7; Isa 2:11) is the most extensive God-to-human mode in the cluster (Char 2). (3) God as worth-assigner — assigning standings of honour or dishonour according to his sovereign purpose: the potter's right (Rom 9:21; Char 3). (4) God as moral standard — being the sight before which conduct bears or does not bear scrutiny: "in the sight of God" (2Cor 4:2; Char 4). (5) God as innocence-confirmer — acknowledging the genuine innocence-claim and acting accordingly: God's response to Abimelech (Gen 20:6; Char 6). These five modes are not in tension: they are different expressions of the same God's character operating in M07's field — guardian, sovereign, assigner, standard, and confirmer.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — CHAR-1 does not operate from God toward the human person — God does not possess or extend arrogant self-elevation. What the evidence consistently shows is God's active response to CHAR-1 in the human person: sustained, structural divine opposition. Jam 4:6 (vc=33931, M08-A4-VCG-01): "God opposes the proud, while granting grace to the humble" — the opposition is named as the direct relational response to CHAR-1. 1Pe 5:5 (vc=33934, M08-A4-VCG-01): "God opposes the proud" — repeated citation of the same principle, confirming it as a structural divine disposition. 2Sa 22:28 (vc=34236, M08-A4-VCG-02): "your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down" — God's watchful attention specifically directed at the proud as a target for reversal. Luk 1:51 (vc=33930, M08-A1-VCG-03): "he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts" — active divine dispersal of the proud at the level of their inner thoughts. The God-to-human direction in CHAR-1's evidence is not extension of the characteristic but active, sustained opposition to it.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 does not operate from God toward the human person — God does not possess presumptuous defiance. What the evidence shows is God's consistent opposition and judicial response to CHAR-2. Deu 17:12 (vc=34110, M08-B-VCG-02): the presumptuous man "shall die; so you shall purge the evil from Israel" — God's judicial response through the appointed legal system. Neh 9:10 (vc=34125, M08-B-VCG-01): "you performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants and all the people of his land, for you knew that they acted arrogantly against our ancestors" — divine counter-action to CHAR-2. Mal 4:1 (vc=34107, M08-B-VCG-02): "the arrogant and all evildoers will be stubble; the day that is coming shall set them ablaze" — God's eschatological judgment of CHAR-2.

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 does not operate from God toward the human person. The characteristic therefore operates from God toward the human person as a moral verdict, a relational exclusion, and a persistent divine response.

**[CHAR-4]** E — God does not extend idolatrous abomination toward humans — he is the party offended by it. What operates from God toward the person in the context of this characteristic is the divine response: (1) jealousy — Deu 32:16 (vc=65938 — VCG-02): "stirred him to jealousy"; (2) hatred/anger — Jer 44:4 (vc=65966 — VCG-04): "this abomination that I hate"; Deu 12:31 (vc=1683 — VCG-02): "every abominable thing that the Lord hates"; (3) withdrawal — Eze 5:11 (vc=65969 — VCG-05): "I will withdraw"; (4) unprecedented judgment — Eze 5:9 (vc=65968 — VCG-05): "I will do with you what I have never yet done"; (5) desolation — Eze 33:29 (vc=65999 — VCG-05): "the land a desolation and a waste because of all their abominations." The characteristic's divine-to-human operation is therefore entirely a response: divine judgment, withdrawal, and desolation as consequences of the characteristic's human expression.

**[CHAR-5]** E — God does not extend iniquity toward the human person — he is the moral authority who perceives and judges it. What operates from God toward the person in the context of this characteristic is: (1) active hatred — Psa 5:5 (vc=38237 — VCG-03): "you hate all evildoers" — God's settled moral hatred directed at those who work iniquity; (2) retributive return — Psa 94:23 (vc=38249 — VCG-03): "He will bring back on them their iniquity and wipe them out" — God returns the accumulated iniquity upon the schemer; (3) responsive judgment — Deu 28:20 (vc=38439 — VCG-05): "curses, confusion, and frustration… because of the evil of your deeds" — God's response to evil deeds; (4) instruction-through-opening — Job 36:10 (vc=38215 — VCG-04): "He opens their ears to instruction and commands that they return from iniquity" — the divine initiative in creating the possibility of departure.

**[CHAR-6]** E — God does not extend evil speech toward the human person — he is its target (VCG-01) or the one whose name is dishonoured by others' speech and conduct (VCG-02). What operates from God toward the person in the context of this characteristic is the divine response: the plagues and judgments that the Rev 16 corpus (VCG-01) shows humans blaspheming rather than receiving correctly. Rev 16:9 (vc=14352 — VCG-01): "God who had power over these plagues" — the divine power directed toward the human person through judgment is the context within which the blasphemy occurs. Additionally, 1Pe 2:12 (vc=14377 — VCG-03): "glorify God on the day of visitation" — the day of visitation is the divine movement toward humanity that eventually exposes the false accusation. God's movement toward the person is through judgment and visitation, not through evil speech.

**[CLUSTER]** E — None of the six M10b characteristics operates from God toward the human person as a gift or extension — God does not bestow inner evil on anyone. What operates from God toward the person constituted by M10b characteristics is consistently the divine response: judgment, hatred, withdrawal, retributive return, and instruction. The cluster maps five distinct divine response-modes across its six characteristics: (a) active hatred (Char 1: Psa 11:5 — "his soul hates the wicked"; Char 5: Psa 5:5 — "you hate all evildoers"); (b) retributive return (Char 5: Psa 94:23 — "bring back on them their iniquity"; Char 1: Psa 94:23 same); (c) withdrawal of presence (Char 4: Eze 5:11 — "I will withdraw"; Char 3: Pro 3:32 — exclusion from divine confidence); (d) judgment and desolation (Char 4: Jer 44:22 — land desolation; Chars 3, 6: eschatological judgment); (e) restorative instruction (Char 5: Job 36:10 — opening the ear to instruction; Char 4: Eze 14:6 — command to repent and turn). The cluster reveals that God's operations toward the M10b-constituted person are two-sided: responding to the evil with judgment/withdrawal AND maintaining the offer of instruction and return (in all six characteristics, restoration or return is possible prior to the eschatological terminus).

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, in two distinct modes. First, God is the source of the clean/unclean categorical system: throughout Lev 11-15 and Lev 13-14, the laws are delivered as divine speech ("the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying..."); the categories are divinely established, not humanly constructed. God's delineation of which animals are clean and unclean (Lev 11, M10c-A-VCG-02), which bodily conditions produce defilement (Lev 12, 15, M10c-A-VCG-05 and -06), and which disease states require examination (Lev 13-14, M10c-B-VCG-02) are all expressions of God's determination of the sacred/common boundary. Second, God's remedial provision operates toward the human: the red-heifer ash designated as "the water for impurity for the congregation of the people of Israel; it is a sin offering" (Num 19:9, M10c-A-VCG-07) is God's own provision for resolving the most severe defilement — God provides the remedy, not merely the requirement.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, in one specific and theologically significant mode: divine judicial abandonment. Rom 1:24 (VCG-02): "God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves" — God's action of giving over (paredōken) is an active divine movement that deepens the person's moral-inner defilement-state as a consequence of their prior rejection of him. This is the characteristic operating from God toward the human: God does not cause the defilement but acts in a way that removes the restraint on it, allowing the condition to deepen as judicial consequence. This is the inverse of the divine remedial action of Characteristic 1 (where God provides standing remedy); here God's action is judicial withdrawal of the constraint that had limited the defilement's spread.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, in three modes. (1) Divine perception and declaration: Eze 23:13 (VCG-02) — "I saw that she was defiled" — God perceives and holds the defilement as a spiritual fact; Hos 5:3 — "I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; Israel is defiled" — divine omniscience confronts the community with what they cannot see about themselves. (2) Judicial deepening of defilement: Eze 20:26 (VCG-02) — "I defiled them through their very gifts" — God uses their defiant offering of firstborn as the instrument of their own further defilement as judicial punishment. (3) Cleansing promise as divine gift: Eze 37:23 (VCG-05) — "I will save them... and will cleanse them"; Zec 13:1 (VCG-05) — "a fountain opened... to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness" — the divine movement toward the defiled community is ultimately one of cleansing and restoration.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, in two modes. (1) Divine authority confronting and expelling the spirits: Mar 5:8 — "Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!"; Mar 9:25 — "I command you, come out of him and never enter him again"; Luk 9:42 — "Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy" — divine actions operating toward the person by removing the characteristic's source. (2) Delegated authority given to the disciples: Mat 10:1 (VCG-03) — "he gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out" — God's authority extended through Christ to the disciples.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics show God acting toward the human person in relation to the characteristic, but his mode of action differs significantly across the four. Characteristic 1: God as the source of the clean/unclean categorical system (the laws are delivered as divine speech throughout Lev 11-15 and 13-14) and as the provider of remedial resources (Num 19:9 — the red-heifer ash designated as a sin offering for the congregation). Characteristic 2: God acting judicially — "gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity" (Rom 1:24 VCG-02) — a divine withdrawal of restraint that deepens the condition as consequence of prior human rejection of God. Characteristic 3: God acting in three modes — divine perception and declaration (Eze 23:13 — "I saw that she was defiled"), judicial deepening (Eze 20:26 — "I defiled them through their very gifts"), and cleansing promise (Eze 37:23 — "I will save them... and will cleanse them"). Characteristic 4: God acting through sovereign expulsion (Mar 5:8; Mar 9:25; Luk 9:42) and delegated authority (Mat 10:1 — "he gave them authority over unclean spirits"). The cluster pattern: God is never the cause of the defilement-state (it is creaturely) but is always involved in its management, judgment, and resolution. His disposition ranges from covenantal provision (Char 1) through judicial withdrawal (Char 2) through covenantal seriousness and restorative promise (Char 3) to sovereign compassionate expulsion (Char 4).

questions.question_text: On what basis does God extend the characteristic — conditional, unconditional, covenantal, or responsive — as the evidence shows?

findings.session_b_note:
The data reveals a nuanced answer — the basis varies by context and the variation is analytically significant:

**Covenantal:** The OT cultic mode is covenantal — forgiveness is granted on the basis of correct covenantal performance (sacrifice, priestly mediation). The mechanism is external and the basis is covenant-compliance (Lev 4:20). F-006 answer confirms: "the OT cultic mode — the mechanism (correct sacrifice) defines the conditions."

**Character-based (unconditional within its scope):** Psa 86:5 — "to all who call upon you." The basis is God's own character (goodness, steadfast love) and the only condition is calling. H5546 (sal.lach) names forgiveness as an attribute of God's essential goodness — not conditioned on the quality of the petitioner but on the character of God. Similarly, Jer 31:34 — the new covenant declaration has no stated inner-being prerequisite beyond covenant membership.

**Responsive (to access-postures):** NT access-postures (repentance, faith, confession) name the basis as responsive — God forgives when the inner-being conditions are met. F-007: "These are access-postures, not merit-conditions." The basis is not merit but orientation — God responds to the inner posture of repentance, faith, and confession.

**Christological:** Eph 1:7 — "according to the riches of his grace." The ultimate basis in the NT is grace — divine character overflowing in the Christ-event. The basis is neither covenantal compliance nor human merit but divine generosity grounded in the atoning act.

The basis therefore moves historically: covenant mechanism (OT cultic) → divine character appeal (OT intercessory) → new covenant declaration (prophetic) → grace through atonement (NT). The trajectory is toward increasing unconditionality, with the NT access-postures naming not conditions of merit but orientations of reception.

findings.session_b_note:
The data reveals that God's compassion operates on multiple bases simultaneously, and these are not in contradiction:

**Sovereignly free (unconditional at the divine initiative level):** Rom 9:15 — oikteirō — "I will have compassion on whom I have compassion." This is the most direct statement in the data: divine compassion is sovereignly free, not earned or elicited by human merit or condition. God's compassion is not a response to human worthiness.

**Covenantal (constitutive of the covenant relationship):** The chesed vocabulary is definitionally covenantal — steadfast love is the loyalty that holds the covenant from God's side regardless of Israel's faithfulness. Lam 3:22 — "his mercies never come to an end" — names chesed as the unbreakable covenantal commitment. This is not unconditional in the sense of indifferent to covenant — it is the covenant's foundation on the divine side.

**Responsive (to need and suffering):** The splanchnizō pattern in the Gospels shows God-in-Christ responding to what he sees — the crowd without a shepherd, the widow's grief, the leper's condition. This responsiveness does not contradict sovereign freedom — it is the form that sovereign compassion takes when it encounters actual human suffering.

**Temporally asymmetric with judgment:** Isa 54:8 — a moment of anger, then everlasting chesed/racham. God's compassion is the characteristic that re-asserts itself after judgment. This is responsive in a temporal sense: it is what God returns to. The anger is real but temporary; the compassion is permanent. This temporal structure is itself data about the basis of divine compassion — it is the ground state of God's orientation toward the human person.

**Key finding:** The data does not support a reading of divine compassion as merely conditional (earned by human behaviour) or merely unconditional (indifferent to the human situation). It is sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, and situationally responsive — all simultaneously.

findings.session_b_note:
The divine response to contrition — reviving, nearness, dwelling, attention — is extended on the basis of **divine character, not human merit**. Isa 57:15 grounds the divine promise in God's own self-identification: "the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy." The divine dwelling with the contrite is an expression of who God is, not a reward for the quality of the person's contrition.

The principle is not merit-based exchange but **character-consistent divine disposition**: the holy God's character includes attention to the lowly. This is not unconditional in the sense of indifference to the human posture — the posture of contrition is required (Jer 44:10 shows the alternative clearly). But neither is it earned — the contrite person brings no merit, only disclosed need. The operative principle is divine holiness-and-nearness responding to creaturely openness.

findings.session_b_note:
Finding 062-EXTEN-001 addresses this. The basis is mixed:

**Grace-based (not merit-based):** 2Pe 1:4 — God grants the promises that enable divine nature participation based on divine character and initiative, not on recipient merit. The extension is from divine character, not in response to human achievement.

**Covenantal:** Mal 2:14 — God as witness to the companion-wife covenant. The divine fellowship-protection operates within a covenantal framework. God's witness is covenant-based.

**Redemptive/substitutionary:** Isa 53:5 — the wound-fellowship of the servant produces healing in others through substitutionary bearing of their transgressions. The basis is redemptive, operating through the servant's vicarious suffering.

**Responsive within the covenantal frame:** Eze 37:19 — God's joining of the divided sticks is responsive to the prior division caused by human faithlessness (the split kingdom). The divine fellowship-action is a response to a prior condition, but the initiative of the response is entirely God's.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence reveals a structural tension between the unconditional and conditional registers — and this tension is itself the analytical finding. On the unconditional side: Gen 1:31 establishes goodness as a creative-ontological act prior to any human response — God declares creation good without condition. The doxological refrain "for he is good, his steadfast love endures forever" names an enduring, non-contingent character attribute. On the conditional side: Rom 11:22 names a condition on the ongoing experience of divine chrēstotēs — "provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off." This is not a condition on God's character but on the human's ongoing reception of its benefits. Rom 2:4 implies responsiveness — God's kindness "is meant to lead you to repentance," with an implied expectation that repentance follows. The resolution: God's goodness as a character attribute is unconditional; the human's ongoing experience of its relational benefits is covenantal-responsive. This distinction is analytically significant and carries to SP-067-018 (the conditionality question). (OBS-067-OBS-006, OBS-067-OBS-043, OBS-067-OBS-044, SP-067-018)

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-004: T4 as a whole reveals that goodness operates across all relational directions simultaneously — God-to-human, human-to-God, and human-to-human — but with a fundamental asymmetry: the God-to-human direc…
findings.finding_value: T4 as a whole reveals that goodness operates across all relational directions simultaneously — God-to-human, human-to-God, and human-to-human — but with a fundamental asymmetry: the God-to-human direction is prior, generative, and abundant in evidence; the human-to-God direction is responsive and derivative; the human-to-human direction is overflow from prior reception. This is not a simple tripartite scheme but a structured cascade: God's goodness initiates and flows toward the human person (Q&A-099-101); the human responds in trust, seeking, and worship (Q&A-103-105); the goodness received overflows toward others through instruction, justice, and kindness (Q&A-107-109). The most structurally significant T4 finding is the unconditional/conditional distinction (Q&A-100): God's goodness as a character attribute is unconditional; the human's ongoing experience of its relational benefits is conditional on continued trust. This distinction has direct implications for how goodness is taught, received, and sustained. The spiritual beings interface is largely silent — the relational architecture of goodness is thoroughly human-divine in orientation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-023: T4 identified that God's goodness as a character attribute is unconditional while the human's ongoing experience of its relational benefits is conditional (Q&A-100). T5 named the transformation arcs t…
findings.finding_value: T4 identified that God's goodness as a character attribute is unconditional while the human's ongoing experience of its relational benefits is conditional (Q&A-100). T5 named the transformation arcs through which the conditional dimension operates: the positive transformation arc (encounter → trust → reorientation → overflow) is the arc in which the conditional relational experience is deepened; the moral awareness arc (recognition → loathing → repentance) is the arc that recovers the relational experience when it has been lost through departure. T4's human-to-God enabling inner postures (waiting, seeking, trust — Q&A-104) correspond to T5's formation mechanisms: the posture of waiting corresponds to the encounter mechanism (sustained receptive openness); the moral awareness arc is the recovery mechanism for the person who has departed from the relational posture. Together: T5's formative processes are the mechanisms through which T4's relational conditions are entered, sustained, and restored. Transformation and relationship are inseparable in goodness.

findings.finding_value: T4 confirmed that the God-to-human direction of goodness is initiatory, generous, and sustaining (Q&A-101). T7 confirms that the primary literary form carrying divine goodness (prophetic covenantal address at Mic 6:8, doxological Psalm declarations, Pauline epistolary) all use forms that emphasise divine initiative and human receptivity. T7's literary analysis (Q&A-178-179) reveals that the literary forms carrying goodness are theologically intentional: the covenant lawsuit form (Mic 6:8) establishes divine initiative in defining the good; the invitation form ("taste and see" — Psa 34:8) establishes divine initiative in the encounter; the indicative-imperative structure of Col 3:12 (God has made you chosen → therefore put on kindness) establishes divine prior action before human response. T7's literary analysis confirms T4's relational architecture through the literary forms that carry them: the literature itself models the God-initiates-human-responds structure.

findings.session_b_note: Divine love as gift has two structural features in the data: (a) **Priority** — 1Jo 4:19 ('we love because he first loved us') — divine love precedes all human love; it is not responsive to human merit but prior to it. Jer 31:3 ('with an everlasting love I have loved you') — the love predates the present moment and will outlast it. (b) **Sufficiency** — Heb 13:5 (OBS-103-138): the promise 'I will never leave you nor forsake you' is the ground for freedom from love-of-money — divine love is sufficient to displace the need for material security. The gift of divine love reorders the inner economy: receiving it makes other attachments unnecessary. As gift, divine love is both prior (unconditioned by merit) and sufficient (displacing rival loves by its own fullness).

findings.finding_value: Love's relational architecture is structured by three directional axes — GOD → HUMAN, HUMAN → GOD, HUMAN → HUMAN — with divine love structurally prior and causally generative of all subsequent love. 1Jo 4:19 ('we love because he first loved us') is the axis-precedence statement: the first axis is not responsive to but constitutive of the second and third. The GOD → HUMAN direction moves through four mechanisms: covenantal declaration (naming the beloved — Jer 12:7, Mat 3:17), Spirit-infusion (Rom 5:5), redemptive acts (Joh 3:16), and covenantal covering (Eze 16:8). The HUMAN → GOD direction requires total inner mobilisation (Mat 22:37 — all heart, soul, mind) and the clearing of rival loves as its condition (1Jo 4:19, 1Ti 6:10). The HUMAN → HUMAN direction spans five structural types (neighbour, enemy, community, friendship, family) and creates the social architecture described in Q&A-088 (restructured kinship, public legibility, competitive generosity). The most significant finding in T4: the human-to-God direction is conditioned by prior reception of divine love — the capacity for human love toward God is itself a gift. The one structural gap: T4.6 (spiritual beings) is absent from the evidence.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence reveals multiple bases that are not mutually exclusive: (1) Sovereign/unconditional: Rom 9:15 — "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy" — the ground is divine will, not human merit. (2) Covenantal: Heb 8:12 — mercy as new covenant structure; Luk 1:54 — mercy in remembrance of covenant. (3) Responsive: 2Ch 33:13 (God moved by Manasseh's entreaty, OBS-111-059); Gen 25:21 (God grants Isaac's prayer). (4) Compassion-motivated: Psa 78:38 (being compassionate, he atoned). *New finding: divine mercy operates on all four bases simultaneously — sovereignty grounds the possibility, covenant structures the framework, compassion motivates the act, and responsive movement actualises it in the specific encounter. These are not competing accounts but different perspectives on the same act.* OBS-111-038, OBS-111-052, OBS-111-059.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-111-004: Reading T4 as a whole reveals mercy's relational architecture as directional and asymmetric in all three interface directions (God→human, human→God, human→human), with a structural requirement that re…
findings.finding_value: Reading T4 as a whole reveals mercy's relational architecture as directional and asymmetric in all three interface directions (God→human, human→God, human→human), with a structural requirement that receiving precedes giving. The key synthesis across T4: (a) God-to-human direction is the most extensively evidenced and is the source of mercy in all other directions; (b) human-to-God direction is characterised by normative ongoing supplication — not exceptional crisis-response; (c) human-to-human direction requires prior receipt from God and solidarity-knowledge of the condition being addressed; (d) mercy operates characteristically across relational distance and rupture (Q&A-117), not within maintained relationships; (e) the scope is wide (crossing covenantal boundaries) but not unconditionally permanent (withdrawal is named possibility). The T4 synthesis: mercy's relational architecture is an asymmetric chain — divine mercy → received human mercy → extended human mercy — with the chain requiring the prior link at each stage.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-010: T1's four modes of mercy's operation (dispositional, mechanical, dialogic, institutional) map directly onto T4's four relational directions. The dispositional mode corresponds to God→human mercy (sove…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes of mercy's operation (dispositional, mechanical, dialogic, institutional) map directly onto T4's four relational directions. The dispositional mode corresponds to God→human mercy (sovereign disposition). The mechanical mode corresponds to the atoning mechanism of the God→human direction. The dialogic (petition-response) mode corresponds to the human→God direction. The institutional mode (mercy seat, Day of Atonement) structures all three directions simultaneously. T1 and T4 together: mercy's operational modes are relationally differentiated — each mode is specific to a relational direction, and together they constitute the full relational architecture of mercy.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-023: T4's relational chain (God→human→human mercy) and T5's formative arc (mercy received forms mercy-giving capacity) are structurally identical processes described at different levels. T4 describes the r…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational chain (God→human→human mercy) and T5's formative arc (mercy received forms mercy-giving capacity) are structurally identical processes described at different levels. T4 describes the relational structure (who gives, who receives, under what conditions); T5 describes the developmental process (what changes in the person as a result). Reading together: T4's relational chain is the structure within which T5's formative arc occurs. The transition from receiving mercy (T4, God→human direction) to giving mercy (T4, human→human direction) is not automatic but requires the formative arc T5 describes — specifically the character formation through suffering (T5.4) and the sustained effects of mercy-reception (T1, confirmed by T5). T4's normative mercy-seeking posture (Q&A-107) is the relational expression of T5's sustained developmental practice (Dan 6:11 daily prayer, Q&A-137).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-024: T4's asymmetric relational chain (God→human→human) and T6's sequential positioning of mercy as bridge-between-conditions are structurally related. T6 shows mercy appearing between negative conditions …
findings.finding_value: T4's asymmetric relational chain (God→human→human) and T6's sequential positioning of mercy as bridge-between-conditions are structurally related. T6 shows mercy appearing between negative conditions (guilt, despair, distress) and positive outcomes (forgiveness, joy, peace, identity). T4 shows mercy flowing asymmetrically from greater-to-lesser. Reading together: the bridge function T6 identifies is made possible by the asymmetric relational structure T4 describes — mercy can bridge from negative to positive precisely because it flows from a position of greater (God, or the human who has received from God) toward a position of lesser (the guilty, the suffering, the despairing). T4's power-asymmetry requirement is T6's bridge-enabling mechanism.

findings.session_b_note: God's response to contrition is grounded in divine character, not human merit. Isa 57:15 frames the divine promise with self-identification (the holy One who inhabits eternity) — God draws near the contrite because of who God is, not because the contrite person has earned nearness. The contrite posture is the absence of merit-claims; the divine response is the gift of nearness to that absence. OBS-030-045, OBS-030-053.
