findings.session_b_note: God's extension of peace reveals his constitutive orientation of goodwill and wholeness toward the human person. Three dimensions: (1) God delights in the welfare of his servant (Psa 35:27 — OBS-117-149) — peace-giving is the expression of divine delight, not merely duty; (2) God plans for welfare and not for evil (Jer 29:11) — the divine intention toward the human person is purposively peaceful; (3) God identified as peace (YHWH-Shalom, 406-001) — God's own identity includes peace as a constitutive attribute, meaning his extension of peace is not situational but essential to who he is. The convergence of these three dimensions reveals that God's peace-giving is not a response to human deserving but the overflow of his own identity — the God who IS peace gives peace because that is what he is.

findings.session_b_note: God's giving reveals a complex of inner-being dispositions toward the human person. (1) Covenantal commitment: God's giving of land and promise over generations reveals that his orientation toward Abraham and his offspring is one of binding, persistent faithfulness — a commitment that does not lapse with time or circumstance. (2) Attentive compassion: God hears Leah's inner condition and gives in response — his orientation is one of attentiveness to the inner suffering of the creature, not detachment. (3) Formative care: God gives Spirit and wisdom to equip the person for formation and service — his orientation is developmental, not merely transactional. (4) Moral seriousness: God gives-over in response to faithlessness — his orientation includes moral consistency and covenantal accountability. He is not sentimentally lenient. (5) Hos 11:8 holds all of these in tension: the heart that recoils in compassion is also the heart that had determined judgement — God's orientation is a complex of justice and compassion held together by sovereign grace.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-004: T4 as a whole reveals that the relational architecture of this characteristic is directionally structured and asymmetrical. The dominant direction is God-to-human (6 of 7 groups, confirmed across T4.1…
findings.finding_value: T4 as a whole reveals that the relational architecture of this characteristic is directionally structured and asymmetrical. The dominant direction is God-to-human (6 of 7 groups, confirmed across T4.1); the human direction is responsive (T4.2: human gives back what was first given). The basis of divine giving is plural — covenantal, responsive, formative, moral-consequential, eschatological-grace (Q&A-102) — revealing that faithfulness is not a single relational mode but a relational orientation that differentiates itself across relational conditions while remaining unified in character. The human-to-God direction reveals responsive correspondence as the relational structure (Q&A-107): the proper relational form is one in which the human gives back to God what is his (glory, praise, self), having first received. The human-to-human direction is thinner in the data (Q&A-109) — reflecting the registry's God-subject dominance. T4.6 is substantially silent on spiritual beings. What T4 reveals as a whole: faithfulness-as-giving is constitutively a divine-initiative relational reality that the human enters through responsive participation. The human's giving is always downstream of divine giving; the correspondence is the proper form of the relationship.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-008: The constitutional locations where the characteristic operates (T2 — heart, soul/nephesh, spirit, body) and the relational interfaces through which it operates (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal…
findings.finding_value: The constitutional locations where the characteristic operates (T2 — heart, soul/nephesh, spirit, body) and the relational interfaces through which it operates (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal a mirroring structure. God's giving proceeds from his leb (heart, Hos 11:8) and his nafshi (soul, Jer 12:7) — the deepest divine inner-being locations are engaged in the God-to-human direction. The human's giving toward God is expressed through the body (back, cheeks, face — Isa 50:6) and from the deepest inner orientation (Job 1:21 — recognition of divine sovereignty). The constitutional depths engaged in both directions are commensurate: God gives from his heart and soul; the human gives from the whole self, expressed bodily. What this pair reveals: the divine-human relational correspondence (DHC dimension, group 872-006) has a constitutional depth structure — the correspondence is not merely behavioural but engages the deepest constitutional levels of both parties. The giving that constitutes the correspondence is heart-to-body deep.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-012: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — perception, affect, volition, relational capacity all engaged) and the relational interface structure (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal a faculty-interface …
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — perception, affect, volition, relational capacity all engaged) and the relational interface structure (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal a faculty-interface correspondence. In the God-to-human direction: divine hearing (T3.1 — perception) precedes compassionate giving (T4.1 — responsive basis); divine affect (T3.4 — rahamim, leb) determines the direction of giving (T4.1 — basis of extension); divine relational capacity (T3.11) is the prior orientation that makes the giving possible. In the human-to-God direction: human perception (Q2 — recognising divine sovereignty), human affect (blessing under loss), human volition (choosing to give glory), and human relational capacity (genuine correspondence) are all required for the giving to be genuine (T4.2 — inner posture). What this pair reveals: the relational interfaces are not external channels through which giving flows; they are relational events in which the inner faculties of both parties are engaged simultaneously and correspondingly. The correspondence is not mechanical but genuinely personal.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-016: The relational interfaces (T4 — divine-initiative, human-responsive, covenantal scope) and the formation arc (T5 — constitutive endowment, sustained narrative, eschatological orientation) reveal that …
findings.finding_value: The relational interfaces (T4 — divine-initiative, human-responsive, covenantal scope) and the formation arc (T5 — constitutive endowment, sustained narrative, eschatological orientation) reveal that formation happens through relational interfaces. The God-to-human interface is the channel through which constitutive formation occurs (Spirit given, wisdom deposited — T5.5). The human-to-God interface is both the goal of formation (glory-giving as the proper orientation of the formed person) and a constituent of the formation process (practising glory-giving forms the person who gives glory). What this pair reveals: formation is not an individual inner process — it is a relational event. The person is not formed in isolation from God and others; they are formed through the giving and receiving that constitutes the relational interfaces. The formation arc (T5) is the temporal dimension of the relational structure (T4): what the interfaces do over time is formation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-018: The relational interface analysis (T4 — six of seven groups are God-to-human; the divine disposition ranges from covenantal to compassionate to formative to moral-consequential) and the primary anchor…
findings.finding_value: The relational interface analysis (T4 — six of seven groups are God-to-human; the divine disposition ranges from covenantal to compassionate to formative to moral-consequential) and the primary anchor identification (T7 — Hos 11:8 as the verse that uniquely reveals the divine inner-being decision structure) converge. Hos 11:8 is the primary anchor precisely because it holds the full complexity of T4 in a single verse: it shows the God-to-human relational direction (the giving is addressed at Ephraim/Israel), the multiple bases of divine giving (deserved-judgement vs. compassionate restraint), and the divine disposition (heart recoiling, compassion warming). The full vocabulary arc (T7.1.10 — enacted + constituted poles) maps onto the two directions of T4: the enacted pole (na.tan) is the God-to-human and human-to-God relational act; the constituted pole (emunah/hesed/pistis) is the dispositional quality that makes the relational giving faithful rather than merely generous. What this pair reveals: the relational architecture and the vocabulary architecture are the same structure described at two levels of abstraction.

God's hatred of evil and of those who persistently choose it reveals the depth and seriousness of his moral commitments. He is not indifferent to wickedness — his inner being (nephesh) is set against it. This means that when God acts in judgment against evil, he is not merely applying an external rule but expressing an inner disposition. Psa 5:5-6 shows the dual face: God hates evildoers and abhors the bloodthirsty — this is paired with God's grace toward those who seek him (v.7). The hatred and the welcome exist in the same God, directed toward different objects.

Across all seven sub-groups, God's extension of the cluster's characteristics reveals a consistent divine disposition: unconditional, initiatory, covenantal, and transformatively purposive gracious engagement with the human person. God does not merely respond to human goodness; he precedes, initiates, and grounds the possibility of the human's receiving and expressing these characteristics. The cluster reveals a God who is constitutively for the human person — who loves, compassionates, mercifully overrides condemnation, gives gracious goodwill, stoops in gentleness, actively comforts, and calls into fellowship with himself.

**[CLUSTER]** E. The comprehensive range of God's extension of righteousness toward the human person reveals a disposition that is simultaneously just and gracious: God's righteousness is not indulgent (he condemns sin and wickedness) and not merely juridical (he justifies the ungodly through Christ). The same righteousness that requires condemnation provides justification — through the cross, where "he is just and the justifier" (Rom 3:26). God's disposition toward the human person is that of a righteous judge who is also a gracious Saviour — not despite his righteousness but through it.

findings.finding_value: God's disposition toward the M20-experiencing person is consistently one of movement toward, not withdrawal. The anxious person is not condemned but invited to cast (1Pe 5:7); the despairing person receives the ground of resurrection hope (2Cor 1:9); the discouraged person receives daily inner renewal (2Cor 4:16); the doubting person receives the hand of Christ (Mat 14:31). God's character as revealed in M20 contexts: responsive, proximate, sustaining, and ahead of the person's resolution of their characteristic.

findings.finding_value: God's disposition is constitutively toward-the-person in grace: the verse evidence (particularly the Exo 34:6 formula and its echoes — 2330-001) reveals that graciousness is not an occasional attitude but God's settled relational character toward humans. He bends toward the lesser (the CHANAN root meaning). He gives what the person cannot generate (Eph 2:8). He accepts those he has been petitioned by (984-001). He takes personal pleasure in those he has formed (Isa 42:1 — 795-002). God's disposition toward the human person in M39-A is one of constitutive favour, initiating love, and personal engagement.

findings.finding_value: God's command to fear him, combined with his pledge to implant that fear (Jer 32:40), reveals a disposition of **covenant commitment and pastoral care**: God is not indifferent to whether the human person has the right inner orientation — he actively works to produce it. Psa 25:14 (offering covenant friendship to those who fear him) reveals God's disposition as intimate and relational — the fear-posture opens access to God's friendship.

God's repeated "do not fear" commands in M01-B-VCG-06 (Isa 43:1 anchor: "you are mine" as the ground for releasing fear) reveal a disposition of **possessive care and relational nearness**: God addresses the frightened person directly, names himself as their ground of security, and commands the release of fear from a position of personal commitment.

God's deployment of terror against enemies (M01-C-VCG-01) and imposition of dismay as judgment (M01-D-VCG-02) reveals his disposition as **sovereignly just**: he uses fear as an instrument of historical governance, not arbitrarily but in response to opposition to his covenantal purposes.

God's deployment of terror against enemies (M01-C-VCG-01) and imposition of dismay as judgment (M01-D-VCG-02) reveals his disposition as **sovereignly just**: he uses fear as an instrument of historical governance, not arbitrarily but in response to opposition to his covenantal purposes.

God's disposition toward the human person as revealed through M01 is: (1) intimately relational and care-ful toward those who fear him; (2) actively formative — working to produce the right inner orientation; (3) sovereignly just — deploying fear as an instrument of historical governance. The cluster reveals God as both the object of human fear and the sovereign producer of it.

Rom 9:22 (M02-A-VCG-03): "God's wrath is something he desires to display against vessels prepared for destruction, yet he withholds it with great patience" — reveals that even toward objects of wrath, God's disposition includes patience and restraint. Isa 57:16 (M02-A-VCG-04): "God will not sustain his anger indefinitely because unrelenting wrath would crush the very spirit and breath of life he created" — reveals that God's disposition toward the human person includes concern for the creaturely life he made, which moderates his wrath's expression.

Psa 78:38 (M02-B-VCG-05): "God's rage, though fully warranted, is repeatedly held back — his compassion leads him to atone for iniquity" — reveals that God's wrath toward his covenant people is consistently moderated by compassionate disposition. The wrath is real but the disposition toward the people is not purely punitive.

God's extension of grief toward the human person reveals a God who is seriously engaged with the inner life and its conditions. Two dispositions are evidenced simultaneously. First, seriousness about sin and covenant: God's grief-bestowal as discipline and judgment shows that he takes sin's inner consequences seriously — the heart must register what sin costs. Second, compassion and responsiveness: God hears the groan of the oppressed (Exo 2:24 — M03-E-VCG-01), sees and records tears (2Ki 20:5 — M03-A-VCG-02 anchor; Psa 56:8 — M03-A-VCG-02), wipes away tears eschatologically (Isa 25:8 — M03-A-VCG-02). God governs grief with the intention of its resolution: mourning is what God reverses (Psa 30:11 — M03-B-VCG-03 anchor), what he abolishes in the new creation (Rev 21:4 — M03-B-VCG-04). God's disposition is that grief is a real and serious inner-being state that he takes seriously, governs purposively, and intends ultimately to remove.

**[CHAR-1]** E — God's exultation over his people reveals his disposition as one of genuine relational delight — not merely governance or provision but a surging inner joy directed at his people. Jer 32:41's "with all my heart and all my soul" is the strongest constitutional language applied to God's inner disposition in the entire corpus: it locates his rejoicing at the deepest level of his inner being. Zep 3:17's pairing of exultation with love that quiets — "he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing" — shows exultation as the expression of God's deepest relational tenderness alongside his triumphant joy. God delights in his people.

**[CHAR-2]** E — God's Joy-giving reveals: (1) **Relational investment** — Luk 15:7, 10 (heaven's joy over one repentant sinner — God's investment in individual persons' restoration produces his own inner joy); (2) **Fatherly desire for human flourishing** — Neh 8:10 ("the joy of the Lord is your strength" — God intends his people to be strong through joy); Rom 15:13 ("may the God of hope fill you with all joy") — God desires abundance of joy for his people; (3) **Delight in covenant relationship** — Jer 32:41 ("I will rejoice in doing them good… with all my heart and all my soul") — God's Joy in doing good to his people is not reluctant duty but whole-hearted delight; (4) **Eschatological commitment** — the restoration-Joy passages (Isa 35:10; 51:11; Jer 31:13; Zec 8:19) reveal God's purpose to give everlasting Joy as the final state of his people.

**[CHAR-7]** E — God's extension of Suffering-Joy through the Spirit reveals: (1) **His presence with the suffering person** — the Spirit's production of agalliao within the suffering context means God is not absent in suffering but intensely present; (2) **His eschatological commitment** — the "reward in heaven" and "glory to be revealed" show God's disposition to honour the suffering of faithful witnesses with ultimate eschatological vindication; (3) **His desire for the inner life to transcend circumstances** — the Spirit's production of joy within suffering shows God's aim for the human inner being to be constituted by divine reality rather than circumstantial reality; (4) **His fatherly delight** — Luk 10:21's Jesus rejoicing in the Father's gracious will shows that Suffering-Joy at its most intense is the shared inner life between Father and Son that the Spirit also makes available to the human person.

**[CHAR-3]** E — God's extension of Gladness as his character-goodness reveals: (1) **Constancy** — "his steadfast love endures forever" (ki-tov formula repeated) — God's goodness is not fluctuating but permanent and reliable; (2) **Generosity** — Psa 145:9 ("good to all, mercy over all he has made") — divine goodness extends universally, not selectively; (3) **Protective care** — Nah 1:7 ("a stronghold in the day of trouble") — God's goodness translates into refuge and protection; (4) **Covenantal fidelity** — Jos 21:45 ("not one word had failed") — divine goodness is demonstrated in complete promise-fulfilment; (5) **Instructive character** — Psa 25:8 ("good and upright… therefore he instructs sinners in the way") — divine goodness manifests as patient instruction toward the good path.

**[CHAR-4]** E — God's extension of Delight reveals: (1) **Tender relational attachment** — Jer 31:20 (sha.a.shu.im persisting through rebuke; "my heart yearns for him") — God's Delight includes visceral yearning for the person; (2) **Purposeful favor** — 1Ki 10:9 (delighted in Solomon → set on the throne) — God's Delight is not merely affective but purposively active, producing exaltation; (3) **Life-orientation** — Eze 18:23; 33:11 ("no pleasure in the death of anyone… so turn, and live") — God's deepest Delight is oriented toward human life and restoration, not judgment; (4) **Faithful constancy** — Deu 30:9 ("as he took delight in your fathers") — divine Delight is not a new mood but a continuation of original covenantal pleasure; (5) **Unconditional grounding** — even where Delight is conditioned on the person's faithfulness (Psa 37:23), the ground is God's own prior Delight that makes faithfulness possible (Psa 37:4 — delight in the Lord produces the desires God gives).

**[CHAR-5]** E — (1) **Lavish generosity** — Psa 36:8's river of delights shows God as extravagant in his pleasantness-supply; (2) **Covenant faithfulness** — the ni.cho.ach corpus shows divine Pleasure as reliable and consistent toward those who worship rightly; (3) **Personal beauty** — Psa 27:4's no.am as God's own quality shows his disposition as inherently beautiful and agreeable — he is not merely useful but genuinely pleasant to encounter; (4) **Restorative orientation** — Eze 20:41's future-oriented acceptance shows God's disposition toward restored relationship as the ultimate goal; (5) **Eternal supply** — Psa 16:11's "forevermore" shows God's Pleasure-giving as permanently available, not exhausted.

**[CHAR-6]** E — (1) **Redemptive orientation** — the overwhelming weight of VCG-01 shows God's wonder-acts as redemptive: Exodus, conquest, healing, rescue at sea, restoration; his disposition is toward his people's salvation through extraordinary means; (2) **Exclusivity** — Psa 72:18; 86:10 ("who alone does wondrous things") — God's disposition to be the exclusive worker of genuine wonders reveals his jealousy for his own incomparable status; (3) **Exceeding generosity** — Psa 40:5 ("your wondrous deeds and your thoughts toward us; none can compare with you! They are more than can be told") — wonder-acts multiplied without limit; (4) **Pedagogical intent** — Exo 34:10 ("all the people among whom you are shall see the work of the Lord, for it is an awesome thing") — God extends wonders with the explicit purpose of being witnessed and acknowledged.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The comparative evidence reveals five dimensions of God's disposition: (1) **Tender relational attachment** — Delight (Char 4): Jer 31:20's sha.a.shu.im persisting through rebuke and God's heart yearning for Ephraim is the warmest relational-attachment evidence in the cluster; Exultation (Char 1): Jer 32:41's "with all my heart and all my soul" applied to God's rejoicing in doing good to his people — the fullest constitutional language applied to God's inner disposition; (2) **Pedagogical generosity** — Wonder (Char 6): God performing wonders with the explicit purpose of being witnessed and acknowledged (Exo 34:10 — "all the people among whom you are shall see"); (3) **Life-orientation** — Delight (Char 4): Eze 18:23; 33:11 — God's deepest Delight is toward life and restoration, not judgment; (4) **Lavish supply** — Pleasure (Char 5): Psa 36:8's river of delights; Psa 40:5's "more than can be told"; Psa 16:11's "pleasures forevermore"; (5) **Eschatological commitment** — Joy (Char 2): God's intention is everlasting Joy (Isa 35:10; 51:11); Suffering-Joy (Char 7): God commits to the suffering person through the Spirit's presence and the eschatological reward. The cluster's God-to-human pattern reveals a God whose inner life is characterised by the seven positive characteristics he extends toward the human person — he gives what he himself has.

**[CHAR-1]** E — God's extension of shame as judgment reveals his holiness and justice — he takes moral reality seriously enough to expose and reverse what opposes it. God's extension of shame as corrective mercy toward his own people reveals his pastoral investment in their inner moral integrity — he does not want them to receive his grace without moral self-awareness, because the grace that bypasses shame-recognition is grace that cannot transform. The command "be ashamed" before "I will act for you" (Eze 36:32) reveals a God who is committed to the whole person's inner life, not merely their external circumstances. This disposition is consistent throughout M07-C: God arranges encounters (the temple design, Eze 43:10) specifically to produce shame in the inner person because shame before holiness is what opens the person to receive what God offers.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Extensively evidenced in VCG-03. God extends CHAR-2 to the proud as a judicial act: "your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down" (2Sa 22:28); "the Lord God of hosts will lop the boughs with terrifying power" (Isa 10:33); "I will change their glory into shame" (Hos 4:7). God also extends CHAR-2 redemptively through the mortal body's state (1Cor 15:43) — the dishonored mortal condition is God-ordained as the seed-state for the glorified body. The judicial basis is moral cause (pride, idolatry, opposition to God's servant); the redemptive basis is eschatological purpose.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — God extends CHAR-3 in the structural-assignment mode (VCG-02): the potter's sovereign assignment of vessels for dishonorable use (Rom 9:21) is God's prerogative in the creation and governance of persons. The basis is God's authority over his own creation; the content is the objective assignment of standing according to God's sovereign purpose.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — God is the standard against which CHAR-4's evaluative operation works ("in the sight of God," 2Cor 4:2). God's giving over of persons to dishonorable passions (Rom 1:24; 1:26) — "God gave them up" — shows God as the agent who permits the VCG-02 moral disorder as a consequence of idolatry. This is not God extending shamefulness but God releasing the person into the shamefulness their own choices have generated.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — God acts against CHAR-5 rather than extending it: 1Cor 1:28 — God choosing the despised to nullify things that are — is God's counter-movement against the world's contempt-verdicts. God's sovereign reversal of CHAR-5 is the theological foundation for why the recipient of contempt need not be defined by the contempt-verdict. God does not extend contempt-producing-shame toward persons; he extends the reversal of contempt and the vindication of the despised.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — God confirms and validates CHAR-6: Gen 20:6 (contextually) — God's response to Abimelech's appeal to innocence is to confirm it and grant protection. God is the authoritative validator of the innocence-claim: whether CHAR-6 is present is not merely a self-assessment but a reality confirmed or denied by God. God also reveals the incapacity for innocence (Hos 8:5) — the divine question "how long will they be incapable of innocence?" reveals that God tracks the moral condition of CHAR-6 and names its loss.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — God's movement toward the human person across M07 is the most theologically differentiated dimension in the cluster. Five distinct modes are evidenced. (1) God as shame-bearer's guardian — protecting those who trust him from being put to shame: the repeated Psalm formula "let me not be put to shame" (Psa 25:2; 31:1; 119:31) presupposes this guardianship; 1Cor 1:28 shows God choosing the despised to nullify the world's contempt-assessments (Chars 1, 5). (2) God as sovereign abaser — bringing the proud low as a judicial act: the sha.phel VCG-03 corpus (1Sa 2:7; Psa 75:7; Isa 2:11) is the most extensive God-to-human mode in the cluster (Char 2). (3) God as worth-assigner — assigning standings of honour or dishonour according to his sovereign purpose: the potter's right (Rom 9:21; Char 3). (4) God as moral standard — being the sight before which conduct bears or does not bear scrutiny: "in the sight of God" (2Cor 4:2; Char 4). (5) God as innocence-confirmer — acknowledging the genuine innocence-claim and acting accordingly: God's response to Abimelech (Gen 20:6; Char 6). These five modes are not in tension: they are different expressions of the same God's character operating in M07's field — guardian, sovereign, assigner, standard, and confirmer.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — God's consistent opposition to CHAR-1 reveals three dimensions of his disposition. First, jealousy for his sole exaltation: Isa 2:11 (vc=34601, M08-A3-VCG-04) and 2:17 (vc=34602, M08-A3-VCG-04) — "the Lord alone will be exalted in that day" — the day of judgment re-establishes the divine monopoly on true exaltation that CHAR-1 has trespassed. Second, care for the lowly as the preferred relational posture: 2Sa 22:28 (vc=34236, M08-A4-VCG-02) — "you save a humble people, but your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down" — divine saving-movement toward the humble paired with opposing-movement toward the proud. Psa 138:6 (vc=12086, vc=34300, M08-A4-VCG-02) — "he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar" — relational proximity to the lowly contrasted with relational distance from the proud. Third, judicial commitment to accountability: Psa 94:2 (vc=33952, M08-A4-VCG-02) — "repay to the proud what they deserve" — the judicial frame confirming that God's opposition to CHAR-1 is not arbitrary but grounded in the justice of the creaturely-Creator order.

**[CHAR-2]** E — God's response reveals his disposition as the sovereign ordainer and defender of legitimate authority structures. Deu 17:13 (vc=34124, M08-B-VCG-01): "all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" — God's judgment is educative as well as punitive; it is designed to generate the fear that blocks CHAR-2. Jer 50:31 (vc=34116, M08-B-VCG-02): "behold, I am against you, O proud one" — direct divine opposition. Neh 9:10 (vc=34125): God "performed signs and wonders" as counter-response to Egypt's CHAR-2 — the divine protective care for his people against those who presumptuously defy his order.

**[CHAR-3]** E — God's design to redirect boasting toward himself reveals: (a) his jealousy for his own glory as the legitimate object of all exultation (1Cor 1:31: "boast in the Lord" as the commanded alternative); (b) his care for the community's relational integrity (1Cor 5:6: community boasting spreads corruption — God's concern is for the whole community's health); (c) his sovereign purpose to use human weakness as the arena for his glory (2Cor 12:9, vc=33870, M08-C-VCG-02: "my power is made perfect in weakness" — God designs that CHAR-3 be redirected toward his glory precisely through what humans would not choose to boast about).

**[CHAR-4]** E — God's response reveals: (a) His role as the accurate Measurer — he is the one whose assessment is the true standard against which all cognitive self-assessment should be calibrated (Rom 12:3, vc=60866); (b) His commitment to judicial consistency — the condemnation of the devil (1Ti 3:6, vc=33924) applies equally when humans replicate the same cognitive self-inflation. God's disposition is toward accurate self-knowledge within proper creaturely bounds as the created order; CHAR-4 transgresses this order and receives the judicial response that the adversary's original transgression received.

**[CHAR-5]** E — God's consistent breaking of proud might across nations (Israel — Lev 26:19; Egypt — Eze 30:6/30:18/32:12; Edom — Jer 49:16; Babylon — Jer 51:53) reveals: (a) His sovereignty over all structural power — no national or individual structural power is beyond his ability to break; (b) His particular concern for the vulnerable who are failed by CHAR-5's social indifference — Eze 16:49 (vc=33979, M08-E-VCG-01): the failure to aid the poor is God's indictment of Sodom's proud power; (c) His purpose to redirect all structural goods toward his own glory and the service of others rather than toward human self-exaltation.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The God-toward-human response across all five reveals a consistent divine disposition: God is simultaneously the sovereign who opposes pride at every level and the generous provider who gives what pride falsely claims to generate. CHAR-1's divine opposition reveals the sole-exaltation prerogative. CHAR-2's reveals the authority-ordaining sovereignty. CHAR-3's reveals God as the legitimate boasting-object who redirects the glorying-impulse toward himself. CHAR-4's reveals God as the accurate-measure giver (Rom 12:3, M08-D-VCG-02). CHAR-5's reveals God as the provider of all structural goods (1Ti 6:17, M08-E-VCG-02). The cluster-synthesis: God's disposition toward M08 is not only judicial (opposing and breaking pride) but also generous — he provides the genuine version of what each characteristic falsely claims. He is both the judge of pride and the provider of what pride misattributes.

**[CHAR-2]** E — God's extension of submission-capacity through the Spirit (1Pe1:2) reveals his disposition as actively formative: God does not merely command submission but works to produce it in the person from within. The fact that God requires obedience of faith (Rom1:5; 16:26) as the telos of gospel proclamation reveals that God seeks the person's genuine inner yielding, not merely their outward compliance — he values the will's genuine orientation toward him. Heb5:8 (the Son learning obedience through suffering) reveals God's willingness to enter the creaturely experience of submission to form the paradigm from within — God's disposition is one of solidarity in the formation of the characteristic he requires.

**[CHAR-3]** E — God's response reveals his disposition as one of *active movement toward the broken* rather than requiring the broken person to somehow restore themselves before approaching him. Both verses show God as the initiating party in drawing near (Psa34:18 — "the Lord is near") and dwelling with (Isa57:15 — "I dwell with him"). The divine disposition evidenced is that of one who is attracted toward the contrite and broken inner state rather than repelled by it — a disposition that inverts the ordinary human assumption that strength and achievement attract attention while weakness and brokenness are avoided.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Heb5:2's high priestly metriopatheō images God's disposition as one of measured compassionate restraint toward the "ignorant and wayward" rather than immediate severe judgment. The priestly mediation as a divinely-instituted structure reveals that God has built into his covenantal order a mechanism for gentle engagement with erring humanity — the institution of priesthood is itself a disclosure of the divine disposition of measured compassionate dealing with the wayward.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The requirement for semnotēs in leadership (1Ti3:4; Tit2:7) and in the community's manner of life (1Ti2:2) reveals God's disposition as one who values settled, non-self-assertive moral gravity in those who represent him and his community. God does not value anxious self-promotion or social performance as the mark of his people and leaders — the requirement for semnotēs reveals a divine valuation of grounded, authentic inner gravity over performance and display.

**[CHAR-6]** E — God's operation reveals a disposition of valuing genuine, uncoerced giving over compelled compliance (Exo35:5 — he calls for willing-hearted contribution rather than mandating uniform levies), and of actively restoring the inner capacity for free-giving when it is lost (Psa51:12 — upholding the willing spirit after failure). God's disposition is thus oriented toward genuine freely-given devotion — he desires the person's inner willing orientation, not merely external compliance — and he is active in sustaining that orientation beyond what the person can maintain alone.

**[CHAR-1]** E — God's operation of humility toward humans reveals his disposition as both *corrective* and *restorative*. The imposed-lowering instances (Psa107:12 — bowing hearts down through hard labor; 2Ch28:19 — humbling Judah) are not punitive ends in themselves but corrective means: the humbling produces dependence and turns the person back toward God. Psa107:12 evidences this most acutely — "they fell down with none to help" — the experience of complete dependence is the created condition for turning to God. The responsive-mercy instances (2Ch12:7; 1Ki21:29; Luk18:14) reveal God's disposition as genuinely receptive to the inner posture of humbling — he does not remain opposed when the posture shifts. Jam4:6 ("gives more grace to the humble") reveals God's disposition as actively generous toward the humble: not merely neutral but positively oriented toward the person who takes the lowly posture.

**[CLUSTER]** E — God's operation across the six characteristics reveals a consistent divine disposition: actively oriented toward the person's genuine inner orientation rather than their outward compliance. Humility (CHAR-1): God is both corrective and restorative — the imposed-lowering instances (Psa107:12; 2Ch28:19) are corrective means producing dependence and turning; Jam4:6 reveals a disposition actively generous toward the inner posture of self-lowering. Submission (CHAR-2): God does not merely command submission but works through the Spirit to produce it from within (1Pe1:2), and his solidarity in the formation process is evidenced by the Son's own learning of obedience through suffering (Heb5:8). Contrition (CHAR-3): God is characterologically attracted toward the broken rather than repelled — "the Lord is near to the brokenhearted" (Psa34:18) is a generalising wisdom-principle naming a stable divine disposition, not an occasional event. Meekness and Gentleness (CHAR-4): God has built compassionate-mediation structures (priesthood) into his covenantal order, revealing a disposition that sends mediators who share the erring person's creaturely weakness. Dignity (CHAR-5): God values settled, non-self-assertive moral gravity in leaders — the Pastorals' standard reflects what God requires and shapes in his community. Willing-heartedness (CHAR-6): God calls for freely-given devotion rather than compelled compliance, and actively restores the willing capacity when it is lost (Psa51:12). Cluster-level: the common divine disposition across all six is that God values genuine inner orientation over managed external compliance.

---

**[CHAR-1]** S — Since God does not extend wilful sinning (T4.1.2), this prompt cannot be answered from the corpus as framed. What the corpus reveals about God's disposition toward sinning humans is: (1) *Moral seriousness* — "the soul who sins shall die" (Eze 18:4/20); (2) *Preventive care* — Gen 20:6 (active restraint to protect both Abimelech and Abraham's wife); (3) *Forgiveness available upon confession* — 2Sa 12:13; 1Ki 8:33/35/50 (Solomon's prayer structure). God's disposition toward sinning humans is one of moral seriousness combined with covenantal availability of forgiveness — not extension of the sinning characteristic itself.

**[CHAR-10]** E — 2Pe 2:14's "Accursed children" reveals a disposition of judicial seriousness toward those who deliberately practise enticement against the vulnerable. The specific targeting of "unsteady souls" (2Pe 2:18) — those barely escaping from error — intensifies the moral severity. God's disposition is not indifference to the mechanism's operation but active judicial opposition to those who exploit it against the vulnerable.

**[CHAR-11]** E — God's disposition is one of *engaged mercy within maintained holiness*. (1) *Mercy*: Mat 1:21 — "he will save his people from their sins" — God's purpose is salvific, not merely judicial; the mission of Jesus names mercy as God's disposition toward those in the condition; (2) *Maintained holiness*: Heb 5:1/3 — the persistent need for sacrifice for sins reveals that God's holiness does not simply absorb the condition — the condition requires addressed mediation; (3) *Patience*: 1Th 2:16 — the accumulated measure of sins that brings wrath "at last" implies that God's response has been withheld while the measure fills — patience is part of the disposition toward those in the condition.

**[CHAR-12]** E — God's disposition is one of purposive liberating provision. (1) *Purposive imprisonment leading to promise*: Gal 3:22 — the confinement under sin is not God's final word but the penultimate condition that makes the faith-promise possible; God's disposition is toward liberation through faith, not permanent confinement. (2) *Protective guardianship*: 1Jo 5:18 — "he who was born of God protects him" — God's disposition toward the liberated person is one of active ongoing protection against re-enslavement; the disposition is not withdrawal after liberation but continued guardianship.

**[CHAR-13]** E — God's disposition is one of *patient scrutiny moving toward either judgment or erasure*. The sevenfold discipline of Lev 26:18-28 reveals a patient escalating response designed to provoke turning rather than immediately destroying. Exo 32:34 — "in the day when I visit" — the deferred reckoning reveals patience. Isa 43:25 — "for my own sake" — the erasure reveals mercy grounded in God's own character. Amos 5:12 — "I know how many are your transgressions" — God's complete knowledge of the record does not require the person to confess what God already knows; the knowledge is already complete. The disposition is thus patient-knowing-and-ready-to-erase rather than eager to condemn.

**[CHAR-14]** E — God's disposition is one of *welcoming and ready forgiveness grounded in provided mechanism*. Mar 3:28 — "all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter" — the scope of divine willingness to forgive is total (all sins, all blasphemies) with a single exception (Mar 3:29). Eph 1:7 — "according to the riches of his grace" — the richness of the forgiveness reveals the richness of the disposition: God does not forgive grudgingly but abundantly. Act 10:43 — "everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness" — the universality of "everyone" reveals no favouritism in the disposition; the forgiveness is available to all who believe.

**[CHAR-15]** E — God's disposition is one of *morally engaged anger moving toward sovereign redemption*. Isa 64:5 — "you were angry, and we sinned" — the anger is real and provoked by the sinning-pattern; God is not indifferent to the accumulated condition. Jer 8:14 — doom declared — the judgment is the consequence of the sustained sinning. But Eze 37:23 — "I will save them... I will cleanse them... they shall be my people, and I will be their God" — the disposition moves through judgment toward restoration: God's ultimate purpose is not the community's destruction under the generational burden but their cleansing and covenant-restoration.

**[CHAR-16]** E — God's disposition is one of *holy opposition moving through judgment toward redemption*. Isa 13:9 and Psa 104:35 name the judgment-disposition; 1Ti 1:15 and Rom 5:8 name the redemptive-disposition. Both are simultaneously operative. The defining statement is Rom 5:8 — "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" — God's love is directed toward the person in their worst moral condition. Psa 25:8 — "he instructs sinners in the way" — God's disposition toward sinners includes ongoing moral guidance rather than mere abandonment to judgment. The twin disposition (judgment of unrepentant extreme sinners; redemptive engagement with repentable sinners) characterises the full corpus.

**[CHAR-17]** E — God's disposition is one of *precise moral justice moving toward purposeful mercy*. Job 11:6 — "God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves" — mercy moderates justice. Hos 5:15 — the withdrawal until guilt is acknowledged reveals a patient relational strategy rather than immediate destruction; God waits for the acknowledgment. Jer 33:8 — "I will cleanse them from all the guilt" — the totality of the cleansing-promise ("all the guilt") reveals an intention to fully resolve rather than partially address. The disposition is neither indifferent (God sees and responds — Jer 2:22) nor punitive-only (mercy moderates — Job 11:6; cleansing promised — Jer 33:8).

**[CHAR-18]** E — God's disposition is one of *precise moral justice held in tension with enduring steadfast love*. Exo 34:7 — God both forgives iniquity and visits it on children — both responses flow from the same character; Psa 78:38 — "yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them; he restrained his anger often" — compassion repeatedly moderates full justice; Job 11:6 — "God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves" — mercy consistently moderates the full punitive application. The disposition is neither indifferent (Hos 13:12 — the record is maintained) nor implacably punitive (Mic 7:18 — he delights in steadfast love). The defining eschatological posture: Jer 50:20 — iniquity shall be sought and none found — total removal is God's ultimate goal.

**[CHAR-19]** E — God's disposition is *patient justice sustained by steadfast love*. Amos 1:3 — the three-and-four threshold formula shows patience exhausted only at a specific limit; God has counted and waited. Isa 43:25 — "for my own sake" — the pardon flows from God's own character rather than the transgressor's merit. Isa 48:8 — "from before birth you were called a rebel" — God identifies the rebel-identity before birth yet still speaks to the person through Isaiah; identification of the transgressor does not equal abandonment. The defining eschatological statement: Dan 9:24 — "to finish the transgression" — God has appointed an end to transgression; his ultimate disposition is toward transgression's completion and termination.

**[CHAR-2]** E — God's provision of a comprehensive remedial system for unintentional sinning (Lev 4:2 — the entire sin-offering structure; Num 15:27/28 — the individual inadvertent offering; Exo 29:36 — daily altar purification) reveals a disposition of *gracious moral realism* toward the creature. God holds moral standards that apply even when the creature acts without knowing (Lev 4:2 — the sin is real even when unintentional); simultaneously he provides the precise remedy that addresses the resulting liability (Num 15:28 — "he shall be forgiven"). The disposition is neither moral laxity (the sin is treated as real and requires remedy) nor moral severity without provision (the remedy is prescribed and forgiveness follows its use). God's disposition is structured around the creature's epistemic limitation — he provides for what he knows the creature will inadvertently do.

**[CHAR-20]** E — God's disposition is one of *personally wounded faithfulness sustaining covenant-memory toward restoration*. Ize 39:23 — "I hid my face" — the face-hiding is a personal response to personal betrayal; it is not mere judicial distance but relational withdrawal. Lev 26:42 — God remembers the covenant that was betrayed — the willingness to remember the very covenant whose breaking caused the wound reveals a disposition that sustains loyalty even through the experience of disloyalty. The eschatological resolution (Eze 39:26 — "they shall forget their shame") confirms: God's ultimate goal is not retribution but the restoration in which even the shame of the treachery is eclipsed.

**[CHAR-21]** E — God's disposition is one of *holy opposition to perversity combined with disciplinary love toward the perverted person*. Pro 8:13 — wisdom hates perverted speech (holy opposition to the characteristic); 2Sa 7:14 — "my steadfast love will not depart from him" (disciplinary love toward the person). The distinction is important: God's hatred is of the perversity itself; his sustained commitment is to the person even as he disciplines the perverse conduct. Deu 32:20's face-hiding is for a time ("I will see what their end will be") rather than permanent abandonment.

**[CHAR-22]** E — God's disposition is one of *righteous opposition to injustice combined with sustained moral patience toward the unjust person*. 2Pe 2:9 — "keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment" — not immediate destruction but sustained custody; Rev 18:5 — God "remembers" (retains in mind rather than acting immediately) — patience before final reckoning. Eze 33:15 — the wicked who stops doing injustice "shall surely live" — God's disposition sustains the possibility of reversal. The eschatological judgment (Rev 18:5; 2Pe 2:9) is deferred precisely because God's disposition holds open the path to repentance while maintaining the certainty of final accountability.

**[CHAR-3]** E — God's disposition toward the confessing person is one of *merciful reception*. Eze 33:16 — sins not remembered when the person has turned — reveals a God who does not hold the confessed sin against the person indefinitely. Mic 7:9 — "He will bring me out to the light; I shall look upon his vindication" — the confessor trusts God's disposition to be ultimately restorative, moving from indignation to vindication. The corporate confessions (Judg 10:10/15; 1Sa 7:6/12:10) show God as the one before whom Israel prostrates in confession and to whom they appeal for deliverance — presupposing a God whose disposition is to receive corporate confession and respond with covenantal intervention. God's disposition is holy-and-merciful: he does not ignore the sin, but he does not permanently hold it against the one who confesses and turns.

**[CHAR-4]** E — God's disposition toward the conscience-suppressed person is one of *unflinching moral honesty*: he does not accept the false innocence claim (Jer 2:35), does not allow the perceptual blindness to go unchallenged (Jer 16:10 — the prophetic word has been sent), and does not exempt the person from accountability (Jer 2:35 — "I will bring you to judgment"). God's response also reveals patience through the very existence of the prophetic word (Jer 2:35; 16:10): he has spoken before the judgment falls, giving opportunity for the suppressed conscience to be re-engaged. The disposition is: morally serious, unwilling to collude with the denial, and persistent in providing the moral truth that the suppressed conscience needs to hear.

**[CHAR-5]** E — God's disposition toward the refusing person is: (1) *Patient and persistent in invitation*: Neh 9:29 — "you warned them" — the warnings are given before judgment; God does not immediately move to judgment but warns repeatedly. (2) *Morally serious in consequence*: Eze 18:24; Heb 10:26 — when refusal persists, the consequences are real and severe. God's disposition is not one of indifference to the refusal (he continues to warn) nor one of unlimited tolerance (the consequence is real and announced). The disposition is holy patience that does not capitulate to the refusal: God maintains his moral standard ("the law") while continuing to call the refusing person toward it.

**[CHAR-6]** E — God's disposition toward the habitually sinning person is one of *patient holiness that reaches a consequence*. Heb 3:17 — provoked for forty years before the bodies fall — reveals patience: God sustained the relationship through prolonged habitual rebellion. 1Ki 8:46 — Solomon's prayer presupposing that God will hear the prayer of those who sin and then are taken captive — implies God's continuing receptivity to prayer and repentance even after habitual sinning. The disposition is not one of immediate retributive termination but sustained moral seriousness that both endures the habitual sinning and eventually brings its consequence. Pro 11:31 — "how much more the wicked and the sinner!" — the amplified consequence reveals a disposition of moral proportionality: the sinner's habitual defection receives proportionally amplified consequence.

**[CHAR-7]** E — God's disposition toward the leader who practises contagious sin is one of *direct personal accountability without diminishment of the community's responsibility*. 1Ki 16:2 — "you have made my people Israel to sin" — God claims the people ("my people") even while the leader has corrupted them; the relational claim over the community is not dissolved by the leader's contagious sin. 1Ki 21:22 — house-destroying judgment — God's disposition is morally decisive when the leader's contagious sin has reached the scope of drawing the whole nation away. The disposition is not arbitrary severity but proportional moral seriousness: the scale of the leader's contagious sin determines the scale of the divine response.

**[CHAR-8]** E — God's disposition toward the person who forsakes him is revealed by the consequence: the political order sustained by God's covenantal presence begins to fragment when that presence is forsaken. God does not impose the revolt directly — the revolt is the natural consequence of the forsaking. The disposition is: *covenantal faithfulness sustains order; faithlessness allows fragmentation*. The political revolt is God's providential consequence for the ruler's forsaking — not a punitive imposition from outside but the structural result of the ruler's own abandonment of the covenantal ground of legitimate governance.

**[CHAR-9]** E — God's disposition is: (1) *Merciful toward those whose sinful speech arose from ignorance*: 1Ti 1:13 — Paul the former blasphemer received mercy — God's mercy is not withheld from those who spoke sinfully in ignorant unbelief; (2) *Forgiving toward most forms of sinful speech*: Mar 3:28 — "whatever blasphemies they utter" fall within the scope of forgiveness — the breadth of God's forgiveness extends to the category of sinful speech generally; (3) *Irrevocably judicial toward Spirit-blasphemy*: Mat 12:31 — a single specific form of sinful speech exceeds the scope of forgiveness entirely. The disposition is thus characterised by wide mercy and a single threshold of irreversible judgment.

**[CHAR-1]** E — God's response to the wicked person reveals the conjunction of two dispositions: his moral loathing of wickedness and his genuine desire for the wicked person's turning. Eze 33:11 (VCG-07) is the most theologically concentrated statement: "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" — God's disposition is anti-wickedness and pro-life-for-the-wicked simultaneously. His soul hates the wicked as a type (Psa 11:5) but desires the wicked person as an individual to turn (Eze 18:23). This reveals that God's disposition toward the wicked human is not indifferent — it is actively engaged: with loathing of what they have become and with desire for what they might become through turning.

**[CHAR-2]** E — God's response reveals a dual disposition: moral seriousness about the constitutional evil combined with transformative intent for the person. Wrath is revealed against the unrighteousness (Rom 1:18 — VCG-05) — this reveals God's non-neutrality about the constitutional condition. But Act 3:26 (vc=14410 — VCG-05) reveals a mission of transformation: God's servant is sent "to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness" — the blessing-intent is toward the person even while the condemnation is toward the condition. Heb 10:22 (VCG-06) reveals God's provision of a cleansed conscience for the constitutionally evil person through the new covenant — the divine disposition is toward making the impossible approach to God (blocked by the evil conscience) possible again.

**[CHAR-3]** E — God's revulsion-verdict reveals his moral character as both actively rejecting and genuinely caring. The active rejection: Pro 11:20 (vc=1677 — VCG-01): "those of crooked heart are an abomination to the Lord" — God's holiness does not merely tolerate but actively responds with revulsion to the abominable inner condition. The genuine care: Eze 14:6 (vc=65984 — VCG-04): "repent and turn away from your idols, and turn away your faces from all your abominations" — God issues the command to turn, showing that the revulsion verdict does not mean abandonment; the call to repentance shows God's desire for the human person to depart from the abominable condition. Eze 36:31 (vc=1681 — VCG-04): the divine action of restoring memory that produces self-loathing is a gracious act enabling conscience-reawakening. God's disposition is thus one of active moral revulsion toward the abominable condition combined with active desire for the person to be transformed.

**[CHAR-4]** E — God's response reveals a disposition of covenantal faithfulness that makes idolatrous betrayal genuinely painful and provocative. Deu 32:16 (vc=65938 — VCG-02): jealousy — this is the emotion of a covenant partner who experiences betrayal; it reveals that God's disposition toward the human person is one of genuine covenantal attachment that is hurt by infidelity. Eze 6:9 (vc=1697 — VCG-05): "I have been broken over their whoring heart that has departed from me" — the divine heart is "broken" — a personal, relational response to betrayal. Despite this, God's desire is for restoration: Eze 37:23 (vc=65913 — VCG-05): "I will save them from all the backslidings in which they have sinned, and will cleanse them; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God" — the restorative desire is present even through the judgment responses.

**[CHAR-5]** E — God's response reveals a disposition that takes iniquity seriously as a moral-relational violation while maintaining the possibility of return. Psa 5:5 (VCG-03): active hatred of evildoers — God's holiness creates a disposition of settled moral revulsion toward those constituted by iniquity. Job 36:10 (vc=38215 — VCG-04): "He opens their ears to instruction" — the divine initiative in enabling return reveals that the hatred-posture does not preclude redemptive desire; God acts to create the possibility of departure from iniquity. Isa 55:7 (vc=38200 — VCG-02): "he will abundantly pardon" — the promise of abundant pardon for those who forsake iniquitous thoughts reveals God's disposition as willing to restore, even after prolonged iniquity-scheming, upon genuine return.

**[CHAR-6]** E — God's disposition revealed through the characteristic is morally serious and relentlessly pursuing. The Rev 16 sequence (vc=14352; 14350; 14353 — VCG-01): God sends three successive judgments even as blasphemy follows each one — this reveals that God does not abandon the pursuit of response even in the face of sustained defiance. The persistent judgment is not indifference but a morally serious engagement with the hardened human will. 1Pe 2:12 (vc=14377 — VCG-03): the day of visitation reveals God as one who evaluates and will ultimately vindicate the falsely accused — his disposition toward the unjustly slandered is one of eventual public vindication. Rom 2:24 (vc=14357 — VCG-02): his name's dishonour among the Gentiles moves him — God cares about the testimony of his name through his people's conduct.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's cross-characteristic pattern reveals God's disposition as simultaneously morally serious and redemptively inclined. The moral seriousness: all six characteristics evidence active divine hatred or revulsion toward the evil-forms (Char 1: Psa 11:5; Char 5: Psa 5:5; Chars 3/4: to.e.vah framework — divine revulsion). The redemptive inclination: all six also evidence divine desire for return and transformation prior to the eschatological terminus (Char 1: Eze 18:21-27 — divine desire for turning; Char 2: Act 3:26 — turning from wickedness through divine blessing; Char 3: Eze 14:6 — command to repent; Char 4: Eze 37:23 — divine cleansing; Char 5: Job 36:10 — divine ear-opening; Char 6: Rev 16:9's implied missed opportunity for repentance). The cluster reveals God as the morally serious, actively just responder to M10b evil who simultaneously maintains the offer of redemptive return — a disposition of simultaneous moral seriousness and salvific desire that defines the cluster's theological frame.

**[CHAR-1]** E — God's establishment of the defilement-state system alongside its remedial provisions reveals a disposition of protective care for the human person's access to his presence. Lev 15:31 (M10c-A-VCG-08) — "lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle" — shows the system as life-preserving: the defilement categories are given so that the defiled person does not unwittingly destroy themselves through unauthorized access to divine holiness. The provision of a standing remedy (Num 19:9, M10c-A-VCG-07) shows God's disposition as remedial — the goal is restored access, not permanent exclusion. The accommodation for involuntary defilement (Num 9:10-11, M10c-A-VCG-07 — provision for a secondary Passover date for those with corpse-contact defilement) shows a disposition of gracious accommodation for creaturely vulnerability.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The judicial giving-over (Rom 1:24, VCG-02) reveals a disposition of serious moral seriousness: God does not treat moral defection as inconsequential. The removal of restraint is a judicial act of taking human choice seriously — if the person chooses the direction of impurity, God permits the deepening of that trajectory as a consequence of choice. Alongside this: 1Th 4:7 (VCG-02) — "God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness" — reveals the divine disposition as fundamentally oriented toward the person's holiness, not toward their defilement. The judicial giving-over is therefore not God's desired outcome but his response to the human rejection of the better outcome he intended.

**[CHAR-3]** E — God's action in this characteristic reveals a disposition of covenantal seriousness: he treats the defilement of his name, sanctuary, and land as real violations that require real response (Eze 5:11 — withdrawal of compassion). But the eschatological cleansing promises (Eze 37:23, Zec 13:1, VCG-05) reveal that the disposition is ultimately restorative rather than permanently punitive — the goal of the judicial response is the community's future non-defilement ("they shall not defile themselves anymore") and the restored covenant relationship ("they shall be my people, and I will be their God"). The characteristic reveals God as one who takes covenantal betrayal with ultimate seriousness and who also provides the ultimate remedy.

**[CHAR-4]** E — God's consistent expulsion of unclean spirits and restoration reveals a disposition of sovereign compassion: (1) Luk 6:18 — "were cured" — comprehensive, without exception; (2) Luk 9:42 — "healed the boy, and gave him back to his father" — relational restoration as important as the physical; (3) Act 5:16 — "they were all healed" — universal healing scope within the gathering. The disposition is both power (authority over all spirits — Mar 3:11) and care for the specific relational restoration of each person.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The four dispositions together reveal the cluster's theology of divine character in relation to the defilement domain. Characteristic 1 reveals protective care: God's establishment of the defilement system alongside its remedial provisions is life-preserving (Lev 15:31 — "lest they die in their uncleanness") and accommodating of creaturely vulnerability (Num 9:10-11 — secondary Passover provision for the corpse-defiled). Characteristic 2 reveals moral seriousness: God does not treat moral defection as inconsequential; the giving-over (Rom 1:24) takes human choice seriously by allowing it to run its natural course. Characteristic 3 reveals covenantal seriousness and ultimate restoration intention: God's withdrawal (Eze 5:11) and judicial deepening (Eze 20:26) are responsive to real violations; his cleansing promise (Eze 37:23, Zec 13:1) reveals that judgment is not his final word. Characteristic 4 reveals sovereign compassion: the consistent, comprehensive healing of all who are brought (Luk 6:18 — "all cured"; Act 5:16 — "all healed") and the relational restoration priority (Luk 9:42 — "gave him back to his father") reveal a God whose power and care are expressed together. The cluster's unified picture: a God who is protective (Char 1), morally serious (Char 2), covenantally faithful (Char 3), and sovereignly compassionate (Char 4) — different emphases of one consistent character engaged across the defilement domain's four registers.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-004: T4 reveals the most structurally developed relational architecture for compassion's scope. God's compassion operates simultaneously on three bases: sovereignly free (Rom 9:15 — "I will have compassion…
findings.finding_value: T4 reveals the most structurally developed relational architecture for compassion's scope. God's compassion operates simultaneously on three bases: sovereignly free (Rom 9:15 — "I will have compassion on whom I have compassion"), covenantally grounded (chesed as the bond-loyalty that grounds the characteristic), and situationally responsive (splanchnizō — triggered by the specific sight of suffering). These three bases are not in tension but in integration: divine compassion is free, covenanted, and responsive simultaneously. The scope finding is among the most analytically significant in the registry: compassion explicitly and repeatedly crosses covenantal boundaries (Nineveh, the Samaritan/Jew axis, the power-asymmetric relationship). Scope is defined by perceived need, not moral standing or covenantal membership — this is formally confirmed in the data and distinguishes compassion from many other relational characteristics. The chesed/splanchnizō distinction maps onto distinct relational registers: chesed sustains within established bonds; splanchnizō extends across distance and difference. T4.4 (receiver's inner-being experience) is the most significant gap — four P-rated prompts, entirely absent from the data. T4.6 (spiritual beings interface) is entirely silent across all four prompts.

findings.finding_value: T1's scope finding (compassion requires a suffering other; scope is determined by perceived need, not moral standing) is precisely confirmed in T4's relational analysis. The explicit crossing of covenantal boundaries (Nineveh, Samaritan/Jew) evidenced in T4 is the relational expression of T1's boundary-definition: compassion ends where the condition (pitiable need) is absent, not where covenantal membership ends. T1's four modes of operation (T1.4) — intra-covenantal, cross-boundary, anticipatory, Christological — map onto T4's chesed/splanchnizō distinction (within-bond sustaining vs across-distance extending) and the scope analysis (covenantal and transcovenantal registers). Definition and relational scope are structurally co-determining.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-015: T2's constitutional origin analysis (somatic-relational-covenantal triple ground) and T4's relational direction analysis are structurally aligned. The somatic origin (womb, gut) grounds the cross-boun…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional origin analysis (somatic-relational-covenantal triple ground) and T4's relational direction analysis are structurally aligned. The somatic origin (womb, gut) grounds the cross-boundary relational direction in T4: splanchnizō's somatic immediacy is precisely what enables it to cross covenantal boundaries — the gut-movement toward the suffering other precedes any covenantal assessment of the relationship. The covenantal origin (chesed) grounds the within-bond sustaining direction in T4. The constitutional origin therefore predicts the relational direction: somatic = cross-boundary; covenantal = within-bond. T2's soul-body interface classification explains T4's scope-by-need finding: because compassion originates at the soul-body interface (before covenantal-rational assessment), its scope is determined by the pre-rational recognition of need rather than the post-rational assessment of covenantal standing.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-019: T3's perceptive-trigger finding (compassion is activated by sight — splanchnizō is perceptively dependent) and T4's scope-by-need finding (scope is determined by perceived need, not covenantal standin…
findings.finding_value: T3's perceptive-trigger finding (compassion is activated by sight — splanchnizō is perceptively dependent) and T4's scope-by-need finding (scope is determined by perceived need, not covenantal standing) are the same finding from two analytical perspectives. T3 names the faculty (perception) and its function (triggering compassion by seeing the pitiable condition); T4 names the relational consequence (scope defined by what is seen). The cross-boundary extension in T4 (Nineveh, Samaritan/Jew) is the relational expression of T3's merit-independence: compassion is perceptively dependent (it must see the need) but merit-independent (it does not assess the moral standing of the one seen). The three relational modes in T3.11 (building/sustaining, restoring/repairing, extending across difference) correspond precisely to T4's chesed/splanchnizō/cross-boundary structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-023: T4's finding that divine compassion operates on three simultaneous bases (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, cove…
findings.finding_value: T4's finding that divine compassion operates on three simultaneous bases (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological) are structurally isomorphic. The sovereignly-free basis corresponds to the encounter/sudden mechanism: divine compassion operating freely produces the sudden compassion-event (splanchnizō). The covenantally-grounded basis corresponds to the covenantal-sustaining mechanism: chesed as the sustaining relational ground operates gradually and consistently. The situationally-responsive basis opens toward the participatory-ontological mechanism: formation at the deepest constitutional level produces a person who is dispositionally responsive to every situation of need. T4's relational architecture and T5's formation mechanisms are the same structural reality described from relational and developmental perspectives respectively.

findings.finding_value: T4's three bases of divine compassion (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) are each grounded in specific textual evidence from T7. The sovereignly-free basis is evidenced in Rom 9:15 (T7's argument structure analysis — divine compassion as sovereign determination). The covenantally-grounded basis is evidenced in Exod 34:6 (T7's most multiply-anchored verse — the divine self-declaration in the covenant context). The situationally-responsive basis is evidenced in the Synoptic splanchnizō pattern (T7.2 — the sight-event structure of the Gospels). T7's framework divergences (sovereignty vs automaticity) map directly onto T4's relational analysis: the framework correctly identifies that divine compassion's sovereign freedom (T4.1) is what exceeds the natural empathic automaticity that human science frameworks describe.

findings.finding_value: T4 establishes the most precisely articulated relational architecture of any characteristic in the review set. The God-to-human direction is primary and dominant (groups 888-001, 889-001, 5471-001 — all God-as-subject). The basis of divine extension is the giver's character and prior knowing (Exo 33:17 — "I know you by name"), not the receiver's merit — neither merit-based nor arbitrary. The human-to-God direction is specifically supplication: tachanum (H8469) is the receiving side's corresponding vocabulary built into the same root family as the giving side (chen/chanan) — the vocabulary embeds the two-directional circuit in a single root. The human-giving direction extends grace horizontally through three modes: forgiving (charizō — Eph 4:32), gracious conduct (chen as character quality — 889-003), and gracious speech (SD022). The receiving direction is the most underexamined (T4.4 — P-rated throughout); the scope analysis (T4.5) reveals grace crossing covenantal and social boundaries (Ruth narrative — grace in the context of foreign status and vulnerability). T4.6 (spiritual beings) is evidenced at one point: Luk 1:28 (kecharitōmenē — the angel's announcement), which implies angelic ministry as a vehicle of grace rather than grace operating independently in the spiritual-beings register. T4 synthesis: the relational architecture of grace is unique in the programme — it is the only characteristic where the giving-side vocabulary and the receiving-side vocabulary are built from the same root (chen/tachanum), encoding the grace-circuit's two-sidedness at the lexical level.

T4 describes the relational shape of each mechanism; T5 describes the inner formation process each mechanism produces.

God extends CHAR-2 to the proud as a judicial act: "your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down" (2Sa 22:28); "the Lord God of hosts will lop the boughs with terrifying power" (Isa 10:33); "I will change their glory into shame" (Hos 4:7). God's sovereign reversal of CHAR-5 is the theological foundation for why the recipient of contempt need not be defined by the contempt-verdict. God does not extend contempt-producing-shame toward persons; he extends the reversal of contempt and the vindication of the despised.

**[CHAR-6]** E — God confirms and validates CHAR-6: Gen 20:6 (contextually) — God's response to Abimelech's appeal to innocence is to confirm it and grant protection. God is the authoritative validator of the innocence-claim: whether CHAR-6 is present is not merely a self-assessment but a reality confirmed or denied by God. God also reveals the incapacity for innocence (Hos 8:5) — the divine question "how long will they be incapable of innocence?" reveals that God tracks the moral condition of CHAR-6 and names its loss.

(1) God as shame-bearer's guardian — protecting those who trust him from being put to shame: the repeated Psalm formula "let me not be put to shame" (Psa 25:2; 31:1; 119:31) presupposes this guardianship; 1Cor 1:28 shows God choosing the despised to nullify the world's contempt-assessments (Chars 1, 5). (2) God as sovereign abaser — bringing the proud low as a judicial act: the sha.phel VCG-03 corpus (1Sa 2:7; Psa 75:7; Isa 2:11) is the most extensive God-to-human mode in the cluster (Char 2). (3) God as worth-assigner — assigning standings of honour or dishonour according to his sovereign purpose: the potter's right (Rom 9:21; Char 3). (4) God as moral standard — being the sight before which conduct bears or does not bear scrutiny: "in the sight of God" (2Cor 4:2; Char 4). (5) God as innocence-confirmer — acknowledging the genuine innocence-claim and acting accordingly: God's response to Abimelech (Gen 20:6; Char 6). These five modes are not in tension: they are different expressions of the same God's character operating in M07's field — guardian, sovereign, assigner, standard, and confirmer.

findings.session_b_note:
Yes — the human-to-God direction is the second major direction in the corpus, concentrated in the intercessory vocabulary (group 5379-002) and the access-posture evidence:

**Intercession as the primary human-to-God movement:**
- Dan 9:19 — "O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive." Daniel's intercessory cry is the paradigm: the human person turns toward God in urgent, dependent appeal, seeking the divine act of forgiving. The inner act of intercession is the human-to-God movement that corresponds to the God-to-human act of forgiving.
- Group 5379-002 description: "the act of seeking God's pardon on behalf of oneself or others, and God's response of pardoning or withholding." The seeking-act is the human movement; the pardoning is the divine response.

**Access-postures as human-to-God orientations:**

findings.session_b_note:
Yes — the human-to-God direction is well-evidenced through the supplication vocabulary, which is structurally embedded in the compassion data as a significant XREF set.

**Supplication as the human-to-God compassion-interface:** H8467 techinah (supplication, 24 XREF occurrences) and H8469 tahanun (entreaty, 18 XREF occurrences) both derive from the CHANAN root (grace/favour/compassion). They name the verbal acts through which the human person appeals for divine compassion. The structural relationship established by this vocabulary: God's compassion is the presupposed ground that makes earnest appeal possible (SD-021). The human person who approaches God in supplication is acting on the knowledge that God is compassionate — the appeal would be irrational if God were not.

**Psalm vocabulary of seeking chesed:** Psa 25:7 (group 1633-003) — "according to your steadfast love remember me" — is directed toward God. Psa 48:9 — "we have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple." These are human-to-God movements in which the human inner being orients itself toward and rests in divine chesed. This is not supplication under duress but contemplative orientation — the human person's inner being actively seeking and dwelling in the reality of divine compassion.

**Covenantal return enabled by compassion (Joel 2:13):** "Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and merciful (rachum ve-channum)." The divine compassion-character is the basis and motivation for the human movement back toward God. The human-to-God direction here is one of return — the inner act of repentance and reorientation toward God, enabled and motivated by the certainty of his compassion.

findings.session_b_note: Human-to-God operation is evidenced through three modes: (1) Doxological worship — the liturgical refrain "for he is good, his steadfast love endures forever" (group 884-001) is goodness operating as the content of the human's praise and confession toward God. The human declares God's goodness in worship — this is goodness moving upward from the human toward God as acknowledgement and adoration. (2) Seeking and trust — Psa 34:8 ("blessed is the man who takes refuge in him") and Lam 3:25 ("the soul who seeks him"): the human's movement toward God in trust and seeking is enabled by the encounter with divine goodness. Goodness produces the movement toward God. (3) Covenantal request — Psa 119:68 ("you are good and do good; teach me your statutes"): the human addresses God's goodness as the ground for petition. God's goodness is invoked as the basis of the human's request — "because you are good, teach me." (OBS-067-OBS-025, OBS-067-OBS-026, OBS-067-OBS-033)
