**[CHAR-21]** E — Yes — through social corruption and the great-prostitute archetype. (1) *Social corruption contagion*: 1Cor 15:33 — "bad company ruins good morals" — the perverse person's company corrupts the morals of those in proximity; the perversion extends outward through social influence; (2) *Cosmic-scale corruption*: Rev 19:2 — "the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality" — the archetype of the perverted agent whose corruption extends to the whole earth; (3) *False-teacher corruption*: 2Cor 7:2 — "we have corrupted no one" — Paul's denial implies the false teachers did corrupt — they extend perversion to their hearers; 2Cor 11:3 — "as the serpent deceived Eve... your thoughts will be led astray" — the external corrupting agent working on the hearers.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Yes — as the characteristic's defining mode. (1) *Judicial extension*: Psa 82:2 — "how long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked?" — judges extending injustice to those who appear before them; (2) *Violent extension*: 2Sa 7:10 — "violent men shall afflict them" — the violent extending harm; Psa 58:2 — "your hands deal out violence on earth" — distributing injustice outward; (3) *Commercial extension*: Lev 19:35 — "do no wrong in judgment, in measures of length or weight or quantity" — commercial relationships as the context for extending injustice to counterparties; (4) *Civic-structural extension*: Mic 3:10 — "who build Zion with blood" — leaders extending injustice to the whole city through structural wrongdoing.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Person-to-person confessions appear in several instances. (1) Exo 10:16 — Pharaoh confesses "against the Lord your God, and against you" — Moses as a human recipient alongside God. (2) 2Sa 19:20 — Shimei confesses "I have sinned" to the returning King David — a direct interpersonal confession. (3) Mat 27:4 — Judas confesses "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood" to the chief priests — a person-directed confession. (4) 1Sa 26:21 — Saul confesses "I have sinned" in the context of David's mercy — a relational confession between king and subject. The person-to-person direction is present but secondary to the God-directed primary axis.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Limited evidence. Tit 3:11 — the divisive person who is "warped and sinful" operates within a community, and the divisiveness itself is an extension of the conscience-suppressed character into the community — the person is causing division without apparently registering the sinfulness of doing so. 1Cor 15:34 — "some have no knowledge of God" — the knowledge-absence that enables ongoing sinning within a community of faith suggests that conscience suppression operates at a communal level where it may influence others through modelled behaviour. However, the corpus does not show one person explicitly extending conscience suppression to another.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes — the transmission dimension is extensively evidenced. The Jeroboam-sin formula includes the phrase "which he made Israel to sin" (2Ki 3:3; 10:29; 13:2/6/11; 14:24; 15:9/18/24/28) — each king's refusal to repent is extended to the people through leadership. The king's non-departure from Jeroboam's sins draws the whole nation into the same non-departure. 1Ki 16:31 — Ahab's treatment of Jeroboam's sins as "a light thing" while going further to serve Baal: the leader's refusal extends and escalates the communal sinful course. The characteristic is transmitted from leader to people through the leadership's continued walking in the sinful pattern.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes. Ecc 9:18 — "but one sinner destroys much good" — the habitually sinning person's settled sinning orientation has a destructive extension toward others: the one sinner dismantles much accumulated good in the surrounding community. 1Sa 2:25 — Eli's sons' habitual defection ("sinned against the Lord") operates in a priestly-leadership context where their sinning directly affects the people they serve and the sacred functions they perform. Hos 8:11 — altars multiplied for sinning — the institutionalised sinning extends through community structures to shape the sinning orientation of all who participate in the misdirected worship.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes — this is the characteristic's defining relational operation. The Hiphil causative formula "made Israel/Judah to sin" appears across 12+ verses, each naming the leader extending the sinning direction to the community. 1Ki 14:16 — "the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and made Israel to sin" — the personal sinning and the extending to Israel are named side by side. 1Ki 16:2 — "made my people Israel to sin" — God explicitly identifies the giving-direction as the indictment. Jer 32:35 — "they built the high places of Baal... to cause Judah to sin" — a deliberate constructive act whose stated purpose is causing the community to sin.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Yes — this is the defining relational operation of political revolt: a subordinate community extending the revolt against a governing community. 2Ki 1:1 / 3:5 — Moab extending revolt against Israel; 2Ki 8:20 / 2Ch 21:8 — Edom extending revolt against Judah; 2Ki 8:22 / 2Ch 21:10 — Libnah extending revolt against Jehoram. The direction is always upward (subordinate breaking from governing authority) rather than downward (governing authority imposing revolt on subordinate). The giving-direction is the subordinate extending the revolt to the governing authority by breaking submission.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Yes — VCG-01 slander is constitutively directed from one person toward another. Eph 4:31 — "slander be put away from you" — the community context shows slander as the speech that one community member directs toward others. Act 6:11 — "We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God" — false witnesses direct blasphemous claims against Stephen, extending sinful speech as a weapon against him. Rev 2:9 — "the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not" — a false identity claim directed against the true community. The person-to-person giving direction is present throughout VCG-01.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The question asks about "extending" wickedness as one might extend love or wisdom. The evidence shows the wicked person imposing their characteristic on others through: (a) social-moral contagion — Num 16:26 (VCG-04): proximity to the wicked risks "being swept away with all their sins" — the characteristic has a social-contagious dimension; (b) alliance-recruitment — Exo 23:1 (VCG-04): "you shall not join hands with a wicked man to be a malicious witness" — the wicked person actively recruits others into complicity; (c) evil counsel — Psa 1:1 (VCG-04): the blessed person avoids the wicked person's counsel — the counsel of the wicked is extended outward and capable of drawing others into alignment; (d) systemic imposition — Eze 7:21 (VCG-03): the wicked of the earth serve as instruments of profanation. The wicked person extends their characteristic's influence outward as harm and recruitment, not as a gift.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. The characteristic is extended toward others through several mechanisms. (1) Social contagion: 2Jo 11 (vc=14453 — VCG-04): "whoever greets him takes part in his wicked works" — the constitutionally evil person communicates their characteristic through voluntary association; greeting is the mechanism. (2) Social disruption: Act 17:5 (vc=14452 — VCG-04): "wicked men of the rabble…formed a mob, set the city in an uproar" — the constitutional inner disposition is organised and deployed collectively as social harm. (3) Community control: 3Jo 10 (vc=14454 — VCG-04): Diotrephes's characteristic is extended through speech ("wicked nonsense"), refusal of hospitality, and obstruction of others — the characteristic flows outward through the person's social power. (4) Teaching and leadership: 2Ti 3:13 (vc=14451 — VCG-06): "evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse, deceiving" — the characteristic is extended through false teaching as a communicative act.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, though extension operates differently from a gift characteristic. The characteristic is extended toward others primarily through: (1) the scoffer's contemptuous derision — Pro 24:9 (vc=65957 — VCG-01): "the scoffer is an abomination to mankind" — the inner disposition of contemptuous derision is extended toward others and makes the scoffer repugnant to the human community; (2) perverted judgment — Pro 17:15 (vc=1690 — VCG-01): justifying the wicked and condemning the righteous — the inverted moral verdict is directed toward other persons, doing them harm; (3) the Babylon-figure of Rev 17:5 (vc=65878 — VCG-05): the "mother of prostitutes and of earth's abominations" — the characteristic is generative, extending abomination toward others through the generation and propagation of moral corruption; (4) Mal 2:11 (vc=66004 — VCG-04): faithless betrayal in the covenant-marriage relationship — the abomination is extended toward the covenant partner.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. Idolatrous abomination extends from person to person through multiple mechanisms. (1) Royal/institutional extension: 1Ki 11:7 (vc=65899 — VCG-03): Solomon building high places extends the idolatrous abomination to the entire community; 2Ki 21:11 (vc=65942 — VCG-03): Manasseh "made Judah also to sin with his idols" — active communal extension; 2Ch 36:14 (vc=65948 — VCG-03): leaders "following all the abominations of the nations" leading the people in the same. (2) Cultural-educational extension: Deu 20:18 (vc=65932 — VCG-02): the nations "teach you to do according to all their abominable practices" — the teaching of abominable practices is a specific extension mechanism. (3) Social-relational extension: Ezr 9:14 (vc=65950 — VCG-03): intermarriage with abomination-practicing peoples as the relational channel of extension.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. The extension of iniquity toward others is extensively documented. Direct harm-infliction: Psa 55:3 (vc=38188 — VCG-01): "they drop trouble upon me" — iniquity is actively dropped onto victims. Predatory exploitation: Psa 14:4 (vc=38229 — VCG-03): "evildoers who eat up my people as they eat bread" — the characteristic is extended through predatory consumption of others. Institutional oppression: Isa 10:1 (vc=38191 — VCG-02): "those who decree iniquitous decrees… the writers who keep writing oppression" — iniquity is extended through institutional power structures that systematically harm the weak. Social deception: Psa 28:3 (vc=38232 — VCG-03): speaking peace while evil is in the heart — iniquity is extended through relational deception. Entrapment: Psa 141:9 (vc=38231 — VCG-03): "the trap that they have laid for me and from the snares of evildoers" — the characteristic is extended through cunning entrapment of the innocent.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes. The characteristic is constitutively extended toward others. VCG-01: Rev 13:6 (vc=14356 — VCG-01): blasphemy extended toward God, his name, his dwelling, and heaven's inhabitants — the extension is deliberate and sustained. VCG-02: 1Cor 4:13 (vc=14351 — VCG-02): "when slandered" — the slandering speech is extended by some toward the apostle; Rom 3:8 (vc=14358 — VCG-02): "slanderously charge us with saying" — false attribution extended toward Paul. VCG-03: Joh 18:30 (vc=14378 — VCG-03): the accusers extend the false charge toward the accused (Jesus); 1Pe 2:12 (vc=14377 — VCG-03): opponents "speak against you as evildoers" — the false accusation is extended toward the community of believers.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics evidence extension of their respective evil-forms toward others. The extension mechanisms vary: Char 1 (the wicked person's social harm — Psa 37:12-14 — plots and acts against the righteous), Char 2 (the evil person extending malice toward others — 3Jo 10 — VCG-04), Char 3 (the scoffer's contempt as abomination extended toward the community — Pro 24:9 — VCG-01), Char 4 (kings extending institutional abominations to whole communities — VCG-03; Solomon's high places for foreign gods — 1Ki 11:7), Char 5 (evildoers eating up the people — Psa 14:4; iniquitous decrees against the weak — Isa 10:1), Char 6 (blasphemy directed at God, slander at persons, false accusation at the innocent). The cluster's extension pattern: all six M10b characteristics are active in their social extension — they seek victims, communities, and institutional structures through which to propagate.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, though not as a gift but as a transmission. The defilement-state transmits from person to person through contact: Lev 15:7-11 (M10c-A-VCG-06) — touching the body of the discharge-person, sitting on surfaces they used, being touched by them with unwashed hands, all transmit the unclean state. Hag 2:13 (M10c-A-VCG-07) — the corpse-defiled person transmits impurity to whatever they touch. This transmission is not an intended giving but an inherent feature of the condition's contagious nature. The person in the defilement-state is a source of transmission, and the social-relational duty is to prevent this transmission (Lev 15:11 — washing hands before contact; self-declaration, Lev 13:45 — to warn others to maintain distance).

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, in a morally corrupting environmental sense. 1Cor 8:7 (VCG-03): "through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol" — the former association with defiling practices is a formative context through which the person's conscience was shaped toward susceptibility. The "former association" implies that a defiling social environment can form the inner person's moral vulnerability. 2Cor 6:17 (VCG-03): "go out from their midst" — the command to separate from "their midst" implies that the community of defilement poses a risk of moral-inner defilement to the person in it; the characteristic can be transmitted through sustained immersion in a defiling moral environment. The extending mode is environmental/formative rather than direct personal transmission.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, in two modes. (1) Sexual violation of another person: Gen 34:5/13/27 (VCG-01) — Shechem's violation of Dinah defiles her; the defilement is extended from one person (the violator) to another (the violated). Eze 23:17 (VCG-02) — "the Babylonians came to her into the bed of love, and they defiled her with their whoring lust" — external agents extend defilement to the community through corrupt relational engagement. (2) Corporate contagion: Lam 4:15 (VCG-05) — "Unclean! Away!" — the community in exile extends the defilement-condition to its social environment; the surrounding nations treat the community as a source of contagion.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The defilement-by-external-spiritual-agency characteristic is not extended by one human person to another within the 21-verse corpus. The only transmission evidenced is the spirit moving between entities (Mar 5:13 — spirits leaving the man and entering the pigs). The characteristic is imposed by an external spiritual agent, not transmitted through human interpersonal interaction.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Three of four characteristics show the defilement being extended or transmitted from person to person; Characteristic 4 does not. Characteristic 1: involuntary transmission through bodily contact (Lev 15:7-11 VCG-06; Hag 2:13 VCG-07 — the corpse-defiled person transmits to what they touch), governed by the duty of non-transmission (Lev 15:11 — washing before contact). Characteristic 2: environmental-formative transmission — sustained immersion in a defiling community shapes the inner person's moral formation (1Cor 8:7 — "former association with idols"; 2Cor 6:17 — "go out from their midst" implies the community poses a risk). Characteristic 3: sexual violation of another (Gen 34 — defilement imposed through violent violation; Eze 23:17 — the Babylonians' "whoring lust" defiling the community) and corporate contagion (Lam 4:15 — the exilic community extends defilement to its social environment). Characteristic 4: no human-to-human transmission — the only transmission is the spirit moving between entities (Mar 5:13 — spirits from the man to the pigs). This 3:1 pattern is analytically significant: three forms of defilement have human-transmission mechanisms; Characteristic 4 is the only one that does not, confirming its structural uniqueness as entirely agent-driven.

questions.question_text: What inner conditions or orientations in the giver accompany genuine extension of the characteristic?

findings.session_b_note:
The data identifies several enabling inner conditions for genuine giving:

**Prior receipt of divine forgiveness:** F-003 — the structural enabling condition. The person who has genuinely received divine forgiveness has the inner ground from which horizontal giving flows. The parable of Mat 18 makes this the logical prerequisite: having received much enables (and obligates) giving much. OBS-064-029: "vertical reception → inner transformation → horizontal extension."

**Heart-level reception (not merely formal):** Mat 18:35 — "from your heart." The inner condition of genuine giving is heart-level engagement — the volitional release must reach the deepest level of the inner person. Formal or verbal forgiveness without heart-level release is the misuse identified in F-002.

**Visceral compassion:** Mat 18:27 — splagchnizomai as the felt motivational origin of the master's forgiving act. Compassion is the affective inner condition that enables and motivates the giving. The gut-level responsiveness to the other's condition opens the path to the volitional act.

**The love-orientation produced by received forgiveness:** OBS-064-029 — "forgiveness received generates love-orientation." The love-disposition toward others is the inner state from which horizontal giving flows most naturally. The more deeply forgiveness is received, the more the love-orientation is established, and the more the giving of forgiveness to others becomes natural rather than forced.

findings.session_b_note:
One must have received before genuinely giving. Eph 4:32: "as God in Christ forgave you" — the pattern is the divine gift received, and the human extension is grounded in that receipt. SD030 (eusplanchnos as mediating state): grace received → tenderheartedness produced → kindness and forgiveness extended. Grace extended from pride or self-righteousness is not grace in the structural sense.

*Consistent with prior analysis (SD030). Adds T4 framing.*

findings.session_b_note:
Four inner conditions emerge from the data:

**Perceptive openness (sight of the other's condition):** As established at T3.1, compassion-giving requires seeing the other's condition genuinely. The Good Samaritan sees and is moved; the priest and Levite see and pass by. The enabling inner condition is not merely physical sight but the perceptive openness that allows what is seen to produce inner movement. This cannot be forced — it is the condition of the person who has not closed their inner perception against the reality of suffering.

**Eusplanchnos — tender heart (1 Pet 3:8):** The constitutional pre-condition for compassion-giving is a tender inner being — one that has not been hardened against the suffering of others. This is the inner quality from which the splanchnizō movement can arise naturally. A hardened heart cannot give compassion because it cannot be moved.

**Inner purity as the ground of authentic giving (Luke 11:41; Matt 6:2-4):** Genuine compassion-giving requires that the inner disposition match the outer act. Matt 6:2 identifies the failure mode: almsgiving done "to be praised by others" is compassion-giving divorced from its inner ground. The enabling condition is that the giving flows from the actual inner movement of compassion rather than from social motivation.

**Prior reception (implied by the mirroring principle, 2 Sam 22:26):** The data suggests that genuine compassion-giving is enabled by having received compassion — the person who has been shown mercy by God has the inner ground from which to show mercy to others. The mirroring principle (with the merciful you show yourself merciful) implies that God's compassion toward the person constitutes the inner ground from which the person's compassion toward others flows. This is implicit in the data rather than directly stated, but it is consistent with the structural logic of the vocabulary.

findings.session_b_note: Three enabling inner conditions for giving goodness (SBF-067-Q039): (1) Prior Spirit-transformation — Rom 15:14's community goodness is a Spirit-enabled capacity. Col 3:12's "put on" is explicitly grounded in prior identity transformation ("God's chosen ones, holy and beloved") — the giver must first have received a transformation before they can genuinely give. (2) Encounter with and reception of divine goodness — Psa 73:28's inner reorientation produces the overflow toward others in Psa 73's conclusion (telling of God's works). The person who has genuinely encountered divine goodness has a source of goodness to extend. (3) Spirit-filling — Gal 5:22 / Rom 15:14: the Spirit-produced chrēstotēs and agathōsunē are inner capacities the Spirit supplies. Without Spirit-filling, the person lacks the genuine internal resource for extending goodness. Source is transformation; discipline may shape expression but cannot generate the capacity. (OBS-067-OBS-025, OBS-067-OBS-039, SBF-067-Q039)

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-004: T4 as a whole reveals that goodness operates across all relational directions simultaneously — God-to-human, human-to-God, and human-to-human — but with a fundamental asymmetry: the God-to-human direc…
findings.finding_value: T4 as a whole reveals that goodness operates across all relational directions simultaneously — God-to-human, human-to-God, and human-to-human — but with a fundamental asymmetry: the God-to-human direction is prior, generative, and abundant in evidence; the human-to-God direction is responsive and derivative; the human-to-human direction is overflow from prior reception. This is not a simple tripartite scheme but a structured cascade: God's goodness initiates and flows toward the human person (Q&A-099-101); the human responds in trust, seeking, and worship (Q&A-103-105); the goodness received overflows toward others through instruction, justice, and kindness (Q&A-107-109). The most structurally significant T4 finding is the unconditional/conditional distinction (Q&A-100): God's goodness as a character attribute is unconditional; the human's ongoing experience of its relational benefits is conditional on continued trust. This distinction has direct implications for how goodness is taught, received, and sustained. The spiritual beings interface is largely silent — the relational architecture of goodness is thoroughly human-divine in orientation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-015: T2 confirmed that goodness originates externally to the person — the origin is God's character, Spirit, and word; the person is the site of reception, not generation (Q&A-060-061). T4 maps the relatio…
findings.finding_value: T2 confirmed that goodness originates externally to the person — the origin is God's character, Spirit, and word; the person is the site of reception, not generation (Q&A-060-061). T4 maps the relational architecture of this origin: the God-to-human direction (T4.1) is the relational channel through which the external origin reaches the person; the human-to-God direction (T4.2) is the responsive movement that the received goodness enables; the human-to-human direction (T4.3) is the overflow once received. T2's single-origin/multiple-mechanism finding (Q&A-061) maps onto T4's three relational directions: the encounter mechanism corresponds to the human-to-God direction (seeking and tasting); the covenantal-word mechanism corresponds to the God-to-human covenantal direction; the Spirit-infusion mechanism is the Spirit's work in the human constitutional levels (T2.1-2.2). The constitutional and relational architectures are co-extensive — they describe the same reality from inside (constitutional) and outside (relational).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-019: T3 confirmed that goodness engages every inner faculty (except creativity), with particular depth in moral evaluation (goodness as the normative anchor — Q&A-089), conscience (goodness calibrates the …
findings.finding_value: T3 confirmed that goodness engages every inner faculty (except creativity), with particular depth in moral evaluation (goodness as the normative anchor — Q&A-089), conscience (goodness calibrates the standard — Q&A-092), and relational capacity (dual-directional overflow — Q&A-098). T4 confirmed that goodness operates across all three relational directions. The inter-tier connection: the faculty engagements of T3 are the inner mechanisms through which T4's relational directions operate. The God-to-human direction (T4.1) engages the perceptive faculty (tasting and seeing — Q&A-066) and the moral evaluation faculty (calibrating the conscience's standard — Q&A-092). The human-to-God direction (T4.2) engages the affective faculty (trust, praise) and the relational capacity faculty. The human-to-human direction (T4.3) engages agency (doing justice — Q&A-084) and relational capacity (overflow toward others — Q&A-098). T3's faculty map is the inner architecture; T4's relational directions are the external expressions of those faculties in lived relationship. They are not separate dimensions but the inside and outside of the same relational-characterological phenomenon.

findings.session_b_note: The enabling inner conditions for human mercy-giving: (1) Prior reception of divine mercy (Mat 18:33 — the servant received mercy first; failure to extend was inexcusable because of this). (2) Solidarity with the condition of the needy — Heb 2:17 establishes the principle that mercy-extension requires experiential solidarity (OBS-111-033); Christ's incarnational solidarity with humanity is the mechanism for his priestly mercy. (3) The inner character quality of mercifulness (*eleēmōn*, *oiktirmōn*) — which Col 3:12 frames as a garment to be deliberately appropriated. OBS-111-033, OBS-111-055, OBS-111-069.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-111-004: Reading T4 as a whole reveals mercy's relational architecture as directional and asymmetric in all three interface directions (God→human, human→God, human→human), with a structural requirement that re…
findings.finding_value: Reading T4 as a whole reveals mercy's relational architecture as directional and asymmetric in all three interface directions (God→human, human→God, human→human), with a structural requirement that receiving precedes giving. The key synthesis across T4: (a) God-to-human direction is the most extensively evidenced and is the source of mercy in all other directions; (b) human-to-God direction is characterised by normative ongoing supplication — not exceptional crisis-response; (c) human-to-human direction requires prior receipt from God and solidarity-knowledge of the condition being addressed; (d) mercy operates characteristically across relational distance and rupture (Q&A-117), not within maintained relationships; (e) the scope is wide (crossing covenantal boundaries) but not unconditionally permanent (withdrawal is named possibility). The T4 synthesis: mercy's relational architecture is an asymmetric chain — divine mercy → received human mercy → extended human mercy — with the chain requiring the prior link at each stage.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-010: T1's four modes of mercy's operation (dispositional, mechanical, dialogic, institutional) map directly onto T4's four relational directions. The dispositional mode corresponds to God→human mercy (sove…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes of mercy's operation (dispositional, mechanical, dialogic, institutional) map directly onto T4's four relational directions. The dispositional mode corresponds to God→human mercy (sovereign disposition). The mechanical mode corresponds to the atoning mechanism of the God→human direction. The dialogic (petition-response) mode corresponds to the human→God direction. The institutional mode (mercy seat, Day of Atonement) structures all three directions simultaneously. T1 and T4 together: mercy's operational modes are relationally differentiated — each mode is specific to a relational direction, and together they constitute the full relational architecture of mercy.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-015: T2 establishes the receiving-before-generating constitutional principle (Q&A-062) and T4 establishes the asymmetric relational chain (God→received human→extended human mercy). These are the constituti…
findings.finding_value: T2 establishes the receiving-before-generating constitutional principle (Q&A-062) and T4 establishes the asymmetric relational chain (God→received human→extended human mercy). These are the constitutional and relational descriptions of the same structural requirement: mercy cannot be generated from within the person (T2) and mercy cannot be extended without prior receipt (T4). T2 explains why T4's relational chain is necessary: the constitutional principle of receiving-before-generating is what creates the structural necessity of the T4 relational chain. The body-soul interface through which mercy's mechanism operates (T2 — blood atonement on nephesh) is the constitutionally specific expression of the God→human directional mercy (T4.1).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-019: T3 shows mercy activating the full faculty system (perception, cognition, memory, affect, volition, agency, moral evaluation, conscience, conscientiousness, relational capacity) and T4 shows mercy ope…
findings.finding_value: T3 shows mercy activating the full faculty system (perception, cognition, memory, affect, volition, agency, moral evaluation, conscience, conscientiousness, relational capacity) and T4 shows mercy operating across three relational directions (God→human, human→God, human→human). Reading together: the faculty activations in T3 are the inner capacities that each T4 relational direction requires. God→human mercy (T4.1) engages mercy's receptive faculty complex — conscience, moral evaluation, affect, memory (asymmetric structure). Human→God mercy (T4.2 — mercy-seeking) engages volition, agency, affect, conscience, and perception (face-toward-God). Human→human mercy (T4.3) engages moral evaluation, agency, volition, and relational capacity. The three relational directions of T4 are served by the specific faculty subsets activated in T3.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-023: T4's relational chain (God→human→human mercy) and T5's formative arc (mercy received forms mercy-giving capacity) are structurally identical processes described at different levels. T4 describes the r…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational chain (God→human→human mercy) and T5's formative arc (mercy received forms mercy-giving capacity) are structurally identical processes described at different levels. T4 describes the relational structure (who gives, who receives, under what conditions); T5 describes the developmental process (what changes in the person as a result). Reading together: T4's relational chain is the structure within which T5's formative arc occurs. The transition from receiving mercy (T4, God→human direction) to giving mercy (T4, human→human direction) is not automatic but requires the formative arc T5 describes — specifically the character formation through suffering (T5.4) and the sustained effects of mercy-reception (T1, confirmed by T5). T4's normative mercy-seeking posture (Q&A-107) is the relational expression of T5's sustained developmental practice (Dan 6:11 daily prayer, Q&A-137).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-004: T4 reveals the most structurally developed relational architecture for compassion's scope. God's compassion operates simultaneously on three bases: sovereignly free (Rom 9:15 — "I will have compassion…
findings.finding_value: T4 reveals the most structurally developed relational architecture for compassion's scope. God's compassion operates simultaneously on three bases: sovereignly free (Rom 9:15 — "I will have compassion on whom I have compassion"), covenantally grounded (chesed as the bond-loyalty that grounds the characteristic), and situationally responsive (splanchnizō — triggered by the specific sight of suffering). These three bases are not in tension but in integration: divine compassion is free, covenanted, and responsive simultaneously. The scope finding is among the most analytically significant in the registry: compassion explicitly and repeatedly crosses covenantal boundaries (Nineveh, the Samaritan/Jew axis, the power-asymmetric relationship). Scope is defined by perceived need, not moral standing or covenantal membership — this is formally confirmed in the data and distinguishes compassion from many other relational characteristics. The chesed/splanchnizō distinction maps onto distinct relational registers: chesed sustains within established bonds; splanchnizō extends across distance and difference. T4.4 (receiver's inner-being experience) is the most significant gap — four P-rated prompts, entirely absent from the data. T4.6 (spiritual beings interface) is entirely silent across all four prompts.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-004: T4 establishes the most precisely articulated relational architecture of any characteristic in the review set. The God-to-human direction is primary and dominant (groups 888-001, 889-001, 5471-001 — a…
findings.finding_value: T4 establishes the most precisely articulated relational architecture of any characteristic in the review set. The God-to-human direction is primary and dominant (groups 888-001, 889-001, 5471-001 — all God-as-subject). The basis of divine extension is the giver's character and prior knowing (Exo 33:17 — "I know you by name"), not the receiver's merit — neither merit-based nor arbitrary. The human-to-God direction is specifically supplication: tachanum (H8469) is the receiving side's corresponding vocabulary built into the same root family as the giving side (chen/chanan) — the vocabulary embeds the two-directional circuit in a single root. The human-giving direction extends grace horizontally through three modes: forgiving (charizō — Eph 4:32), gracious conduct (chen as character quality — 889-003), and gracious speech (SD022). The receiving direction is the most underexamined (T4.4 — P-rated throughout); the scope analysis (T4.5) reveals grace crossing covenantal and social boundaries (Ruth narrative — grace in the context of foreign status and vulnerability). T4.6 (spiritual beings) is evidenced at one point: Luk 1:28 (kecharitōmenē — the angel's announcement), which implies angelic ministry as a vehicle of grace rather than grace operating independently in the spiritual-beings register. T4 synthesis: the relational architecture of grace is unique in the programme — it is the only characteristic where the giving-side vocabulary and the receiving-side vocabulary are built from the same root (chen/tachanum), encoding the grace-circuit's two-sidedness at the lexical level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-019: T3's agency-constituting finding (grace constitutes rather than replaces agency — 1Cor 15:10) and T4's human-to-God direction (supplication as the human posture of appeal — requiring genuine human age…
findings.finding_value: T3's agency-constituting finding (grace constitutes rather than replaces agency — 1Cor 15:10) and T4's human-to-God direction (supplication as the human posture of appeal — requiring genuine human agency in the act of plea) are structurally aligned. The constituted agency (T3.7) is precisely the agency that supplication requires: the creature must genuinely appeal, not merely receive passively. T3's finding that grace and conscience are mutually necessary (T3.9) corresponds to T4's relational-access finding: grace transforms the threshold of human-to-God approach (prosagōgē — SD035) from impassable to open, which is the relational expression of T3.9's constitutional finding that grace creates the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destruction. T3 names the inner-being event; T4 names the relational consequence of the same event.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence identifies: (1) Moral integrity — the person who gives covenant to another must be the kind of person who keeps their word. 3308-002 (OBS-034-053) — oath-keeping as moral character: the inner quality of trustworthiness is what makes covenant-giving genuine rather than empty. (2) Inner faithfulness (amanah-root — OBS-034-008, OBS-034-037): Neh 9:38 — the "firm covenant" is one whose firmness derives from the faithfulness character of those who make it. Genuine covenant-giving flows from a faithful inner character. (3) Committed love: 3304-004 (OBS-034-049) — the covenant of intimate personal loyalty is given from a disposition of committed love toward the other person. The giving cannot be merely formal; it requires an inner orientation of love toward the covenant partner. (4) Freedom from competing covenants: 3304-003 (OBS-034-048) — genuine covenant-giving to the right party requires having one's loyalty free from false covenantal commitments. A person bound to false covenants cannot give genuine covenant-loyalty to the right party.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-004: T4 as a whole reveals that the relational architecture of this characteristic is directionally structured and asymmetrical. The dominant direction is God-to-human (6 of 7 groups, confirmed across T4.1…
findings.finding_value: T4 as a whole reveals that the relational architecture of this characteristic is directionally structured and asymmetrical. The dominant direction is God-to-human (6 of 7 groups, confirmed across T4.1); the human direction is responsive (T4.2: human gives back what was first given). The basis of divine giving is plural — covenantal, responsive, formative, moral-consequential, eschatological-grace (Q&A-102) — revealing that faithfulness is not a single relational mode but a relational orientation that differentiates itself across relational conditions while remaining unified in character. The human-to-God direction reveals responsive correspondence as the relational structure (Q&A-107): the proper relational form is one in which the human gives back to God what is his (glory, praise, self), having first received. The human-to-human direction is thinner in the data (Q&A-109) — reflecting the registry's God-subject dominance. T4.6 is substantially silent on spiritual beings. What T4 reveals as a whole: faithfulness-as-giving is constitutively a divine-initiative relational reality that the human enters through responsive participation. The human's giving is always downstream of divine giving; the correspondence is the proper form of the relationship.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-012: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — perception, affect, volition, relational capacity all engaged) and the relational interface structure (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal a faculty-interface …
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — perception, affect, volition, relational capacity all engaged) and the relational interface structure (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal a faculty-interface correspondence. In the God-to-human direction: divine hearing (T3.1 — perception) precedes compassionate giving (T4.1 — responsive basis); divine affect (T3.4 — rahamim, leb) determines the direction of giving (T4.1 — basis of extension); divine relational capacity (T3.11) is the prior orientation that makes the giving possible. In the human-to-God direction: human perception (Q2 — recognising divine sovereignty), human affect (blessing under loss), human volition (choosing to give glory), and human relational capacity (genuine correspondence) are all required for the giving to be genuine (T4.2 — inner posture). What this pair reveals: the relational interfaces are not external channels through which giving flows; they are relational events in which the inner faculties of both parties are engaged simultaneously and correspondingly. The correspondence is not mechanical but genuinely personal.

findings.finding_value: For the transmission of reverential fear through instruction (Psa 34:11): the giver must themselves possess the fear genuinely (2Ki 17:28 shows that a priest who doesn't know how to fear God cannot teach it authentically — formation precedes transmission).

For the extension of "do not fear" release commands: the person who extends this must stand in a position of genuine authority or covenant assurance relative to the other (Jesus extending release from a position of divine authority; Jonathan extending it to David grounded in divine promise).

For the pastoral anxiety that flows from love: Paul's anxiety is enabled by his genuine love for his churches (Gal 4:11 context: "I am afraid I may have labored in vain for you" — the anxiety flows from the labour of love already invested).

For righteous anger extended toward another (as correction, confrontation, or prophetic challenge): the enabling condition is conscience-grounded moral perception of genuine wrongdoing. Nehemiah (Neh 5:6) — righteous anger toward oppressors — requires that the person has accurately perceived a real injustice and the inner state arises from that perception. Elihu's anger toward Job (Job 32:2) requires that the person has a genuine theological concern, not personal grievance.

For destructive anger extended toward another: the enabling condition is wounded pride meeting non-compliance. Peninnah's sustained provocation of Hannah (1Sa 1:6) is a form of anger-extension enabled by rivalry and status-competition.

Three enabling conditions for giving grief: (1) genuine relational bond — Job's soul weeping for the needy (Job 30:25 — M03-A-VCG-04) shows that empathic grief requires genuine inner solidarity with the other's condition; (2) moral seriousness about what matters — the prophet's compassion-grief (Jer 9:1) requires genuine inner engagement with the catastrophe befalling others, not detachment; (3) love — Paul's apostolic travail is "intense inner travail of love" (Gal 4:19 — M03-E-VCG-02 anchor meaning). Love is the inner condition that enables grief to be given as a relational act.
