findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-099-004: T4 reveals that kindness operates across all four relational directions for which evidence exists — God-to-human (most extensively evidenced), human-to-God (appeal/chasid identity mode), human giving,…
findings.finding_value: T4 reveals that kindness operates across all four relational directions for which evidence exists — God-to-human (most extensively evidenced), human-to-God (appeal/chasid identity mode), human giving, human receiving, and communal — with spiritual beings being the only direction that is genuinely absent from the evidence. The structural finding: the four evidenced directions form a coherent circuit, not parallel independent operations. Divine kindness flows to the human → the human receives it and appeals to it (human-to-God) → the human, having received, is equipped and obligated to give it to others (human giving, grounded in Eph 4:32's "as God in Christ forgave you, be kind") → kindness given and received forms the communal relational fabric (chasidim assembly). The circuit is both moral and ontological: it is not merely that we ought to be kind because God is kind, but that the human person is constituted to be a bearer of the divine kindness in the relational world. T4's most significant intra-tier finding: the divine-to-human direction is the source and ground of all other directions — human giving of kindness is explicitly grounded in received divine kindness, making T4 a circuit with a single originating source.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-010: T1's definition of kindness as other-oriented loyal goodwill is perfectly reflected in T4's relational interface structure: kindness has no meaningful existence except in the relational directions T4 …
findings.finding_value: T1's definition of kindness as other-oriented loyal goodwill is perfectly reflected in T4's relational interface structure: kindness has no meaningful existence except in the relational directions T4 maps. The T4 finding that divine-to-human is the most extensively evidenced direction grounds T1's working definition — kindness in its primary form is God's stable outward-oriented goodwill toward the creature, and the human analogue is derived from and dependent on this. The T4 circuit (divine → human → reproduced in giving toward others → communal) maps onto T1's conditions of reception (Q&A-031): the person who has received divine kindness and responded with trust and covenant orientation is precisely the person positioned to extend it to others. T1's finding that kindness explicitly excludes self-serving motivation (Q&A-020) is structurally necessary for T4's circuit to function: if kindness at any point in the circuit becomes self-serving (chrēstologia), the transmission is severed — which is why Eph 4:32 grounds human giving not in the recipient's desert but in the received divine kindness.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-019: T3's faculty analysis and T4's relational interface analysis are structurally interdependent in a specific way: the faculties that kindness most strongly engages (volition, agency, relational capacity…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty analysis and T4's relational interface analysis are structurally interdependent in a specific way: the faculties that kindness most strongly engages (volition, agency, relational capacity, conscientiousness) are precisely the faculties required for the T4 relational circuit to operate. Relational capacity (T3.11) is what makes the T4 interfaces possible at all — the person must have the constitutional equipment for genuine connection before kindness can flow in any direction. Agency (T3.7) is what makes the T4 giving direction concrete — not passive benevolence but enacted care. Conscientiousness (T3.10) is what makes the T4 circuit sustainable across time — the chasid who reliably keeps covenant. The T4 communal interface (Moses's intercession; the chasidim assembly) requires an intercessory capacity (T3 — memory + relational capacity) that knows how to appeal on behalf of others. The two tiers together describe a portrait of the whole inner person oriented outward: T3 names the inner equipment and T4 names the relational directions in which that equipment is deployed.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-024: T4's relational circuit and T6's structural network overlap most clearly at the causal level. The T6 causal network (divine kindness → praise + repentance → reproduced human kindness → sustained coven…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational circuit and T6's structural network overlap most clearly at the causal level. The T6 causal network (divine kindness → praise + repentance → reproduced human kindness → sustained covenant relationships) is a structural description of the T4 circuit in causal terms: T4 identifies the directions; T6 names the causal mechanism connecting them. The T6 finding that Mic 6:8 anchors eight registries is a cluster-level reflection of T4's circuit: Mic 6:8's triadic requirement (do justice / love kindness / walk humbly) is addressed to the covenant community's relational practice — it describes the T4 relational interface requirements in condensed form. The T6 finding that kindness is self-propagating through the causal chain (received kindness → reproduced kindness) is the structural guarantee that the T4 circuit is not a closed loop requiring constant external input but a self-sustaining relational ecosystem once kindness is received and given. The T4 finding that the spiritual beings interface is absent (Q&A-070) is consistent with T6's causal analysis: the causal chain operates within the human-divine-communal relational web, not across spiritual-ontological boundaries.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — the data shows different modes of operation. Within existing covenant relationship: God's covenant of peace (Isa 54:10) is addressed to those already in covenant with him — it deepens and confirms the existing relationship. Within existing friendship: H7965J (2510-001) — the sha.lom-friendship bond is most dramatically revealed when it is violated (Psa 41:9, Jer 20:10) — the betrayal is devastating precisely because the relationship was pre-existing. In new relationships: G1514 eirēneuō (Rom 12:18 — "with all") — the call to peace extends to all people, including strangers; Jer 29:7 — seeking the welfare of the exile city involves extending peace to a new (and hostile) community. Eph 2:14 — Christ making peace between Jew and Gentile is the formation of a new relationship between previously hostile parties. The data does not show a sharp distinction in the characteristic itself — peace is offered in both contexts — but the vulnerability in existing relationships (betrayal wounding) and the cost in new relationships (hostile parties) are different.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-117-004: T4 establishes two key relational findings: (1) Peace's scope expands progressively — covenant-primary (to Israel, Num 6:26) → covenant-expansive (to nations in the prophets, Isa 57:19) → universally …
findings.finding_value: T4 establishes two key relational findings: (1) Peace's scope expands progressively — covenant-primary (to Israel, Num 6:26) → covenant-expansive (to nations in the prophets, Isa 57:19) → universally offered through Christ (Eph 2:14, Col 1:20) — with the only sustained exclusion being moral ("no peace for the wicked"). The covenantal boundaries are overcome in Christ; the moral boundary remains. (2) Peace is a site of cosmic contest: angelic mediation of peace is effective (Dan 10:19), elemental disruption of peace is real (Mar 4:39), and eschatological removal of peace is documented (Rev 6:4). Peace is not only a private inner condition but a publicly contested reality across the cosmic order.

findings.finding_value: T4's God-to-human direction (peace given through covenant, word, cross, Spirit) maps onto T5's mechanisms (proclamation, covenant-ground, cross-accomplishment, Spirit-formation) and sequences (gift received → heart/mind guarded → somatic rest → expressed in community). The developing scope of T4 (covenant → universal) maps onto T5's eschatological trajectory: the expanding relational scope and the deepening eschatological fullness are the same movement outward from its source in God's identity as peace. The T4 finding that peace refused worsens peacelessness (Q&A-114) connects to T5's reversibility finding (T5.1.2) — the experiential peace is reversible in both directions: given and received, or offered and refused.

findings.finding_value: T4's God-to-human direction and T6's causal sequences describe the same reality at different levels of abstraction. T4.1 (God gives peace through covenant/Christ/Spirit) is the relational description of what T6.3.2 catalogues as causal inputs (trust, righteousness, discipline, Spirit, confession, love of law all produce peace). The two analyses are not parallel but nested: T4 names the relational direction; T6 names the structural mechanism through which that direction operates.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-004: T4 as a whole reveals that the relational architecture of this characteristic is directionally structured and asymmetrical. The dominant direction is God-to-human (6 of 7 groups, confirmed across T4.1…
findings.finding_value: T4 as a whole reveals that the relational architecture of this characteristic is directionally structured and asymmetrical. The dominant direction is God-to-human (6 of 7 groups, confirmed across T4.1); the human direction is responsive (T4.2: human gives back what was first given). The basis of divine giving is plural — covenantal, responsive, formative, moral-consequential, eschatological-grace (Q&A-102) — revealing that faithfulness is not a single relational mode but a relational orientation that differentiates itself across relational conditions while remaining unified in character. The human-to-God direction reveals responsive correspondence as the relational structure (Q&A-107): the proper relational form is one in which the human gives back to God what is his (glory, praise, self), having first received. The human-to-human direction is thinner in the data (Q&A-109) — reflecting the registry's God-subject dominance. T4.6 is substantially silent on spiritual beings. What T4 reveals as a whole: faithfulness-as-giving is constitutively a divine-initiative relational reality that the human enters through responsive participation. The human's giving is always downstream of divine giving; the correspondence is the proper form of the relationship.

The cluster's characteristics consistently transcend relational boundaries — they are not restricted to existing bonds but extend toward strangers, enemies, the world. The evidence for universal scope: "do good to everyone" (Gal 6:10 — Group 1098); "kind to the ungrateful and the evil" (Luk 6:35 — Group 1469); "comfort all who mourn" (Isa 61:2 — Group 1742); "God was reconciling the world to himself" (2Cor 5:19 — Group 2069); "show perfect courtesy toward all people" (Tit 3:2 — Groups 1103, 1262). The cluster teaches that these characteristics have a universal relational scope defined by the person's condition of need rather than by pre-existing relational bonds. The community of faith retains priority (Gal 6:10 — Group 1098: "especially to those of the household of faith") but the scope is not restricted to it.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — the cluster contains both bonded (covenant, community) and boundary-crossing examples. Abraham's intercession for Sodom (Gen 18:23–28, VSG M26-A2-015) crosses relational boundaries — he intercedes for a city of strangers. The king who "did justice and righteousness" (Jer 22:15, VSG M26-A2-012) does so in his administrative role — for all within his community. The righteous person's outward-flowing righteousness (Amo 5:24: "like an ever-flowing stream") does not respect relational categories — it flows to whoever is in need.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Yes — the commissioned avenger (Rom 13:4) serves all within the civic jurisdiction, not only those with existing relational bonds. The protection of justice crosses relational distance.

**[CLUSTER — T4.5]** E. Righteousness in M26 operates within existing relational bonds AND crosses relational boundaries. The outward-flowing character of righteousness in A2-012 is not bounded by covenant or community — it reaches toward whoever needs it. However, the covenantal context is the primary context of God's righteousness (A1-003), and the community context is the primary context of the righteous person's social impact (A2-015). Both within-bonds and boundary-crossing modes are present.

findings.finding_value: M01-A operates consistently across relational distance — fear of God applies to the person's treatment of strangers (Lev 25:36-37: not exploiting a stranger's poverty), servants (Lev 25:43: no ruthless domination over a servant who is a fellow Israelite), enemies (Deu 25:18: Amalekites' attack on the weak is evidence of absent God-fear), and foreigners (Act 10:35: "anyone who fears God and does what is right is acceptable to him regardless of nationality"). M01-B's social fear (B-VCG-04) operates across relational difference in the direction of crowd-management: the leaders' fear of the crowd is fear across social distance (the crowd as mass, not individuals in relationship). M01-B's self-preservation fear (B-VCG-05) also operates across relational distance — Jacob's fear of Esau (Gen 32:7-11), the Gibeonites' fear of the covenant community (Jos 9:24).

M01-A's ethical dimension operates specifically in power-asymmetry relationships: Lev 19:14 (the vulnerable deaf and blind), Lev 25:43 (the servant). Fear of God operates precisely where power difference would otherwise enable exploitation. The characteristic does not narrow to relational equals.

M01-A operates consistently across all relational bonds and distances. The characteristic's ethical dimension specifically addresses power-asymmetric relationships where relational exploitation would otherwise be possible. This confirms that fear-of-God is not a parochial characteristic limited to in-group relationships but operates as a universal governing orientation.

The depth of the relational bond (the covenant) makes the refusal more morally serious, not less — refusing to turn within an established covenant is a greater moral act than refusing within no relationship.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes. Within the covenant bond: 2Ki 17:7 — "sinned against the Lord their God, *who had brought them up out of Egypt*" — habitual defection within the established covenant relationship is qualitatively more severe because it operates against a relational foundation of redemptive grace. 1Sa 2:25 — "if someone sins against the Lord, who can intercede for him?" — sinning against the Lord directly (as opposed to against another person) is categorically different because the relationship involves the primary covenantal party. The depth of the established relational bond makes habitual defection within it the more morally weighty instance.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes. Contagious sin operates most powerfully within existing covenantal authority bonds: the Kings corpus shows contagious sin transmitted through the established king-people covenant relationship — a pre-existing bond of authority and accountability. The transmission is effective precisely because the bond is pre-existing: the community already recognises the king's authority. The pre-entry context (Exo 23:33; Deu 20:18) addresses contagious sin across relational distance — from foreign nations who are not yet in a covenant relationship with Israel. The mechanism is different: proximity and teaching rather than authority. The corpus shows contagious sin operating through both existing bonds (covenantal-authority) and across relational distance (proximity-influence), but most severely through existing authority bonds.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Yes. Two relational contexts appear. (1) *Vassal-state bond* (Moab-Israel; Edom-Judah): the revolt breaks a suzerain-vassal political bond — an external governing relationship between distinct peoples. (2) *Intra-covenantal bond* (Israel from house of David — 1Ki 12:19; 2Ch 10:19): the revolt breaks a covenantally grounded internal governing relationship — the Davidic authority structure within the covenant community itself. The intra-covenantal revolt carries greater theological weight because the bond broken is not merely political but covenantally-theologically grounded.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Yes. VCG-01's slander within community context (Eph 4:31; Col 3:8) operates within existing bonds — slander between people who are in relationship damages from the inside: the relational bond is exploited by the sinful speech. Act 6:11's false witness against Stephen operates by introducing sinful speech into a judicial-social context — the speech targets a person across a judicial relationship. VCG-02's blasphemy against Jesus operates in a formal judicial context (the trial) — the charge is brought by religious authorities against one who stands before them. The characteristic operates most destructively within existing bonds of trust and authority.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence shows the characteristic operating with particular intensity within close relational bonds. Psa 28:3 (VCG-08): "speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts" — the deception is maximally operative within close relational proximity where trust is assumed. Psa 37:12 (VCG-03): "the wicked plots against the righteous" — the plotting targets the nearby righteous, not a distant stranger. The social-destruction of Pro 11:11 (city overthrown by the wicked's speech) occurs in a communal context of shared civic life. However, the characteristic also operates across relational distance: Hab 3:13 (VCG-03) — the wicked as an entrenched institutional power structure — suggests the characteristic operates at scale beyond proximate bonds. The evidence does not show a fundamental qualitative difference by relational distance but does show that the characteristic's deceptive mode (Psa 28:3) is most operative within bonds of assumed trust.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence shows the characteristic operating with particular intensity within relational proximity and community bonds. 2Jo 11 (vc=14453 — VCG-04): the transmission through greeting requires proximity. 3Jo 10 (vc=14454 — VCG-04): Diotrephes's constitutional malice is deployed through the specific institutional relationships of church membership and hospitality. 1Cor 5:8 (vc=14363/14412 — VCG-05): the old leaven's spreading effect specifically requires the communal batch it is mixed into — the leaven metaphor implies that close community proximity is the medium through which the characteristic spreads. The evidence does not suggest qualitatively different operation across relational distance — rather, it shows that the characteristic's social harm is most potent and most visible within existing relational bonds precisely because those bonds provide the channels through which it flows.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The evidence shows the characteristic operating with particular intensity within close relational bonds. Mal 2:11 (vc=66004 — VCG-04): faithless covenant-betrayal through mixed marriage — the abomination is specifically the violation of the intimate covenant bond. Pro 26:25 (vc=1694 — VCG-02): seven abominations hidden beneath gracious speech — the gracious speech implies close social relationship; the concealment is operative within relational proximity. The Ezekiel conscience-related abominations (VCG-04: Eze 44:6-7) concern the covenant community's internal violations. VCG-03's corrupt worship abominations concern the personal worship relationship — the most intimate directional bond. The characteristic's most intense expression is within existing bonds of intimacy (covenant, worship relationship, close social proximity) where the violation of trust is compounded by the closeness of the bond violated.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence shows the characteristic operating most powerfully within intimate relational bonds. 1Ki 11:4-5 (vc=65898 — VCG-03): "his wives turned away his heart… Solomon went after Ashtoreth" — the king's intimate marital bonds were the primary mechanism of idolatrous influence. Ezr 9:14 (vc=65950 — VCG-03): intermarriage with abomination-practicing peoples — intimate covenantal bonds as the mechanism. The characteristic is more potent within existing relational bonds (marriage, cultural community, institutional authority) than across relational distance. The Deuteronomic warnings (VCG-02) consistently frame the hazard as relational proximity — being among the nations (Deu 18:9; 20:18 — VCG-02) rather than distance from them.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The evidence shows the characteristic operating with particular damage within close relational bonds. Psa 28:3 (vc=38232 — VCG-03): "workers of evil, who speak peace with their neighbors" — the neighbour-bond is specifically the relational context exploited by the inner-evil/outward-peace deception. Psa 41:6 (vc=38236 — VCG-04): "when one comes to see me, he utters empty words, while his heart gathers iniquity" — the visit (a close relational act) is exploited as cover for inward iniquity-gathering. The characteristic weaponises intimacy: the closer the bond, the more effectively deception operates (speaking peace while evil is in the heart — Psa 28:3 — VCG-03 — requires relational proximity to be plausible). The VCG-01 trouble-suffered register (Psa 55:3 — "they drop trouble upon me") also evidences the characteristic as operating within personal enemy relationships rather than anonymous contexts.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The evidence shows the characteristic operating with particular intensity in contexts of hostile relational proximity. 1Pe 2:12 (vc=14377 — VCG-03): "among the Gentiles" — the false accusation occurs within the shared social space of a minority community (believers) living among a majority culture (Gentiles); the proximity enables the social observation and accusation. Joh 18:30 (vc=14378 — VCG-03): the accusers have specifically observed and evaluated the accused — the false charge requires enough relational proximity to observe and make a judgment. VCG-01 (Rev 16:9/11/21) operates at the most extreme form of divine-human relational distance — yet even this is a direct encounter (God's judgment falling on those who curse him). The characteristic can operate across relational distance (verbal accusation from any social position) but is most intense in contexts of structured social opposition.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster reveals that M10b characteristics operate with greater intensity within existing relational bonds — particularly covenantal and intimate bonds — than across relational distance. Char 4 (Solomon's wives drawing him into idolatrous attachment — 1Ki 11:5; Ezr 9:14 — intermarriage as idolatrous influence channel), Char 6 (1Pe 2:12 — accusation within shared social space; Psa 28:3 — Char 5 — speaking peace to neighbours while evil is in the heart), Char 3 (Mal 2:11 — covenant-betrayal through faithless mixed devotion). The most extreme case is Char 6's VCG-01 — the blasphemy under divine judgment represents the maximum-intimacy-betrayal: the divine-human relationship itself is the relational space within which the most extreme form of evil speech is expressed.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. Existing relational bonds intensify the characteristic's reach: Lev 15:24 (M10c-A-VCG-05) — sexual intercourse with a menstruating woman passes her niddah condition fully to the man for seven days; Lev 15:19-23 (M10c-A-VCG-05) shows the contamination radiating to all surfaces she uses during her condition. The intimacy of the relational bond creates a fuller transmission pathway. Similarly, the Lev 13:46 (M10c-B-VCG-03) exclusion of the diseased person from communal dwelling operates to sever an existing relational bond (community belonging) for protective purposes. Across relational difference, the characteristic operates more simply: touching a stranger's discharge-surface defiles regardless of relational bond (Lev 15:5-10, M10c-A-VCG-06).

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. Within existing relational bonds, the characteristic operates with greater formative force: 1Cor 8:7 (VCG-03) — "former association with idols" — the sustained relational bond with a defiling community shapes the inner person's moral formation over time. Within the community of believers (the Corinthians Paul addresses), the persistence of unrepented impurity (2Cor 12:21, VCG-02) creates a communal moral environment. Mat 23:27 (VCG-04) — the hypocrites' defilement is operating within the existing relational bond of community recognition and reputation, using that bond for concealment. Across relational distance (the general call of 1Th 4:7 — VCG-02 — "God has not called us for impurity") the characteristic is addressed as an interior personal condition without specific relational context.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Within existing covenantal bonds, the characteristic's impact is greatest: the ordeal law (Num 5, VCG-01) specifically governs the marriage bond — adultery within the covenantal marriage produces defilement in a way that sexual act with a stranger does not in the same structural sense. The Gen 34 narrative (VCG-01) shows the characteristic operating within the existing relational bond between a community and the surrounding peoples — the violation of Dinah is perpetrated by those outside the covenant but the inner-being consequence (violated honour driving revenge) operates within the family bond. Within the covenant community (VCG-02): idolatrous self-defilement affects the corporate communal bond and the land they share — the closer the bond, the more comprehensive the defilement's reach.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic does not appear to operate differently based on existing relational bonds. The spirits inhabit: a man in a synagogue community (Mar 1:23 — within a religious community), a man utterly isolated (Mar 5:2 — among tombs), and a child (Mar 7:25 — within a family). The variety of relational contexts shows no pattern of relational-bond dependence. However, the characteristic's resolution does engage existing relational bonds: the mother's bond with her daughter (Mar 7:25), the father's bond with his son (Luk 9:42).

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics show relational-bond-sensitivity in their operation, but the pattern differs by characteristic. Characteristic 1: existing intimate bonds intensify transmission (Lev 15:24 — sexual intercourse with a menstruating woman transmits the full niddah condition; Lev 15:19-23 — contamination radiates to all surfaces she uses); the stronger the relational bond, the fuller the defilement's reach. Characteristic 2: existing relational bonds intensify formative force (1Cor 8:7 — "former association" implies sustained immersive relationship; the Corinthian community in 2Cor 12:21 shows that the community bond amplifies the characteristic's persistence). Characteristic 3: the characteristic operates most acutely within existing covenantal bonds — the ordeal law (Num 5) specifically governs the marriage bond; idolatrous alliance (Eze 23:17) engages existing national bonds; the closer the bond, the more comprehensive the defilement's reach. Characteristic 4: no significant variation by relational bond at the level of reception — a man in a synagogue community (Mar 1:23), an isolated man (Mar 5:2), and a child within a family (Mar 7:25) all receive the characteristic; the spirit's invasion does not depend on relational context. The cluster pattern: Characteristics 1-3 all show that existing relational bonds amplify the defilement's reach (by intensifying transmission, formative force, or covenantal stakes). Characteristic 4 does not depend on relational bonds for its operation — it arrives regardless.

questions.question_text: Does the characteristic operate within covenantal contexts only, or does it cross covenantal boundaries, as the evidence shows?

findings.session_b_note:
The data provides a partially evidenced answer:

**Covenantally bounded (OT):** The OT cultic mode (group 5379-001) is explicitly covenantal — the atonement mechanism operates within the covenant community and its prescribed practices. The salach-root forgiveness is covenantally framed throughout the OT.

**Crossing covenantal boundaries (NT):** Act 10:43 — "everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name." The "everyone" is contextually significant — this verse is the climax of the Cornelius narrative, in which forgiveness is extended beyond the Jewish covenant community to the Gentile household. The NT covenantal expansion explicitly crosses the prior covenantal boundary.

**The new covenant:** Jer 31:34 — the new covenant promise is addressed to "the house of Israel and the house of Judah" (Jer 31:31) but its structural logic — direct knowing, forgiveness without mediation — points toward the broader NT expansion.

The data supports: covenantally bounded in the OT register; explicitly crossing covenantal boundaries in the NT through the universal scope of the forgiveness-offer ("everyone who believes"). This is consistent with OBS-064-014's contrast between OT mechanism-based and NT access-posture-based forgiveness.

findings.session_b_note:
The data clearly establishes that compassion crosses covenantal boundaries — this is one of its most structurally significant features.

**Jon 4:11 — Nineveh:** God's pity (chus) for Nineveh — a pagan city — is one of the data's most pointed boundary-crossings. The 120,000 people who "do not know their right hand from their left" are not covenant members; they are outside Israel's covenantal relationship with God entirely. God's compassion extends to them. Jonah's resistance to this extension (the narrative context of Jon 4) confirms that the covenantal boundary-crossing is deliberate and theologically significant — it is precisely the point of the passage.

**Luke 10:33 — the Good Samaritan:** The Samaritan extends compassion to the Jew, crossing not only an ethnic and cultural boundary but a specifically religious and covenantal one. In this parable, compassion defines who the neighbour is — and the answer explicitly includes the person outside one's own covenantal community.

**Matt 18:27 — the king's mercy:** The parable's king shows compassion (splanchnizō) toward his servant — a relationship of power and obligation rather than covenant. Compassion here is not contingent on covenantal membership.

The covenantal vocabulary (chesed) does operate primarily within covenantal relationships. But the wider compassion vocabulary (splanchnizō, chus, oikteirō) explicitly crosses covenantal boundaries. The data supports a reading in which compassion's inner character is broader than the covenantal forms through which it is often expressed.

findings.session_b_note:
All instances of contrition in the penitential-relational mode are within covenantal contexts: the psalmists (within Israel's covenant with God), Isa 57:15 and 66:2 (prophetic to Israel), Jer 44:10 (Israel's covenant failure). There is no verse in the registry that addresses contrition in a non-covenantal context.

However, the experiential-anguish mode (Jer 46:5 — Egyptian warriors in terror/panic) involves persons outside the Israelite covenant. Whether this represents a cross-covenantal operation of the crushing vocabulary or simply a general human experience described in covenantal vocabulary is not resolvable from the data.

*Partial: penitential contrition is exclusively covenantal in the verse evidence; the experiential-anguish mode may cross covenantal boundaries but the data does not confirm this.*

findings.session_b_note:
The data shows fellowship operating both within and across covenantal contexts.

**Within covenantal context:** Mal 2:14 (marriage covenant), Psa 119:63 (covenant community of fear-of-God), group 873-001 (fellowship with Father and Son — covenantal relationship). Much of the evidence is covenantally located.

**Across covenantal boundaries:** Ecc 9:4 — *he who is joined with all the living has hope* — this verse uses the joining vocabulary in relation to *all the living*, not a specific covenant community. The fellowship of common life (being alive) crosses covenantal particularity.

**Ecc 4:10** — *if they fall, one will lift up his fellow* — the context does not specify a covenant community. The mutual-support function of fellowship appears to operate at the level of shared human life, not only within covenant boundaries.

**New finding:** Fellowship has a covenantal form (operating within covenant at its highest registers) and a common-life form (operating across the shared boundary of human existence). This distinction parallels the difference between koinōnia vocabulary (highly particular, often covenantally located) and chavar/chaver vocabulary (wider application, including common-life contexts). This has implications for the programme's understanding of fellowship's relational scope.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-004: T4 as a whole reveals that goodness operates across all relational directions simultaneously — God-to-human, human-to-God, and human-to-human — but with a fundamental asymmetry: the God-to-human direc…
findings.finding_value: T4 as a whole reveals that goodness operates across all relational directions simultaneously — God-to-human, human-to-God, and human-to-human — but with a fundamental asymmetry: the God-to-human direction is prior, generative, and abundant in evidence; the human-to-God direction is responsive and derivative; the human-to-human direction is overflow from prior reception. This is not a simple tripartite scheme but a structured cascade: God's goodness initiates and flows toward the human person (Q&A-099-101); the human responds in trust, seeking, and worship (Q&A-103-105); the goodness received overflows toward others through instruction, justice, and kindness (Q&A-107-109). The most structurally significant T4 finding is the unconditional/conditional distinction (Q&A-100): God's goodness as a character attribute is unconditional; the human's ongoing experience of its relational benefits is conditional on continued trust. This distinction has direct implications for how goodness is taught, received, and sustained. The spiritual beings interface is largely silent — the relational architecture of goodness is thoroughly human-divine in orientation.

findings.finding_value: T4 confirmed that goodness operates across all three relational directions (God-to-human, human-to-God, human-to-human). T6's structural relationships and shared anchors data confirms that the cross-registry connections of goodness are organised along the same relational axes. The Mic 6:8 shared anchor (6 co-registries) is organized along the human-to-God and human-to-human axes: humility with God (vertical) and justice/kindness with others (horizontal). The Gal 5:22 shared anchor (5 co-registries) is organized along the human-community axis: Spirit-fruit characteristics that are all expressed in human relationship. The sequential finding (goodness → repentance, goodness → faith — Q&A-147-148) corresponds to the God-to-human relational direction: divine goodness producing these inner-being responses in the human. T6's cross-registry connections are the structural record of goodness's relational reach — the registries it is most connected to are the registries it most closely interacts with in its relational operation. Relational architecture (T4) and structural position (T6) are co-extensive.

findings.session_b_note: Human-to-human love creates a social architecture with three features: (a) **Restructured family** — Mat 12:50 (OBS-103-063): 'whoever does the will of my Father is my brother and sister and mother' — love redraws the family boundary around shared orientation toward God rather than natural kinship. (b) **Public community mark** — Joh 13:35 (OBS-103-129): mutual love is externally legible as the community's identity. The social architecture of love is publicly readable — it creates a community whose internal reality is visible to outsiders. (c) **Competitive generosity** — Rom 12:10 (OBS-103-119): 'outdo one another in showing honor' — love creates a social order where the competition is in giving rather than taking, in honour-showing rather than honour-claiming. These three features constitute a social architecture that is structurally counter to the natural social patterns of kinship, concealment, and rivalry.

findings.finding_value: Love's relational architecture is structured by three directional axes — GOD → HUMAN, HUMAN → GOD, HUMAN → HUMAN — with divine love structurally prior and causally generative of all subsequent love. 1Jo 4:19 ('we love because he first loved us') is the axis-precedence statement: the first axis is not responsive to but constitutive of the second and third. The GOD → HUMAN direction moves through four mechanisms: covenantal declaration (naming the beloved — Jer 12:7, Mat 3:17), Spirit-infusion (Rom 5:5), redemptive acts (Joh 3:16), and covenantal covering (Eze 16:8). The HUMAN → GOD direction requires total inner mobilisation (Mat 22:37 — all heart, soul, mind) and the clearing of rival loves as its condition (1Jo 4:19, 1Ti 6:10). The HUMAN → HUMAN direction spans five structural types (neighbour, enemy, community, friendship, family) and creates the social architecture described in Q&A-088 (restructured kinship, public legibility, competitive generosity). The most significant finding in T4: the human-to-God direction is conditioned by prior reception of divine love — the capacity for human love toward God is itself a gift. The one structural gap: T4.6 (spiritual beings) is absent from the evidence.

findings.finding_value: Reading T4 as a whole reveals mercy's relational architecture as directional and asymmetric in all three interface directions (God→human, human→God, human→human), with a structural requirement that receiving precedes giving. The key synthesis across T4: (a) God-to-human direction is the most extensively evidenced and is the source of mercy in all other directions; (b) human-to-God direction is characterised by normative ongoing supplication — not exceptional crisis-response; (c) human-to-human direction requires prior receipt from God and solidarity-knowledge of the condition being addressed; (d) mercy operates characteristically across relational distance and rupture (Q&A-117), not within maintained relationships; (e) the scope is wide (crossing covenantal boundaries) but not unconditionally permanent (withdrawal is named possibility). The T4 synthesis: mercy's relational architecture is an asymmetric chain — divine mercy → received human mercy → extended human mercy — with the chain requiring the prior link at each stage.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-004: T4 reveals the most structurally developed relational architecture for compassion's scope. God's compassion operates simultaneously on three bases: sovereignly free (Rom 9:15 — "I will have compassion…
findings.finding_value: T4 reveals the most structurally developed relational architecture for compassion's scope. God's compassion operates simultaneously on three bases: sovereignly free (Rom 9:15 — "I will have compassion on whom I have compassion"), covenantally grounded (chesed as the bond-loyalty that grounds the characteristic), and situationally responsive (splanchnizō — triggered by the specific sight of suffering). These three bases are not in tension but in integration: divine compassion is free, covenanted, and responsive simultaneously. The scope finding is among the most analytically significant in the registry: compassion explicitly and repeatedly crosses covenantal boundaries (Nineveh, the Samaritan/Jew axis, the power-asymmetric relationship). Scope is defined by perceived need, not moral standing or covenantal membership — this is formally confirmed in the data and distinguishes compassion from many other relational characteristics. The chesed/splanchnizō distinction maps onto distinct relational registers: chesed sustains within established bonds; splanchnizō extends across distance and difference. T4.4 (receiver's inner-being experience) is the most significant gap — four P-rated prompts, entirely absent from the data. T4.6 (spiritual beings interface) is entirely silent across all four prompts.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-010: T1's scope finding (compassion requires a suffering other; scope is determined by perceived need, not moral standing) is precisely confirmed in T4's relational analysis. The explicit crossing of coven…
findings.finding_value: T1's scope finding (compassion requires a suffering other; scope is determined by perceived need, not moral standing) is precisely confirmed in T4's relational analysis. The explicit crossing of covenantal boundaries (Nineveh, Samaritan/Jew) evidenced in T4 is the relational expression of T1's boundary-definition: compassion ends where the condition (pitiable need) is absent, not where covenantal membership ends. T1's four modes of operation (T1.4) — intra-covenantal, cross-boundary, anticipatory, Christological — map onto T4's chesed/splanchnizō distinction (within-bond sustaining vs across-distance extending) and the scope analysis (covenantal and transcovenantal registers). Definition and relational scope are structurally co-determining.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-015: T2's constitutional origin analysis (somatic-relational-covenantal triple ground) and T4's relational direction analysis are structurally aligned. The somatic origin (womb, gut) grounds the cross-boun…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional origin analysis (somatic-relational-covenantal triple ground) and T4's relational direction analysis are structurally aligned. The somatic origin (womb, gut) grounds the cross-boundary relational direction in T4: splanchnizō's somatic immediacy is precisely what enables it to cross covenantal boundaries — the gut-movement toward the suffering other precedes any covenantal assessment of the relationship. The covenantal origin (chesed) grounds the within-bond sustaining direction in T4. The constitutional origin therefore predicts the relational direction: somatic = cross-boundary; covenantal = within-bond. T2's soul-body interface classification explains T4's scope-by-need finding: because compassion originates at the soul-body interface (before covenantal-rational assessment), its scope is determined by the pre-rational recognition of need rather than the post-rational assessment of covenantal standing.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-019: T3's perceptive-trigger finding (compassion is activated by sight — splanchnizō is perceptively dependent) and T4's scope-by-need finding (scope is determined by perceived need, not covenantal standin…
findings.finding_value: T3's perceptive-trigger finding (compassion is activated by sight — splanchnizō is perceptively dependent) and T4's scope-by-need finding (scope is determined by perceived need, not covenantal standing) are the same finding from two analytical perspectives. T3 names the faculty (perception) and its function (triggering compassion by seeing the pitiable condition); T4 names the relational consequence (scope defined by what is seen). The cross-boundary extension in T4 (Nineveh, Samaritan/Jew) is the relational expression of T3's merit-independence: compassion is perceptively dependent (it must see the need) but merit-independent (it does not assess the moral standing of the one seen). The three relational modes in T3.11 (building/sustaining, restoring/repairing, extending across difference) correspond precisely to T4's chesed/splanchnizō/cross-boundary structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-023: T4's finding that divine compassion operates on three simultaneous bases (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, cove…
findings.finding_value: T4's finding that divine compassion operates on three simultaneous bases (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological) are structurally isomorphic. The sovereignly-free basis corresponds to the encounter/sudden mechanism: divine compassion operating freely produces the sudden compassion-event (splanchnizō). The covenantally-grounded basis corresponds to the covenantal-sustaining mechanism: chesed as the sustaining relational ground operates gradually and consistently. The situationally-responsive basis opens toward the participatory-ontological mechanism: formation at the deepest constitutional level produces a person who is dispositionally responsive to every situation of need. T4's relational architecture and T5's formation mechanisms are the same structural reality described from relational and developmental perspectives respectively.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-024: T4's scope-by-need finding (compassion crosses covenantal boundaries) and T6's co-occurrence landscape (the human-response cluster — peace, faith, will, surrender — co-occurring with compassion) revea…
findings.finding_value: T4's scope-by-need finding (compassion crosses covenantal boundaries) and T6's co-occurrence landscape (the human-response cluster — peace, faith, will, surrender — co-occurring with compassion) reveal a structural pattern: divine compassion reaching across boundaries generates a characteristic cluster of human inner-being responses regardless of the covenantal position of the recipient. The Nineveh response (repentance and turning) and the pattern of peace/faith/will/surrender co-occurring with compassion both confirm this: compassion-received generates a recognisable inner-being response cluster that is structurally consistent across relational positions. T6's mapping of the human-response cluster is the co-occurrence evidence for T4's structural finding about scope and response.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-025: T4's three bases of divine compassion (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) are each grounded in specific textual evidence from T7. The sovereignly-free basis is evidence…
findings.finding_value: T4's three bases of divine compassion (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) are each grounded in specific textual evidence from T7. The sovereignly-free basis is evidenced in Rom 9:15 (T7's argument structure analysis — divine compassion as sovereign determination). The covenantally-grounded basis is evidenced in Exod 34:6 (T7's most multiply-anchored verse — the divine self-declaration in the covenant context). The situationally-responsive basis is evidenced in the Synoptic splanchnizō pattern (T7.2 — the sight-event structure of the Gospels). T7's framework divergences (sovereignty vs automaticity) map directly onto T4's relational analysis: the framework correctly identifies that divine compassion's sovereign freedom (T4.1) is what exceeds the natural empathic automaticity that human science frameworks describe.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-004: T4 establishes the most precisely articulated relational architecture of any characteristic in the review set. The God-to-human direction is primary and dominant (groups 888-001, 889-001, 5471-001 — a…
findings.finding_value: T4 establishes the most precisely articulated relational architecture of any characteristic in the review set. The God-to-human direction is primary and dominant (groups 888-001, 889-001, 5471-001 — all God-as-subject). The basis of divine extension is the giver's character and prior knowing (Exo 33:17 — "I know you by name"), not the receiver's merit — neither merit-based nor arbitrary. The human-to-God direction is specifically supplication: tachanum (H8469) is the receiving side's corresponding vocabulary built into the same root family as the giving side (chen/chanan) — the vocabulary embeds the two-directional circuit in a single root. The human-giving direction extends grace horizontally through three modes: forgiving (charizō — Eph 4:32), gracious conduct (chen as character quality — 889-003), and gracious speech (SD022). The receiving direction is the most underexamined (T4.4 — P-rated throughout); the scope analysis (T4.5) reveals grace crossing covenantal and social boundaries (Ruth narrative — grace in the context of foreign status and vulnerability). T4.6 (spiritual beings) is evidenced at one point: Luk 1:28 (kecharitōmenē — the angel's announcement), which implies angelic ministry as a vehicle of grace rather than grace operating independently in the spiritual-beings register. T4 synthesis: the relational architecture of grace is unique in the programme — it is the only characteristic where the giving-side vocabulary and the receiving-side vocabulary are built from the same root (chen/tachanum), encoding the grace-circuit's two-sidedness at the lexical level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-010: T1's four modes of operation map onto T4's four relational directions. The sovereign-bestowal mode corresponds to the God-to-human direction (T4.1 — primary and dominant). The covenantal-relational-su…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes of operation map onto T4's four relational directions. The sovereign-bestowal mode corresponds to the God-to-human direction (T4.1 — primary and dominant). The covenantal-relational-sustaining mode corresponds to the relational scope (T4.5 — grace operating within and across covenantal boundaries). The capacity-conferring mode corresponds to the human-to-God direction in its supplication register (T4.2 — SD026: grace giving even the capacity to appeal). The character-forming mode corresponds to the human-giving direction (T4.3 — gracious conduct and speech as the horizontal expression of received grace-character). The vocabulary's structural insight (T4 synthesis: giving-side and receiving-side built from the same root, chen/tachanum) explains T1's finding that grace requires the receptor's inner engagement to complete its operation — the vocabulary encodes the two-sidedness because grace is constitutively a two-sided circuit.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-024: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 vers…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T4.2 (the human-to-God supplication direction): seeking is the relational posture, and R140 is the registry that names it. The sequential relationship confirmed in T6.2 (grace precedes and enables faith, repentance, supplication, mourning — SD003, SD006, SD026, SD038) is the causal expression of T4's architectural finding: grace is the enabling condition for every positive human-to-God relational posture. The boundary questions in T6.5 (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-chesed) correspond to T4.5's scope analysis: the characteristics that share grace's scope (particularly love and mercy) are the same characteristics whose relational scope overlaps with grace's at T4.5.

findings.session_b_note: The covenant characteristic is inherently a boundary-creating reality — it operates by establishing and maintaining the boundary between those who are within the covenant and those who are outside. (1) The boundary is constitutive: covenant defines who belongs ("you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples" — Exo 19:5; "you are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant" — Act 3:25; "Israel, and to them belong... the covenants" — Rom 9:4). The covenantal community is defined by the covenant boundary. (2) The boundary is not permanent for outsiders — it can be crossed through covenant-entry: "foreigners who join themselves to the Lord... and hold fast my covenant" (Isa 56:6 — Group 765-002 context) are included. The new covenant is explicit about this: "all the families of the earth" (Act 3:25), "in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek" (Gal 3:28 context). (3) The new covenant specifically crosses the ethnic-cultural-legal boundary of the old covenant's administration: Eph 2:12-14 context — those once "strangers to the covenants of promise" (OBS-034-060) are brought near in Christ. The covenantal boundary is permeable in the new covenant direction.

findings.session_b_note: Both — with a clear movement across the canon from primarily covenantal to universally-extended. OT: most explicit peace-giving is within covenant (Num 6:26 — to Israel; Isa 54:10 — to the covenant people; Psa 85:8 — to "his saints"). However: Jer 29:7 (seeking welfare of the exile city), Isa 52:7/Nah 1:15 (peace proclaimed to nations), Zec 9:10 (messianic king speaking peace to the nations) — peace crosses covenantal boundaries in the OT prophets. NT: Eph 2:14-16 — Christ makes peace between Jew and Gentile, creating one body; G1515 group 426-002 — apostolic peace-blessing in every letter extends to Gentile recipients; Col 1:20 ("all things, whether on earth or in heaven") — the scope of cosmic peace-making is universal. The trajectory: covenant-primary → covenant-expansive → universally offered through Christ.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-117-004: T4 establishes two key relational findings: (1) Peace's scope expands progressively — covenant-primary (to Israel, Num 6:26) → covenant-expansive (to nations in the prophets, Isa 57:19) → universally …
findings.finding_value: T4 establishes two key relational findings: (1) Peace's scope expands progressively — covenant-primary (to Israel, Num 6:26) → covenant-expansive (to nations in the prophets, Isa 57:19) → universally offered through Christ (Eph 2:14, Col 1:20) — with the only sustained exclusion being moral ("no peace for the wicked"). The covenantal boundaries are overcome in Christ; the moral boundary remains. (2) Peace is a site of cosmic contest: angelic mediation of peace is effective (Dan 10:19), elemental disruption of peace is real (Mar 4:39), and eschatological removal of peace is documented (Rev 6:4). Peace is not only a private inner condition but a publicly contested reality across the cosmic order.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-003: T1 names peace as integrative wholeness; T4 shows its relational structure is not incidental but constitutive. The peace-wholeness of T1 is not achievable in isolation — it is given by God (T4.1), ori…
findings.finding_value: T1 names peace as integrative wholeness; T4 shows its relational structure is not incidental but constitutive. The peace-wholeness of T1 is not achievable in isolation — it is given by God (T4.1), oriented toward God (T4.2), extended toward others (T4.3), and contested cosmically (T4.6). The interiority (T1) and the relationality (T4) are co-constitutive (confirmed from T3.11.3): the person at peace is the person in right relation — with God, with others, and with themselves. T4's expanding scope (covenant → universal) maps onto T1's eschatological dimension (the peace that has no end, Isa 9:7): the scope expands toward the same fullness that the essence reaches toward.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-017: T4's God-to-human direction and T6's causal sequences describe the same reality at different levels of abstraction. T4.1 (God gives peace through covenant/Christ/Spirit) is the relational description …
findings.finding_value: T4's God-to-human direction and T6's causal sequences describe the same reality at different levels of abstraction. T4.1 (God gives peace through covenant/Christ/Spirit) is the relational description of what T6.3.2 catalogues as causal inputs (trust, righteousness, discipline, Spirit, confession, love of law all produce peace). The covenant-of-peace (T4.1 — Isa 54:10) is the relational framework for what T6.4.2 names as the SHA.L root shared between peace and covenant at the structural level. The two analyses are not parallel but nested: T4 names the relational direction; T6 names the structural mechanism through which that direction operates.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-018: T4's relational scope findings (peace given to Israel → expanding to nations → universal in Christ) are lexically grounded in T7's vocabulary arc. The greeting-blessing (H7965K, T4.3 — human giving of…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational scope findings (peace given to Israel → expanding to nations → universal in Christ) are lexically grounded in T7's vocabulary arc. The greeting-blessing (H7965K, T4.3 — human giving of peace) has its person-type lexical ground in T7.1.6 (ish sha.lom — the man of peace as person-type). The absence of a dedicated antonym term (T7.1.5) confirms T4's finding that peace is primarily defined by its presence and relational giving, not by its absence — the vocabulary is positive-directional, matching the God-to-human direction of peace's primary flow (T4.1). The NT coinage eirēnopoieō (T7.1.9) names what T4.1.2 describes as the basis of God's peace-giving through Christ — the cross-accomplishment has its own unique verbal form precisely because it is a unique relational act.

findings.session_b_note: Primarily within covenantal contexts but with boundary-crossing capacity through mediation. The dominant mode (872-001) is explicitly covenantal. However, the compassionate giving (872-002) includes instances where the relational basis is need rather than formal covenant: Leah's condition (Gen 29:33) is within the covenant community but the giving is responsive to her individual inner suffering, not to her covenant membership per se. Isa 61:3 addresses "those who mourn in Zion" — the covenantal community, but the giving is to the condition of mourning, not to a specific covenant transaction. Isa 42:6 — "a covenant for the people, a light for the nations" — the servant mediates the giving beyond the covenant boundary. The characteristic operates primarily within covenant but is not constitutionally limited to it.

findings.finding_value: M01-A crosses covenantal boundaries. The Gen 20:11 material (Abraham assuming absence of God-fear in Gerar's people — implying fear-of-God is expected in non-Israelites), Act 10:35 ("anyone who fears God and does what is right is acceptable to him regardless of nationality"), and the nations-fearing-God material (Psa 102:15; Isa 25:3; Rev 14:7; 19:5) all show that reverential fear of God is not limited to covenant members. God demands and expects it of all peoples; the goal is universal fear-of-God (Mal 1:14: "God's name will evoke genuine reverent fear among all nations").

M01-C and M01-A-VCG-07 show God deploying fear across covenantal boundaries as a historical governance instrument: God instilling fear of Israel in surrounding nations, God producing fear in Egyptian overseers at the Exodus. The covenantal-cross operation is explicit.
