**[CHAR-1]** E — It crosses covenantal boundaries in at least one clear instance (Jethro, Exo 18:9) and in the cosmic-rejoicing passages (Psa 96:11; 97:1 — the whole earth and its coastlands called to rejoice). The eschatological passages (Isa 66:10 calling "all who love Jerusalem") also suggest a scope broader than ethnic Israel. Exultation is covenantally grounded but not covenantally restricted in its ultimate scope.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Joy crosses covenantal boundaries: Luk 2:10 — "good news of great joy that will be for all the people" — the gospel joy is for all peoples; Act 13:48 (Gentiles rejoicing at the word of eternal life — covenantal outsiders receiving gospel Joy); Psa 67:4 ("let the nations be glad and sing for joy") — all nations called to Joy; the cosmic-rejoicing passages (Psa 96:11; 97:1) call all creation to Joy. The Deuteronomic feast-joy includes sojourners and the vulnerable (Deu 16:11, 14) — crossing social and ethnic boundaries within Israel. Joy is covenantally grounded but universally offered in its eschatological fullness.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The agalliao corpus is primarily new-covenant: the characteristic in its Spirit-enabled form operates within the covenant community of faith (the persecuted disciples, the apostles, the Petrine communities). Act 16:34 (the Philippian jailer — a Roman, not an Israelite) shows the characteristic crossing covenantal-ethnic boundaries: Suffering-Joy is given through faith regardless of covenant background. Joh 8:56 (Abraham's anticipatory agalliao) is OT-covenant-located but anticipates Christ's day — making it typologically covenant-crossing.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Gladness crosses covenantal boundaries: Exo 18:17 (Jethro, a Midianite, exercising accurate evaluative-gladness toward Moses); Rut 2:22 (Naomi assessing Ruth's best course — a Moabite within Israel's covenant community); 2Sa 18:27 (Achish's moral assessment of David's blamelessness — a Philistine king exercising the evaluative-gladness faculty). The evaluative-gladness faculty is not covenantally restricted; it is a human-image-bearing capacity that operates wherever persons make moral assessments. The doxological and covenantal registers are more specifically covenant-shaped.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Delight crosses covenantal boundaries in specific instances: (1) **M04-H-VCG-03's diplomatic idiom** — non-Israelite kings (Abimelech — Gen 20:15; Achish — 1Sa 29:6) and non-covenant contexts (the Esther/Nehemiah court of Persia) use the Delight-vocabulary for practical preference — the capacity for directed inner pleasure is pan-human; (2) **1Th 2:8** (Paul's Delight in Gentile believers) — crosses the Jew-Gentile boundary through the new covenant; (3) **Rom 15:26–27** (Macedonia and Achaia's Delight in contributing to Jerusalem's poor) — cross-ethnic new-covenant Delight. The corrupt register (M04-P) crosses any boundary — Eze 23:12's lustful Delight in Assyrians crosses national and covenant lines destructively.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The worship-Pleasure (ni.cho.ach) is explicitly bounded by covenant: Lev 26:31 (withheld from the unfaithful); Eze 20:41 (restored after regathering). However, Num 15:14 shows the worship-Pleasure accessible to any who follow the prescribed form, crossing ethnic boundaries. The relational-Pleasure register (M04-J) is not covenant-restricted — the pleasantness of wisdom's ways (Pro 3:17), gracious speech (Pro 16:24), and communal harmony (Psa 133:1) are available wherever wisdom is practiced and genuine agreeableness exists.

**[CHAR-6]** E — No — Wonder crosses covenantal boundaries in the missional proclamation register. Psa 107:24's seafarers who saw God's wondrous works in the deep are not necessarily Israelites — the sea-rescue wonders in Psa 107 are available to all who encounter divine rescue. Exo 34:10's "all the people among whom you are" explicitly includes non-Israelites as witnesses. The marvellous works in VCG-02's "is anything too hard for the Lord?" (Gen 18:14; Jer 32:17, 27) are directed at universal divine capability, not covenantal restriction.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All seven cross covenantal boundaries, but with different reach: (1) **Most boundary-crossing**: Wonder (Char 6) — Psa 107:24's non-Israelite seafarers; Exo 34:10's non-Israelite observers; 1Ch 16:24's "all peoples"; Joy (Char 2) — Luk 2:10 ("for all the people"); Psa 67:4 (nations invited to Joy); (2) **Crosses boundaries in their pan-human capacity**: Gladness (Char 3) — the evaluative faculty operates wherever persons make moral assessments (Jethro, Exo 18:17; Achish, 1Sa 29:9; Rut); (3) **Crosses boundaries through new-covenant faith**: Suffering-Joy (Char 7) — Act 16:34's Roman jailer; (4) **Partially bounded**: Pleasure (Char 5) — the ni.cho.ach worship register is covenant-conditioned; but the relational and wisdom registers (M04-J) are not covenant-restricted; (5) **Bounded in primary register, universal in scope**: Exultation (Char 1) — covenantally primary but the cosmic-rejoicing passages (Psa 96:11; 97:1) have universal scope. The cluster as a whole is covenantally grounded but not covenantally restricted in its ultimate eschatological scope.

**[CHAR-1]** E — CHAR-1 crosses covenantal boundaries. The psalmist's enemies experience shame; Edom is covered with shame (Obd 10); Babylon's gods are put to shame (Jer 50:2) — these are not covenantal contexts. God's judicial deployment of shame against opponents crosses covenantal boundaries freely. What is covenantally specific is the *corrective and restorative* mode of shame: the commands to "be ashamed" in Eze 16:52; 36:32; 43:10 are directed at God's covenant people specifically, not universally. Corrective shame as gateway to renewed relationship appears to operate within the covenantal context, while judicial shame as consequence operates universally.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 operates both within existing bonds (David's king offering compassion to humiliated envoys) and across bonds (military opponents humiliating nations, God humbling the proud). The divine-abasement mode (VCG-03) is universal — God's corrective humiliation of pride crosses all covenantal boundaries. CHAR-2's scope is not covenantally limited.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — The head-covering material (1Cor 11:4-5) operates within the covenant community. Jam 2:6's dishonoring of the poor operates within the community of believers. The dishonoring of Jesus (Joh 8:49) crosses the covenant community's internal boundary. CHAR-3 appears to operate most damagingly within existing relational bonds where worth-recognition is expected and violated.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 operates within community contexts (VCG-01: the shameful conduct of speech in the assembly, the shameful hair practices — all community-embedded evaluations) and within covenantal contexts (the idolatrous shameful-objects of Jer 3:24; 11:13 are specifically about Israel's covenantal infidelity). VCG-02 (disordered passions) crosses community boundaries — Rom 1:26-27 addresses a pattern of moral disorder that is cultural-historical in scope.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — The commands against despising (Rom 14:3; 14:10; 1Cor 16:11; 1Th 5:20) operate within the covenant community. The Boaz-Ruth protection (Rut 2:15, vc=38516) operates across covenantal difference: Boaz protects Ruth, an outsider, from the contempt she would normally receive. The 1Sa 25:7/15 (vc=38530/38531) protection of Nabal's shepherds operates within a social context of armed men restraining themselves. CHAR-5's scope is not covenantally limited — contempt can cross any relational boundary; what is covenantally specific is the community's obligation to protect against contempt within its own relational field.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 operates specifically within the covenant relationship between the person and God: the approach to God's altar (Psa 26:6) is a covenantal act; the divine confirmation of innocence (Gen 20:6) is a covenantal response; the incapacity for innocence (Hos 8:5) is a covenantal failure condition. CHAR-6's scope is specifically covenantal-relational: it is the inner moral condition that the covenant relationship with God requires of the person.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's relational scope shows a consistent pattern: the destructive characteristics (unjust shame, contempt, dishonour) cross covenantal boundaries freely — they can fall on anyone. The constructive characteristics (corrective shame, conscience-activated moral evaluation, innocence-enabled approach) are more covenantally specific. Exceptions: Char 2's God-abasing act crosses all covenantal boundaries (God humbles all pride); Char 5's divine reversal is explicitly extended universally (1Cor 1:28 — God choosing the world's despised). Within the covenant community, specific obligations apply: protect the vulnerable from contempt (Char 5 — Rut 2:15; 1Cor 16:11), honour the worth of all members (Char 3 — Jam 2:6), exercise corrective shame with proper moral grounding (Char 1's entrepō; Char 4). These community-internal obligations are the cluster's most directly applicable finding for relational ethics.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — CHAR-1 crosses covenantal boundaries consistently. Within Israel's covenant: Amo 6:8 (vc=34002, M08-A3-VCG-03) — "I abhor the pride of Jacob"; Hos 5:5 (vc=34000, M08-A3-VCG-03) — "the pride of Israel testifies to his face." Outside the covenant: Isa 16:6 (vc=33989, M08-A3-VCG-01) — Moab's pride; Isa 13:19 (vc=33987, M08-A3-VCG-02) — Babylon's pride. NT evidence confirms the trans-covenantal scope: Rom 1:30 (vc=33932, M08-A4-VCG-01) — haughtiness as a vice of a morally disordered mind generally; 2Ti 3:2 (vc=33933, M08-A4-VCG-01) — arrogance as a characteristic of "people" in the last days without covenantal limitation. Isa 2:12 (vc=33957, M08-A3-VCG-04) addresses "all that is proud and lofty" universally. CHAR-1 is a universal human characteristic whose divine assessment and consequence are consistent regardless of covenantal status.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 crosses covenantal boundaries. Within covenant: Israel's repeated presumption (Deu 1:43; Neh 9:16/29), the false prophet from within Israel (Deu 18:20), the presumptuous judge-defier from within Israel's community (Deu 17:12). Outside covenant: Pharaoh/Egypt (Exo 18:11, vc=34121; Neh 9:10), Babylon (Jer 50:29, vc=34127; Jer 50:31, vc=34116). NT: self-willed false teachers and domineering leaders without covenantal qualification (2Pe 2:10; Tit 1:7). CHAR-2 is a universal human characteristic not limited to covenantal context.

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 crosses covenantal boundaries. Within covenant: Rom 2:17/23 (vc=33882/33883, M08-C-VCG-01) — boasting in the Law from within Jewish covenantal identity. Outside covenant: 1Jo 2:16 (vc=33865, M08-C-VCG-01): "the pride of life" (alazoneia) as a worldly disposition without covenantal qualification. Rom 1:30 (vc=33867): alazōn in a universal vice catalogue. The NT examines CHAR-3 across both Jewish-covenantal and Gentile-universal contexts.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The 12-verse §3.C corpus is entirely from Pauline NT communities (1Cor, 2Cor, Col, Rom, 1Ti, 2Ti). There is no Hebrew OT evidence in CHAR-4's corpus. Within the NT corpus, CHAR-4 is evidenced across multiple communities (Corinthian — 1Cor/2Cor; Roman — Rom 12:3; Colossian — Col 2:18; Pastoral — 1Ti/2Ti). The evidence addresses Christian community contexts without restricting CHAR-4 to a specific covenantal framework — Rom 12:3 addresses believers in general.

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 crosses all covenantal boundaries, evidenced across: Israel (Lev 26:19, vc=33982; Eze 33:28, vc=33999), Sodom (Eze 16:49, vc=33979), Egypt (Eze 30:6–32:12, M08-E-VCG-01), Tyre (Eze 28:5, vc=34046), Edom (Jer 49:16, vc=34167; Obd 3, vc=65674), Babylon (Isa 47:8, vc=9563; Jer 51:53, vc=65670), Judah/Eze 19:11 rulers (vc=54398), and the wealthy in NT communities (1Ti 6:17, vc=60878). CHAR-5 is the M08 characteristic most extensively evidenced across different national and cultural contexts — its structural-power medium operates wherever power and wealth exist.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All five characteristics cross covenantal boundaries. The cluster comparison reveals that M08 is one of the most universal clusters in the programme — it is evidenced within the covenant (Israel's pride: CHAR-1, CHAR-2, CHAR-5) and outside it (Egypt, Moab, Babylon, Edom: CHAR-1, CHAR-5; Gentile vice catalogues: CHAR-2, CHAR-3, CHAR-4). 1Pe 5:5 (M08-A4-VCG-01) and Jam 4:6 (M08-A4-VCG-01) — "God opposes the proud" — are addressed universally without covenantal qualification. Pro 16:5 (M08-A1-VCG-03) — "everyone who is arrogant in heart" — establishes universal scope. The cluster-synthesis: M08 is a universal-human cluster — its characteristics are evidenced across all persons, peoples, and periods without covenantal limitation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries. Gen49:10 — "the obedience of the peoples" (all nations) — the submission characteristic is framed as gathering all peoples, not only Israel. Rom1:5 — "obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations" — the scope is universal. Pro30:17 — obedience to parents as a creational-wisdom principle, not specifically covenantal. The characteristic operates within covenant but also extends to universal scope in its eschatological and wisdom dimensions.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The generalising language of both verses (Psa34:18 — general wisdom-type statement; Isa57:15 — general address) suggests the characteristic may operate across covenantal contexts rather than being restricted to the covenant people. The God who is near to "the brokenhearted" is not specifying Israelites only. However, both verses arise within the OT canonical context which has Israel as its primary frame, so a definitive cross-covenantal claim requires caution from this corpus alone.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Heb5:2 operates within the covenantal-priestly structure. Act9:38 operates within the early Christian community. The evidence is covenantal in frame. However, the generalising quality of metriopatheō (measured-compassionate restraint toward the erring) as an inner capacity suggests it may operate beyond specifically covenantal contexts wherever the person encounters the ignorant and wayward — the capacity is not inherently limited to covenant insiders.

**[CHAR-5]** E — 1Ti2:2 — "a peaceful and quiet life under good governance" in public civic life — the characteristic is called for in the public civic sphere which is not narrowly covenantal. The characteristic thus crosses the covenantal boundary into the broader civic sphere, where the believer's semnotēs shapes their manner of inhabiting public life. Tit2:7's teaching context and 1Ti3:4's household context are community-formational, while 1Ti2:2's civic context is broader.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The five-verse corpus is exclusively within covenantal contexts: the Israel covenant community (Exo35; 1Ch28:21; 2Ch29:31) and the individual covenant-member's relation to God (Psa51:12). The characteristic as evidenced in §3.E operates within the covenant rather than across covenantal boundaries. The generalising principle of free-will offering may extend beyond the covenantal context, but the direct evidence is covenantal.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The primary evidence is covenantal (Israel before God; believers in the body). However, the exaltation-of-the-humble pattern (Luk1:52 — "he has exalted those of humble estate") and the wisdom connexion (Pro11:2 — structural contrast available to any person) operate as wisdom-principles that appear cross-covenantal in their scope. The characteristic's operation is most extensively evidenced in the covenantal context, but its wisdom-principle dimension suggests it operates beyond those boundaries.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's covenantal scope varies systematically. *Most explicitly covenantal* (operating primarily within the Israel or new covenant community): CHAR-3 Contrition (both verses — OT covenant community context) and CHAR-6 Willing-heartedness (exclusively covenantal contexts in its five-verse corpus). *Crosses covenantal boundaries most explicitly*: CHAR-2 Submission — Gen49:10 (all peoples' submission to the coming ruler) and Rom1:5/16:26 (obedience of faith among all nations) are explicitly universal in scope. *Operates in the public civic sphere beyond the covenant community*: CHAR-5 Dignity — 1Ti2:2 situates semnotēs in the believer's civic existence under governance, crossing the narrowly covenantal boundary. *Wisdom-principle basis potentially cross-covenantal*: CHAR-1 (Psa107:12 — generalising wisdom-statement; Pro11:2 — cross-cultural wisdom principle). CHAR-4: the scope of the erring (the "ignorant and wayward" of Heb5:2) is not explicitly covenantal. Cluster-level: CHAR-2 has the widest covenantal scope (universal — all nations); CHAR-3 and CHAR-6 have the narrowest (exclusively covenantal). The cluster thus spans from universal eschatological scope (CHAR-2) to covenant-interior (CHAR-3, CHAR-6).

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries. VCG-01 is primarily covenantal (Israel sinning against the Lord — the covenant framework defines the sin). But VCG-02 includes sinning across non-covenantal boundaries: Gen 20:9 (Abraham sinning against Abimelech — a pagan king outside the covenant); Gen 42:22 (Joseph — a Hebrew sinned against by his brothers before the Sinai covenant). Mat 18:15/21 (community of disciples context — a new covenant setting). The characteristic is not confined to the Mosaic covenant but operates wherever relational bonds and moral claims exist. Eze 18:4/20 (individual soul-level accountability) operates without covenantal specification.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The mechanisms cross covenantal boundaries. Enticement (Jam 1:14; 2Pe 2:14/18) applies universally — "each person is tempted" (Jam 1:14) — regardless of covenant membership. Hypocrisy (Gal 2:13) operates within the covenantal community (Jewish believers) but its principle applies beyond covenant boundaries. Apostasy (Act 21:21) is specifically covenantal in this instance (forsaking Moses), but the apostasia root applies to any covenantal-standing departure.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The condition crosses all covenantal boundaries. Rom 3:9 — "all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin" — the foundational statement that the condition is not restricted to those outside the covenant; Rom 2:12 — "all who have sinned without the law will perish... all who have sinned under the law will be judged" — whether under the law (covenant) or not, the condition applies and produces judgment. The universal scope of the condition (Rom 3:23 — "all have sinned") is not qualified by covenantal membership.

**[CHAR-12]** E — The enslaving power crosses all boundaries. Joh 8:34 — "everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin" — "everyone" is universal, not restricted to covenant membership. Gal 3:22 — "imprisoned everything under sin" — the "everything" encompasses all persons regardless of covenantal standing. 1Jo 3:8 — "whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil" — "whoever" is universal. The enslaving power is not covenantally bounded; it holds all who practice sin regardless of identity or membership.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The record crosses all covenantal boundaries. Gen 18:20 — Sodom (outside the covenant) has a sin-record before God; Amo 5:12 — "I know how many are your transgressions" is addressed to Israel within the covenant; Rom 3:25 — "former sins" encompassed all humanity in divine forbearance. The divine record is not covenantally bounded: every person, in every relationship with or without the covenant, stands with a sin-record before God. What differs across the covenantal boundary is the specific content of the record (covenant-specific obligations generating covenant-specific entries) rather than the record's existence.

**[CHAR-14]** E — The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries in the NT register. Act 10:43 — "everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name" — "everyone" in context (Cornelius the Gentile) explicitly crosses the Jewish-covenant boundary; Mar 3:28 — "all sins will be forgiven the children of man" — "children of man" (sons of Adam) is a universal human category, not a covenantal one; 2Cor 5:19 — "God was reconciling the world to himself" — "the world" is the broadest possible scope. The OT register (VCG-01/03) operates primarily within the covenant community; the NT register explicitly extends to all who believe.

**[CHAR-15]** S — The 8-verse corpus addresses generational sin exclusively within the covenant community of Israel (Isa 43:27 — "your first father"; Psa 78:17/32 — Israel in the wilderness; 1Ki 8:47 — the exiles; Jer 8:14 — Judah; Eze 37:23 — Israel). No verse in the corpus explicitly extends the generational mechanism beyond the covenant community. The question of whether generational sin operates across covenantal boundaries (e.g. in non-Israelite lineages) cannot be answered from this corpus.

**[CHAR-16]** E — The sinner-identity crosses covenantal boundaries. Gal 2:15 — "Gentile sinners" — the label applies to those outside the Jewish covenant. Gen 13:13 — Sodom (outside Israel's covenant) bears the sinner-identity. 1Sa 15:18 — the Amalekites (outside Israel's covenant) are designated sinners by God. Mat 9:10/11 — "tax collectors and sinners" spans Jewish and social categories. The sinner-as-moral-character is not a covenantally bounded category: it applies wherever sinfulness defines a person's moral identity, regardless of covenant membership.

**[CHAR-17]** E — The characteristic operates primarily within covenant contexts (VCG-01's Levitical sequences; VCG-02's accumulation in Israel; VCG-03's priestly transference; VCG-04's punitive consequence in Israel/Judah). However, it also crosses covenantal boundaries: Gen 4:13 — Cain's guilt before God precedes the formal covenant; Gen 42:21 — the brothers' guilt toward Joseph involves inter-personal guilt without explicit covenantal framing; Hab 1:11 — "guilty men, whose own might is their god" — the Babylonian armies bear guilt outside Israel's covenant. The guilt-state is not exclusively covenantal.

**[CHAR-18]** E — The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries. Gen 15:16 — the Amorites (outside Israel's covenant) accumulate iniquity before God; Jer 25:12 — Babylon's iniquity is measured and punished; Eze 28:18 — "the multitude of your iniquities" is addressed to the king of Tyre (outside Israel's covenant). The characteristic is universal in scope: Psa 130:3 — "if you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?" — the universality implies all persons, not merely covenant members, accumulate iniquity before God.

**[CHAR-19]** E — The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries extensively. VCG-03's Amos oracle-series (Amos 1:3–2:6) covers eight nations including six outside Israel's covenant: Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab all accumulate transgression that reaches God's threshold. Dan 8:23 — "when transgressors have reached their limit" — a non-Israelite (Seleucid) context. The parabasis-family NT verses (VCG-04) apply to all law-knowers regardless of ethnic covenant membership (Rom 2:23/25/27 — the law-boaster and the law-keeper, Jew and Gentile).

**[CHAR-2]** E — The primary CHAR-2 evidence base is covenantal throughout: Lev 4:2 and Num 15:27/28 address sinning in the context of Israel's covenant with the Lord. Num 22:34 (Balaam) represents a non-Israelite encountering the characteristic — suggesting that the principle extends beyond the Sinai covenant to any context where God's moral reality intersects with creaturely epistemic limitation. Balaam is not an Israelite under the Mosaic covenant, yet his inadvertent sinning (not knowing the angel stood against him) follows the same pattern of inadvertence → disclosure → confession → offer of reversal. The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries in its logic, even if the prescribed Levitical remedies are specific to the covenant context.

**[CHAR-20]** E — Primarily within covenantal contexts — unlike CHAR-19 (which operated universally across all nations in the Amos oracle-series), CHAR-20 is more bounded by the covenant-relationship as its definitional context. Judg 9:23 — the leaders of Shechem dealing treacherously with Abimelech — a non-explicitly covenantal political context; Hab 1:13 — traitors who swallow up the righteous — a general moral context. These indicate the characteristic can cross beyond explicit covenant contexts into any context where loyalty was owed, but the primary domain is covenantal.

**[CHAR-21]** E — The characteristic crosses all boundaries. Lev 18:23/20:12 (VCG-04) — the sexual perversions apply universally regardless of covenant; Deu 16:19 — bribery-perversion of judgment is addressed to Israel's covenant courts but the principle applies universally; 1Cor 15:33 — "bad company ruins good morals" — a universal principle; Rev 19:2 — Babylon's corruption of the whole earth — crosses all covenantal and non-covenantal contexts. CHAR-21 is universal in scope: any human moral faculty can be twisted regardless of covenant membership.

**[CHAR-22]** E — The characteristic crosses all boundaries. VCG-01's universal Levitical commands (Lev 19:15/35) apply to all Israel regardless of specific relational context; Deu 25:16 — "all who act dishonestly are an abomination" — universal condemnation; Mat 5:45 — "he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust" — God sustains even the unjust regardless of covenant membership; Rev 18:5 — Babylon's accumulated injustice crosses all covenantal and non-covenantal contexts.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Confession crosses covenantal boundaries. Pharaoh's confessions (Exo 9:27/10:16) are confessions by a non-covenant party to the covenant Lord — showing that the confession-form operates across the boundary, even without the covenant relationship that would make it fully operative. Judas (Mat 27:4) confesses to the chief priests — a transactional rather than covenantal relationship. However, the corpus's most substantial and productive confessions are covenantal: the VCG-02 corporate confessions (Judg 10:10; 1Sa 7:6; Dan 9:5) all operate within Israel's covenant framework and produce covenantal renewal. The form crosses the boundary; the full productive effect is covenantal.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries. Ecc 8:12 — "the sinner does evil a hundred times... the absence of the fear of God within" — wisdom literature addresses the human condition generally, not specifically Israel. 1Cor 15:34 — the NT community context. Tit 3:11 — divisive person within a community of faith. The characteristic applies wherever conscience can be suppressed — within and outside the Mosaic covenant structure. The covenantal instances (Jer 2:35; 16:10) are the most fully developed because the moral accountability there is most fully specified, but conscience suppression is a characteristic of human moral failure generically.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The primary corpus is covenantal: Israel's covenant with the Lord is the frame for the Kings corpus and Neh 9:29. However, Rom 6:15 — "are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace?" — extends the characteristic into the new-covenant context: refusing to repent under grace is possible and explicitly rejected. Heb 10:26 — "sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth" — operates in a context where the new covenant's truth has been received. The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries and intensifies within them: the more clearly the covenant's moral requirements are known, the more culpable the refusal to repent.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Habitual defection crosses covenantal boundaries. The Ecclesiastes person-type statements (Ecc 7:26; 9:2/18; Pro 11:31/13:22) address the sinner as a general human type, not specifically as a covenant member. 1Ki 8:46 — "there is no one who does not sin" — universal scope including all humans. The characteristic is covenantally intensified when it operates against the covenant Lord (2Ki 17:7; 1Sa 2:25) but is not confined to the covenantal context: the sinner of wisdom literature is a human type applicable across all moral contexts.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Contagious sin crosses covenantal boundaries. Exo 23:33 and Deu 20:18 address the danger from non-covenantal foreign nations: the Canaanites and their neighbours are not in covenant with Israel or the Lord, yet their sinning influence can transmit through proximity and teaching. The teaching mode (Deu 20:18) requires no prior covenantal bond — proximity and instructional authority are sufficient. The Kings corpus shows contagious sin within the covenant (Israelite kings transmitting to the covenant people). Both registers are present: covenantal-authority transmission (dominant — Kings) and proximity-teaching transmission (pre-entry warning — Exo 23:33; Deu 20:18).

**[CHAR-8]** E — Political revolt crosses covenantal boundaries. Moab's revolt against Israel (2Ki 1:1; 3:5/7) and Edom's revolt against Judah (2Ki 8:20/22; 2Ch 21:8/10) are extra-covenantal: Moab and Edom are not members of the Israelite covenant. The revolt operates in the suzerain-vassal political register regardless of covenantal membership. Israel's revolt from the house of David (1Ki 12:19; 2Ch 10:19) is intra-covenantal. Both registers are present; the covenantal context intensifies the theological weight without being the only context.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Sinful speech crosses covenantal boundaries. VCG-01's slander operates in the general community context (Eph 4:31 — the Ephesian community; Col 3:8). VCG-02's blasphemy-charge occurs within the Jewish covenant context but is directed at Jesus who transcends it. VCG-03's beast-blasphemy (Rev 13:1/5/6) is a cosmic-eschatological context that exceeds any specific covenant — it is universal in scope, directed against God's name, dwelling, and all who dwell in heaven. The characteristic operates across all relational and covenantal contexts without restriction.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries. The Proverbs evidence (VCGs 06, 07, 08, 09) frames wickedness as a universal moral category — the wicked person is addressed as a human type, not specifically as a covenant-community member violating covenant obligations. Job 9:22-24 (VCG-04, 10) frames the wicked as a cosmic category (earth delivered into their hands). The Psalms' structural contrast of wicked vs. righteous is articulated as a fundamental human-moral binary. Mal 3:18 (VCG-02) defines the wicked as those who do not serve God — which applies within and beyond the covenant community. Gen 18:23-25 (VCG-04) frames wickedness and righteousness as universal moral categories in Abraham's dialogue with God about Sodom (a non-covenant city). The characteristic is not covenantally restricted.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries. The baseline constitutional evil (Mat 7:11; Luk 11:13 — VCG-02) is addressed to humans collectively — "you who are evil" — not to covenant community members specifically. Act 17:5 (vc=14452 — VCG-04): wicked men of the rabble — outside the covenant community. Mat 5:45 (vc=14437 — VCG-04): "evil persons" alongside "good" as universal moral categories receiving God's common providence. The characteristic is a universal human constitutional condition, not covenantally bounded. Notably, the Pauline letters address it within the covenant community — Eph 4:31 (VCG-05), Col 3:8 (VCG-05), 1Pe 2:1 (VCG-05) — showing that the characteristic also operates within the covenant community, requiring ongoing address even among believers.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries. The Proverbs evidence (VCGs 01, 02, 03) applies to human moral character generally — the dishonest dealer (Deu 25:16 — VCG-01), the scoffer (Pro 24:9 — VCG-01), and the person with seven abominations in their heart (Pro 26:25 — VCG-02) are moral-character categories that apply universally. Pro 29:27 (vc=65959 — VCG-01): "the unjust man is an abomination to the righteous" — applies to any human community. The NT bdelugma (Luk 16:15; Tit 1:16; Rev 17:4-5; 21:27 — VCG-02/05) also crosses covenantal boundaries: Luk 16:15 is addressed to the Pharisees in a specific religious context but names a principle about divine moral assessment that applies universally. Rev 21:27 is eschatological — applying to all humanity at the end. The characteristic is concentrated in covenantal contexts but not limited to them.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic operates most intensively within the covenantal context — it is a covenantal betrayal (Deu 32:16 — VCG-02: jealousy is provoked within the covenant relationship). The Levitical and Deuteronomic evidence (VCGs 01, 02) is entirely covenantal — laws given to the covenant community. The reform narratives (VCG-03) address the covenant community's kings. The Ezekiel corpus (VCG-05) addresses the covenant people. However, the characteristic also applies to those outside the covenant: the nations' abominable practices (Deu 20:18; 18:9 — VCG-02) are named as abominable even for non-covenant nations — the category of divine revulsion at idolatrous practice is not covenantally bounded. The intensity of the characteristic's expression is concentrated within the covenant relationship (where it constitutes betrayal) but its moral category applies universally.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries. The Psalms' evildoer-class (VCG-03, 24V) addresses iniquity as a universal human category — nations as well as Israel (Psa 59:5 — vc=38242 — VCG-03: "spare none of those who treacherously plot evil" — addressed to nations). Isa 59:7 (vc=38203 — VCG-02): "their feet run to evil" applies universally. The characteristic does have concentrated covenantal expression: Deu 28:20 (VCG-05) addresses Israel specifically; Isa 10:1 (VCG-02) addresses specific Israelite rulers. But the evildoer-type is recognised as a universal inner-character category, not a covenantally bounded one. The characteristic operates most intensively within covenantal contexts (where it constitutes specific betrayal) but is not confined to them.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries. VCG-01 (Rev 16:9/11/21): those cursing God are the general population under eschatological judgment — not specifically the covenant community. Rev 13:6 (VCG-01): the beast's blasphemy is directed at God from a position entirely outside the covenant community. VCG-02: Rom 2:24 (vc=14357 — VCG-02): Gentiles blaspheme God's name because of Jewish believers' moral failure — the characteristic occurs across covenantal boundaries (Gentiles responding to covenant people's failures). VCG-03: 1Pe 2:12 (vc=14377 — VCG-03): Gentile opponents accuse the Christian community — the characteristic crosses from outside to inside the covenant boundary through hostile accusation. The characteristic operates universally across covenantal and non-covenantal contexts.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics cross covenantal boundaries — none is confined to the covenant community. Char 1 (the wicked person is a universal type in Psalms and Proverbs — applied to all nations — Gen 18:23 context). Char 2 (Mat 7:11 — "you who are evil" addressed to general humanity; the cosmic evil framework of VCG-01 extends beyond covenant). Chars 3 and 4 (the nations' abominations named as detestable even for non-covenant nations — Deu 18:9/20:18; Pro 24:9 — scoffer abominable to mankind). Char 5 (the universal evildoer-type in the Psalms applies beyond Israel). Char 6 (Rev 16:9/11/21 — the blasphemers under eschatological judgment are the general population, not the covenant community). The cluster is universally applicable: M10b names inner-being evil conditions that apply to all human persons across covenantal and non-covenantal contexts, with heightened intensity in covenantal contexts (where the evil constitutes specific betrayal).

**[CHAR-1]** E — The system primarily operates within the covenantal context of Israel. However, Num 19:10 (M10c-A-VCG-07) explicitly includes "the stranger who sojourns among them" in the perpetual statute for corpse-contact defilement — showing the characteristic crossing covenantal boundaries to apply to sojourners within Israel's space. The NT revision (Act 10:28, M10c-B-VCG-05) shows the categorical system's covenantal boundaries being revised by divine speech: what was "unclean" (persons of other nations) is declared clean, extending the characteristic's revision across what had been a covenantal boundary.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence shows the characteristic crossing covenantal boundaries. Job 14:4 (VCG-01): "who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one" — this is a universal statement about the human condition as such, not restricted to a covenantal context. Isa 64:6 (VCG-01): "we have all become like one who is unclean" — a corporate confession within Israel, but the condition named (constitutional moral uncleanness) is not presented as covenantally unique. Rom 1:24 (VCG-02): the divine giving-over is described as the consequence of human rejection of divine reality available to all humanity (Rom 1:18-23 context). The characteristic thus operates across covenantal boundaries as a universal human condition, while also having specific applications within covenant communities (the NT epistolary evidence).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primarily within covenantal contexts, but the characteristic extends across boundaries in two ways. (1) The character's consequences extend beyond Israel to the surrounding nations: Eze 22:4 (VCG-02) — "therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations, and a mockery to all the countries" — the nations perceive and respond to Israel's corporate defilement. Lam 1:17 (VCG-05) — "Jerusalem has become a filthy thing among them" — the nations identify the corporate defilement as a marker of Israel's condition. (2) The reforming king's deliberate defilement of idolatrous sites (2Ki 23:8/10/13/16, VCG-02) crosses covenantal boundaries in the sense of defiling what the nations had built within Israel's sacred geography.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries. The 21 NT verses show possession in Jewish contexts (the synagogue — Mar 1:23), among likely Gentiles (the Gerasene region — Mar 5:2, with the pigs characteristic of Gentile territory), and in the broader world (Act 5:16, Act 8:7 — Philip's ministry in Samaria). The characteristic does not respect covenantal boundaries.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster reveals a gradient from primarily-covenantal to boundary-crossing across the four characteristics. Characteristic 1: primarily covenantal (the Sinai system addresses Israel), with extensions to sojourners (Num 19:10) and an NT covenantal revision that crosses the boundary (Act 10:28 — declaring Gentile persons clean). Characteristic 2: crosses covenantal boundaries — Job 14:4 and Isa 64:6 are universal human statements; Rom 1:24 addresses the universal human moral condition (not restricted to Israel); the NT epistolary evidence addresses Gentile believers. Characteristic 3: primarily covenantal, with the community's defilement visible to surrounding nations as consequence (Lam 1:17, Eze 22:4-5); the reforming king's deliberate defilement of idolatrous sites crosses boundary in a different sense (2Ki 23). Characteristic 4: crosses covenantal boundaries — the 21-verse corpus evidences possession in Jewish settings (Mar 1:23 — synagogue), Gentile settings (Mar 5:2 — Gerasene region), and Samaritan settings (Act 8:7 — Philip's ministry). The characteristic does not respect covenantal boundaries. The cluster's boundary pattern confirms the internal gradient: Characteristic 1 is most covenantally bounded; Characteristics 2, 3, and 4 progressively cross covenantal boundaries, with Characteristic 4 the most universally scoped.

questions.question_text: What does the evidence show about the relational scope of the characteristic — who is included and who is not?

findings.session_b_note:
The relational scope evidence in the data:

**Maximally inclusive within the Spirit's work:** Q034 answer draws this directly — "forgiveness is maximally inclusive within the boundary of the Spirit's work; it is exclusively excluded only where the Spirit's work is permanently rejected." Mar 3:28 — "all sins will be forgiven the children of man" — the comprehensive inclusivity is stated before the single exception.

**Psa 86:5 — "all who call upon you":** The only boundary named in this verse is calling — not covenant membership, not moral achievement, not social status. The scope is "all who call."

**Act 10:43 — "everyone who believes":** The NT universal scope — across ethnic, covenantal, and relational boundaries. The Cornelius narrative confirms that the relational scope has expanded beyond the covenant community.

**The one exclusion:** Mar 3:29 — blasphemy against the Spirit. The relational scope includes everyone except the one in the permanent Spirit-rejection condition. This outer limit defines the scope by naming its only exception.

findings.session_b_note:
The scope of grace is determined by the giver's character, not the recipient's relational position. Grace operates toward those who have no basis for it — foreigners, the dead, the morally failed, the incapacitated. The relational scope is: anyone who is in need and without basis — which is, structurally, every creature before God.

*Consistent with prior analysis (SD008, SD032). Adds T4 framing.*

findings.session_b_note:
The data reveals a progressive expansion of relational scope across the vocabulary and the canon:

**Included (evidenced):** The covenant community (chesed toward Israel); individuals within the covenant in specific need (Lot, the widow of Nain, the leper); the morally wayward within the covenant (the prodigal, the unforgiving servant's debtor); those outside the covenant in conditions of suffering or ignorance (Nineveh, the wounded Jew in Luke 10); and those who suffer within the community of faith regardless of merit (the imprisoned believers in Heb 10:34).

**The scope-limiting factor — withheld pity (H2347 chus):** The judicial-prohibition contexts establish that there are cases in which compassion is deliberately withheld — specifically in the execution of divine judgment against covenant-violators (Deut 7:16; 13:8; Ezek 7:4). These are not the absence of compassion but its deliberate suspension. The chus evidence establishes that compassion's scope is not unlimited in all contexts — it is bounded by justice.

**The excluded (by implication):** Those who are wilfully impenitent and who have exhausted the patience of divine judgment may be outside the scope of active compassion-extension in specific judicial moments. However, the temporal asymmetry of Isa 54:8 (anger is momentary; chesed is everlasting) suggests that even these exclusions are temporary rather than permanent.

**Summary:** The scope of compassion as evidenced in the data extends from the covenant community outward to the stranger, the pagan city, and the victim across cultural boundaries. Its outer limit is not ethnic, religious, or moral standing — it is defined primarily by the presence of suffering and need perceived by the one who is moved to respond. Its only evidenced limitation is the deliberate suspension of compassion in specific judicial contexts.

findings.session_b_note:
The primary relational scope is the individual Israelite before God (covenantal, vertical). One instance of corporate scope: Psa 44:19 — the community as a whole in the posture of being broken by God. No individual-to-individual scope is evidenced in the penitential-relational mode.

*Partial: the scope is predominantly individual-vertical and occasionally corporate-vertical. The extent of the scope beyond the covenantal Israelite context is not addressed.*

findings.session_b_note:
The relational scope is graduated:

**Highest scope — divine nature fellowship:** Available to those who receive God's promises and escape corruption (2Pe 1:4). The scope is not ethnically or nationally defined — it follows the receiving of divine promises.

**Covenant-community scope:** Psa 119:63 — those who fear God and keep his precepts. The scope follows moral-spiritual alignment, not ethnic or national identity.

**Moral-compatibility scope:** 2Cor 6:14 — fellowship of righteousness excludes lawlessness. The scope is defined by moral-spiritual character.

**Common-life scope:** Ecc 4:10, Ecc 9:4 — the mutual-support and hope-of-living fellowship extends to all who share in common life. The scope here is the broadest.

**Exclusions:** Moral incompatibility (2Cor 6:14), idolatrous orientation (Hos 4:17), and faithlessness (Mal 2:14) all define who is excluded from genuine fellowship at each register.

findings.session_b_note: The relational scope of goodness is wide but not fully mapped in the data. Inclusion evidenced: creation as a whole (Gen 1:31 — all that God made is good); covenant community (Jos 23:14; Col 3:12; Rom 15:14); those outside the covenant who receive divine chrēstotēs leading to repentance (Rom 2:4); the soul who seeks (Lam 3:25 — the seeking person, without boundary). Possible exclusion: Rom 11:22 names "those who have fallen" as the recipients of severity rather than chrēstotēs — but this is presented as a relational condition rather than a categorical exclusion. The data does not name any class of persons categorically excluded from the scope of divine goodness; the blocking conditions (Q&A-032) describe inner orientations that close reception, not divine decisions to exclude. Whether the human expression of goodness has specific scope limits is not directly addressed. Partial gap. (OBS-067-OBS-006, OBS-067-OBS-043, OBS-067-OBS-044)

findings.session_b_note: Breakdowns evidenced: (a) **False brotherhood** — Gal 2:4 (OBS-103-068): using the community-love structure to serve a contrary agenda — the most dangerous breakdown because it uses love's form; (b) **Betrayal-kiss** — Luk 22:48 (OBS-103-054): love's somatic sign (kiss) used to indicate enmity — betrayal as the weaponisation of love's language; (c) **Desertion for world-love** — 2Ti 4:10 (OBS-103-148): abandonment of love-community for love of world; (d) **Poverty-caused dissolution** — Pro 19:7 (OBS-103-073): friendship tested by adversity may fail when it was conditional; (e) **Pride-driven rivalry** — Luk 22:24 (OBS-103-131): love-of-primacy at the table of the Lord. Conditions for maintenance: honest engagement (Lev 19:17, frank rebuke), soul-purification (1Pe 1:22), shared suffering (1Pe 5:9). The most dangerous breakdown is false brotherhood — it operates inside the love-structure while working against it.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-103-004: Love's relational architecture is structured by three directional axes — GOD → HUMAN, HUMAN → GOD, HUMAN → HUMAN — with divine love structurally prior and causally generative of all subsequent love. 1…
findings.finding_value: Love's relational architecture is structured by three directional axes — GOD → HUMAN, HUMAN → GOD, HUMAN → HUMAN — with divine love structurally prior and causally generative of all subsequent love. 1Jo 4:19 ('we love because he first loved us') is the axis-precedence statement: the first axis is not responsive to but constitutive of the second and third. The GOD → HUMAN direction moves through four mechanisms: covenantal declaration (naming the beloved — Jer 12:7, Mat 3:17), Spirit-infusion (Rom 5:5), redemptive acts (Joh 3:16), and covenantal covering (Eze 16:8). The HUMAN → GOD direction requires total inner mobilisation (Mat 22:37 — all heart, soul, mind) and the clearing of rival loves as its condition (1Jo 4:19, 1Ti 6:10). The HUMAN → HUMAN direction spans five structural types (neighbour, enemy, community, friendship, family) and creates the social architecture described in Q&A-088 (restructured kinship, public legibility, competitive generosity). The most significant finding in T4: the human-to-God direction is conditioned by prior reception of divine love — the capacity for human love toward God is itself a gift. The one structural gap: T4.6 (spiritual beings) is absent from the evidence.

findings.session_b_note: The scope of mercy in the data is wide: the propitiation vocabulary extends mercy to "the whole world" (1Jo 2:2). The Beatitude (Mat 5:7) does not restrict mercy to in-group relations. However, the *lo ruchamah* (Hos 1:6 — OBS-111-058) naming shows mercy can be withdrawn from those who persistently reject the covenant. The scope is wide by design but not unconditionally permanent — withdrawal is a named possibility. The tension is not resolved in the data; it is an SD pointer question. OBS-111-048, OBS-111-058.

Scope is therefore: individual → communal → potentially universal through the Servant. Gap: the boundaries of "who is included" in the contrite-before-God frame are not drawn explicitly. findings.finding_value: T1's five modes correspond directly to T4's relational directions: existential mode = all-the-living (widest scope); companionship mode = human-to-human (giving and receiving); covenantal mode = covenant partner; ontological mode = human-to-God (deepest). The scope-narrows-as-depth-increases finding (T4, Q&A-119) is the relational expression of T1's definition: as the fellowship object becomes more specific (from all-the-living to divine nature), the depth increases while the scope narrows. T1's structural negative (misdirected fellowship) maps onto T4's receiving-direction analysis (Hos 4:17 — prior wrong fellowship blocks reception of right fellowship).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-010: T1's four modes map directly onto T4's relational directions. Covenantal-objective mode = God-to-human (cultic ritual mediated); divine relational-personal = God-to-human (personal declaratory); inter…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes map directly onto T4's relational directions. Covenantal-objective mode = God-to-human (cultic ritual mediated); divine relational-personal = God-to-human (personal declaratory); intercessory = human-to-God on behalf of others; human horizontal = human-giving and human-receiving. The vertical-horizontal interdependence (T4 — the structural claim that receiving divine forgiveness enables extending human forgiveness) is the relational expression of T1's layered modes (the horizontal mode assumes the divine relational-personal mode has operated). T1's structural negative (retained claim = inner torment) is T4's receiving-blocked condition (Hos 4:17 parallel — wrong prior alignment blocks reception of right offering; Mat 18:35 — unforgiveness calling into question whether divine forgiveness was genuinely received).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-004: T4 reveals the most structurally developed relational architecture for compassion's scope. God's compassion operates simultaneously on three bases: sovereignly free (Rom 9:15 — "I will have compassion…
findings.finding_value: T4 reveals the most structurally developed relational architecture for compassion's scope. God's compassion operates simultaneously on three bases: sovereignly free (Rom 9:15 — "I will have compassion on whom I have compassion"), covenantally grounded (chesed as the bond-loyalty that grounds the characteristic), and situationally responsive (splanchnizō — triggered by the specific sight of suffering). These three bases are not in tension but in integration: divine compassion is free, covenanted, and responsive simultaneously. The scope finding is among the most analytically significant in the registry: compassion explicitly and repeatedly crosses covenantal boundaries (Nineveh, the Samaritan/Jew axis, the power-asymmetric relationship). Scope is defined by perceived need, not moral standing or covenantal membership — this is formally confirmed in the data and distinguishes compassion from many other relational characteristics. The chesed/splanchnizō distinction maps onto distinct relational registers: chesed sustains within established bonds; splanchnizō extends across distance and difference. T4.4 (receiver's inner-being experience) is the most significant gap — four P-rated prompts, entirely absent from the data. T4.6 (spiritual beings interface) is entirely silent across all four prompts.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-010: T1's scope finding (compassion requires a suffering other; scope is determined by perceived need, not moral standing) is precisely confirmed in T4's relational analysis. The explicit crossing of coven…
findings.finding_value: T1's scope finding (compassion requires a suffering other; scope is determined by perceived need, not moral standing) is precisely confirmed in T4's relational analysis. The explicit crossing of covenantal boundaries (Nineveh, Samaritan/Jew) evidenced in T4 is the relational expression of T1's boundary-definition: compassion ends where the condition (pitiable need) is absent, not where covenantal membership ends. T1's four modes of operation (T1.4) — intra-covenantal, cross-boundary, anticipatory, Christological — map onto T4's chesed/splanchnizō distinction (within-bond sustaining vs across-distance extending) and the scope analysis (covenantal and transcovenantal registers). Definition and relational scope are structurally co-determining.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-015: T2's constitutional origin analysis (somatic-relational-covenantal triple ground) and T4's relational direction analysis are structurally aligned. The somatic origin (womb, gut) grounds the cross-boun…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional origin analysis (somatic-relational-covenantal triple ground) and T4's relational direction analysis are structurally aligned. The somatic origin (womb, gut) grounds the cross-boundary relational direction in T4: splanchnizō's somatic immediacy is precisely what enables it to cross covenantal boundaries — the gut-movement toward the suffering other precedes any covenantal assessment of the relationship. The covenantal origin (chesed) grounds the within-bond sustaining direction in T4. The constitutional origin therefore predicts the relational direction: somatic = cross-boundary; covenantal = within-bond. T2's soul-body interface classification explains T4's scope-by-need finding: because compassion originates at the soul-body interface (before covenantal-rational assessment), its scope is determined by the pre-rational recognition of need rather than the post-rational assessment of covenantal standing.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-019: T3's perceptive-trigger finding (compassion is activated by sight — splanchnizō is perceptively dependent) and T4's scope-by-need finding (scope is determined by perceived need, not covenantal standin…
findings.finding_value: T3's perceptive-trigger finding (compassion is activated by sight — splanchnizō is perceptively dependent) and T4's scope-by-need finding (scope is determined by perceived need, not covenantal standing) are the same finding from two analytical perspectives. T3 names the faculty (perception) and its function (triggering compassion by seeing the pitiable condition); T4 names the relational consequence (scope defined by what is seen). The cross-boundary extension in T4 (Nineveh, Samaritan/Jew) is the relational expression of T3's merit-independence: compassion is perceptively dependent (it must see the need) but merit-independent (it does not assess the moral standing of the one seen). The three relational modes in T3.11 (building/sustaining, restoring/repairing, extending across difference) correspond precisely to T4's chesed/splanchnizō/cross-boundary structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-023: T4's finding that divine compassion operates on three simultaneous bases (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, cove…
findings.finding_value: T4's finding that divine compassion operates on three simultaneous bases (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological) are structurally isomorphic. The sovereignly-free basis corresponds to the encounter/sudden mechanism: divine compassion operating freely produces the sudden compassion-event (splanchnizō). The covenantally-grounded basis corresponds to the covenantal-sustaining mechanism: chesed as the sustaining relational ground operates gradually and consistently. The situationally-responsive basis opens toward the participatory-ontological mechanism: formation at the deepest constitutional level produces a person who is dispositionally responsive to every situation of need. T4's relational architecture and T5's formation mechanisms are the same structural reality described from relational and developmental perspectives respectively.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-024: T4's scope-by-need finding (compassion crosses covenantal boundaries) and T6's co-occurrence landscape (the human-response cluster — peace, faith, will, surrender — co-occurring with compassion) revea…
findings.finding_value: T4's scope-by-need finding (compassion crosses covenantal boundaries) and T6's co-occurrence landscape (the human-response cluster — peace, faith, will, surrender — co-occurring with compassion) reveal a structural pattern: divine compassion reaching across boundaries generates a characteristic cluster of human inner-being responses regardless of the covenantal position of the recipient. The Nineveh response (repentance and turning) and the pattern of peace/faith/will/surrender co-occurring with compassion both confirm this: compassion-received generates a recognisable inner-being response cluster that is structurally consistent across relational positions. T6's mapping of the human-response cluster is the co-occurrence evidence for T4's structural finding about scope and response.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-025: T4's three bases of divine compassion (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) are each grounded in specific textual evidence from T7. The sovereignly-free basis is evidence…
findings.finding_value: T4's three bases of divine compassion (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) are each grounded in specific textual evidence from T7. The sovereignly-free basis is evidenced in Rom 9:15 (T7's argument structure analysis — divine compassion as sovereign determination). The covenantally-grounded basis is evidenced in Exod 34:6 (T7's most multiply-anchored verse — the divine self-declaration in the covenant context). The situationally-responsive basis is evidenced in the Synoptic splanchnizō pattern (T7.2 — the sight-event structure of the Gospels). T7's framework divergences (sovereignty vs automaticity) map directly onto T4's relational analysis: the framework correctly identifies that divine compassion's sovereign freedom (T4.1) is what exceeds the natural empathic automaticity that human science frameworks describe.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-004: T4 establishes the most precisely articulated relational architecture of any characteristic in the review set. The God-to-human direction is primary and dominant (groups 888-001, 889-001, 5471-001 — a…
findings.finding_value: T4 establishes the most precisely articulated relational architecture of any characteristic in the review set. The God-to-human direction is primary and dominant (groups 888-001, 889-001, 5471-001 — all God-as-subject). The basis of divine extension is the giver's character and prior knowing (Exo 33:17 — "I know you by name"), not the receiver's merit — neither merit-based nor arbitrary. The human-to-God direction is specifically supplication: tachanum (H8469) is the receiving side's corresponding vocabulary built into the same root family as the giving side (chen/chanan) — the vocabulary embeds the two-directional circuit in a single root. The human-giving direction extends grace horizontally through three modes: forgiving (charizō — Eph 4:32), gracious conduct (chen as character quality — 889-003), and gracious speech (SD022). The receiving direction is the most underexamined (T4.4 — P-rated throughout); the scope analysis (T4.5) reveals grace crossing covenantal and social boundaries (Ruth narrative — grace in the context of foreign status and vulnerability). T4.6 (spiritual beings) is evidenced at one point: Luk 1:28 (kecharitōmenē — the angel's announcement), which implies angelic ministry as a vehicle of grace rather than grace operating independently in the spiritual-beings register. T4 synthesis: the relational architecture of grace is unique in the programme — it is the only characteristic where the giving-side vocabulary and the receiving-side vocabulary are built from the same root (chen/tachanum), encoding the grace-circuit's two-sidedness at the lexical level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-010: T1's four modes of operation map onto T4's four relational directions. The sovereign-bestowal mode corresponds to the God-to-human direction (T4.1 — primary and dominant). The covenantal-relational-su…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes of operation map onto T4's four relational directions. The sovereign-bestowal mode corresponds to the God-to-human direction (T4.1 — primary and dominant). The covenantal-relational-sustaining mode corresponds to the relational scope (T4.5 — grace operating within and across covenantal boundaries). The capacity-conferring mode corresponds to the human-to-God direction in its supplication register (T4.2 — SD026: grace giving even the capacity to appeal). The character-forming mode corresponds to the human-giving direction (T4.3 — gracious conduct and speech as the horizontal expression of received grace-character). The vocabulary's structural insight (T4 synthesis: giving-side and receiving-side built from the same root, chen/tachanum) explains T1's finding that grace requires the receptor's inner engagement to complete its operation — the vocabulary encodes the two-sidedness because grace is constitutively a two-sided circuit.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-024: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 vers…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T4.2 (the human-to-God supplication direction): seeking is the relational posture, and R140 is the registry that names it. The sequential relationship confirmed in T6.2 (grace precedes and enables faith, repentance, supplication, mourning — SD003, SD006, SD026, SD038) is the causal expression of T4's architectural finding: grace is the enabling condition for every positive human-to-God relational posture. The boundary questions in T6.5 (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-chesed) correspond to T4.5's scope analysis: the characteristics that share grace's scope (particularly love and mercy) are the same characteristics whose relational scope overlaps with grace's at T4.5.

findings.session_b_note: The relational scope of covenant shifts across the covenantal trajectory — expanding rather than contracting. (1) Noahic: universal — all living creatures (Gen 9:9 — OBS-034-038). Widest possible scope. (2) Abrahamic: a particular people (Abraham's descendants) and through them "all the families of the earth" (Act 3:25). Narrowing to a particular line but with a universal horizon. (3) Sinai: Israel as the specific covenant-community. Explicitly bounded. (4) New covenant: universally offered through Christ — "all the families of the earth" realised, the dividing wall broken down (Eph 2:14 context — OBS-034-060 direction), foreigners who hold fast to the covenant included (Isa 56:6). The scope of the new covenant is the universal scope of the Noahic covenant now realised eschatologically. Those outside the covenant (Eph 2:12) are in a condition of desolation that is a positive, remediable state — the new covenant's scope is intended to encompass all who receive it.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-034-004: T4 as a whole reveals that covenant's relational interface structure is asymmetric but genuinely bilateral. The God-to-human direction (T4.1) is the founding and sustaining axis — God initiates, commi…
findings.finding_value: T4 as a whole reveals that covenant's relational interface structure is asymmetric but genuinely bilateral. The God-to-human direction (T4.1) is the founding and sustaining axis — God initiates, commits, inscribes, and mediates. The human-to-God direction (T4.2) is the responsive axis — the whole person moves toward God through commitment, love, and faithfulness. The horizontal directions (T4.3 giving; T4.4 receiving) are genuine but secondary, and the evidence shows they are grounded in and enabled by the vertical. The relational scope expands progressively across the covenant trajectory — from particular (Abraham) to expanding (Israel) to universal (new covenant in Christ). The spiritual-beings interface (T4.6) is largely absent from the data — the only relevant material is the pagan deity named "lord of covenant" (H1286) and the inferred adversarial spiritual claim. T4 as a whole shows that covenant's relational architecture is constituted by God's prior initiative and realised through the whole person's responsive engagement.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-034-023: T4 reveals that the relational scope of covenant expands progressively from particular (Abraham) to national (Israel) to universal (new covenant in Christ — Q&A-119). T5 reveals that covenant moves to…
findings.finding_value: T4 reveals that the relational scope of covenant expands progressively from particular (Abraham) to national (Israel) to universal (new covenant in Christ — Q&A-119). T5 reveals that covenant moves toward eschatological fullness — from the eternal covenant (Heb 13:20 — Q&A-140) to the new creation (Rev 21:1-5 — Q&A-141). The T4 × T5 synthesis: the expanding relational scope (T4) and the eschatological trajectory (T5) are the same movement described in two registers. The Noahic covenant's universal scope (all living creatures) is the anticipation of the new covenant's universal offer and ultimately the eschatological new creation's universal scope. Covenant moves simultaneously toward wider relational inclusion (T4) and toward deeper fullness of the relationship (T5). The two trajectories are not separate but co-directional — the expansion of who is included (T4) and the deepening of what is included in (T5) are aspects of the same eschatological movement.

findings.session_b_note: Strongly evidenced. (a) Covenant community as relational partner: H5971H/I/L groups 537–539-001 — "covenant community as object of God's relational love and moral claim" [OBS-099-034]. Divine kindness operates toward the community corporately. (b) Intercessory solidarity: Moses's intercession at Num 14:19 — kindness through one person on behalf of many [OBS-099-060]. (c) Chasidim assembly: Psa 149:1/5 — the godly form a community whose gathered character is expressed in common worship [XREG: H2623, OBS-099-095]. Kindness is both individually formed and communally expressed.

findings.session_b_note: The data establishes both inclusion and exclusion: (1) Exclusion: "there is no peace for the wicked" (Isa 48:22, 57:21) — moral condition determines peace-access; (2) Conditional exclusion: Psa 85:8 — "but let them not turn back to folly" — covenant-unfaithfulness risks peace; Deu 23:6 — "you shall not seek their peace" for Ammonites/Moabites — historical covenant boundaries; (3) Expanding inclusion: Isa 57:19 — "peace, peace to the far and to the near" — peace offered to those formerly excluded; Isa 52:7 — the herald of peace to the nations; Eph 2:14 — Gentiles included through Christ. The trajectory of scope is progressive expansion: from Israel → to the nations → to all peoples in Christ → to all things (Col 1:20). The only sustained exclusion in the data is moral: "there is no peace for the wicked." The covenantal exclusions are overcome in Christ.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-117-004: T4 establishes two key relational findings: (1) Peace's scope expands progressively — covenant-primary (to Israel, Num 6:26) → covenant-expansive (to nations in the prophets, Isa 57:19) → universally …
findings.finding_value: T4 establishes two key relational findings: (1) Peace's scope expands progressively — covenant-primary (to Israel, Num 6:26) → covenant-expansive (to nations in the prophets, Isa 57:19) → universally offered through Christ (Eph 2:14, Col 1:20) — with the only sustained exclusion being moral ("no peace for the wicked"). The covenantal boundaries are overcome in Christ; the moral boundary remains. (2) Peace is a site of cosmic contest: angelic mediation of peace is effective (Dan 10:19), elemental disruption of peace is real (Mar 4:39), and eschatological removal of peace is documented (Rev 6:4). Peace is not only a private inner condition but a publicly contested reality across the cosmic order.

findings.session_b_note: The primary scope is the covenantal community — Abraham and his offspring (872-001 corpus), Israel and her sub-communities (Nehemiah, Hosea, Isaiah texts). Within this scope: individuals in need (Leah), the wilderness generation, the mourning in Zion, the depressed Servant. The judicial giving-over (872-004) includes Ephraim/Israel and the nations used as instruments of judgement, expanding the scope negatively. Excluded from covenantal giving: those outside the covenant relationship who have not received its basis (the nations receive the characteristic only through mediation — Isa 42:6). God's non-giving of glory to carved idols (Isa 42:8) establishes the limit at the divine level: idols are explicitly excluded from receiving divine glory-giving. The scope is defined by the relational structure: those in covenant receive covenantal giving; those outside receive at most mediated giving.

findings.finding_value: The relational scope of M06 characteristics is effectively unlimited. They can be directed at family members, neighbours, strangers, enemies, God's servants, and God himself. No relational category is immune. However, the covenantal context makes M06 characteristics more consequential when they operate within it — hate within covenant is treated as more serious precisely because it violates the relational terms the covenant established (e.g., Deu 31:20's sequence: prosperity → contempt → covenant-breaking).

The standard of God's righteousness (A1) applies to all — "the whole world may be held accountable to God" (Rom 3:19, VSG 3208-001 in F-group) — but the reception of righteousness through justification (C) and the practice of righteousness in community (A2-012, A2-015) are primarily described within the covenant community. findings.finding_value: The relational scope of M46 is universal: all four sub-groups operate across covenantal, ethnic, and social boundaries. The cluster's concern is not with a specific community's wealth-ethics but with the systematic inner-being effects of wealth on any person who holds it.
