findings.finding_value: M01-A's scope includes: all Israel (the primary covenant community throughout the Deuteronomy and Psalms corpus), the messianic king (Isa 11:2-3), individual leaders and judges (Exo 18:21; 2Ch 19:9), foreigners who come to know God (Solomon's prayer for foreigners, 1Ki 8:43; Cornelius, Act 10:2), and ultimately all nations (Rev 14:7; 19:5). The scope is universal in aspiration. Exclusions are not based on ethnic identity but on the inner disposition: those whose hearts are hardened (Isa 63:17), whose allegiance is divided (2Ki 17:33), or who do not fear God at all (Psa 36:1) are excluded not from God's demand but from receiving the blessing that fear-of-God confers.

The relational scope of M01-A is genuinely universal: God requires reverential fear of all peoples and rewards it wherever it is found (Act 10:35). The characteristic's scope is as wide as God's sovereignty — which is total.

The relational scope is total: divine anger has no exclusion in terms of who can be its object. Eph 2:3 (M02-A-VCG-02): all humanity is by nature "children of wrath." The scope narrows for specific expressions: covenant anger is more personal, sustained, and morally complex; anger at foreign nations is more categorical and judicial; anger at spiritual enemies (Rev 12:17 / M02-B-VCG-02) crosses into the spiritual-beings interface.

The relational scope is total: divine anger has no exclusion in terms of who can be its object. Eph 2:3 (M02-A-VCG-02): all humanity is by nature "children of wrath." The scope narrows for specific expressions: covenant anger is more personal, sustained, and morally complex; anger at foreign nations is more categorical and judicial; anger at spiritual enemies (Rev 12:17 / M02-B-VCG-02) crosses into the spiritual-beings interface.

The relational scope of M03 is wide: grief is evidenced across personal bonds, family bonds, national bonds, cross-national bonds, human-to-God bonds, and (in M03-E-VCG-02) even the cosmic bond between creation and its Creator. Grief appears to follow wherever genuine bonding exists — the capacity for grief scales with the depth and breadth of relational investment. The widest scope (creation's collective groan, Rom 8:22 — M03-E-VCG-02) represents grief at the widest possible relational scale: all created existence grieving together.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The scope is ultimately universal — cosmic rejoicing (Psa 96:11; 97:1; 1Ch 16:31; Isa 49:13) calls the whole created order to exult. But the primary and most specified locus is within the covenant community (Israel, Zion, the righteous). The characteristic moves from the individual soul (Psa 35:9), through the community (Psa 32:11; 48:11; Zec 9:9), to the cosmos (Psa 97:1), and finally to God himself (Zep 3:17; Jer 32:41) — a concentric relational scope.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Joy has the widest relational scope of any characteristic in M04: from the individual heart (Psa 4:7), through the household (Deu 12:7 — "you and your households"), the community (Neh 12:43), the nation (Est 8:17 — "gladness and joy among the Jews"), all peoples (Luk 2:10), and all creation (Psa 96:11; Isa 55:12 — mountains and trees), to God himself (Zep 3:17; Luk 15:7). The characteristic has a concentrically-expanding relational scope that reaches its fullness in the eschatological wedding of the Lamb (Rev 19:7).

**[CHAR-7]** E — Suffering-Joy's relational scope is: (1) **Primary**: the Spirit-filled faith community (the persecuted disciples, apostles, NT epistolary communities); (2) **Cross-ethnic through faith**: Act 16:34; (3) **Household-encompassing**: Act 16:34's household (the primary social unit); (4) **Anticipatory-historical**: Joh 8:56 (Abraham's faith-joy reaching across millennia). The scope is primarily eschatologically-determined rather than ethnically-bounded: whoever shares in Christ's suffering and faith-orientation participates.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Gladness has a broad but ordered relational scope: (1) **Universal** — Psa 145:9 ("good to all") — divine goodness extends universally; (2) **Covenantal primary** — the ki-tov traditions, the good-hand narratives, and the promise-fulfilment texts are Israel-centred; (3) **Personal and relational** — the good-word and relational-evaluation registers operate at the individual and communal level; (4) **Cross-boundary** — the evaluative faculty operates wherever persons make moral assessments (Jethro, Ruth, Achish). The scope is ordered from divine goodness (universal) → covenantal community → individual relational → cross-boundary.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Delight's scope is: (1) **Primary**: the most intimate bonds — parental, covenantal, friendship; (2) **Hierarchical**: the diplomatic-preference idiom throughout historical books shows Delight structuring all hierarchical relationships (king-subject, captor-captive, general-army); (3) **Universal at the base level**: the human capacity for directed inner pleasure is evidenced across all human relationships; (4) **Eschatologically inclusive**: Isa 62:4 and Mal 3:12 show the scope expanding to encompass the whole restored community as the object of divine Delight.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Scope: (1) **Most intimate bonds** (primary) — David-Jonathan, Song lovers, brotherly unity; (2) **Community** — Psa 133:1's communal pleasantness; (3) **Covenantal-inclusive** — Num 15:14's extension to resident foreigners; (4) **Eschatological** — Psa 16:11 and Eze 20:41's future-oriented Pleasure extending to all the restored community.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Wonder has the widest relational scope of any M04 characteristic: (1) Within Israel (primary); (2) Extending to surrounding nations through witness (Exo 34:10; 1Ch 16:24; Psa 96:3); (3) To all peoples universally (Psa 107's sea-narrative); (4) To the heavenly assembly (Psa 89:5 — "let the heavens praise your wonders"); (5) Eschatologically — Isa 29:14's "wonder upon wonder" reaching all who encounter God's final acts. Wonder's scope is universal and trans-generational.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The comparative relational scopes across the seven reveal a spectrum: (1) **Widest scope**: Wonder (Char 6) — community → nations → heavenly assembly → eschatological universality; Joy (Char 2) — individual → household → community → nation → all peoples → all creation → God; (2) **Intimacy-weighted scope**: Pleasure (Char 5) — most intimate bonds (David-Jonathan; Song lovers; brotherly unity) as the primary register; (3) **Hierarchically-structured scope**: Delight (Char 4) — operates through all hierarchical relationships (diplomatic idiom spans kings, servants, commanders, and citizens); (4) **Community-primary**: Suffering-Joy (Char 7) — primarily faith-community scope; the household as the primary relational unit; (5) **Creation-encompassing**: Exultation (Char 1) — the cosmic-rejoicing passages expand exultation's scope to include the whole created order. The cluster as a whole moves from the most intimate bonds (Pleasure) through community and covenant (Joy, Gladness, Delight) to national witness (Wonder, Exultation) to cosmic celebration (Joy, Exultation) to eschatological consummation (all seven). The concentric-expanding scope is a cluster-wide pattern.

**[CHAR-1]** E — CHAR-1's scope is universal in its judicial form (any moral agent can be put to shame by God's judgment); covenantally specific in its corrective-restorative form (shame as the gateway to knowing God's design is offered to those in covenantal relationship with him); and interpersonally broad in its unjust-wound form (anyone can inflict unjust shame on anyone else, as the psalmist's enemy-evidence shows).

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 operates both within existing bonds (David's king offering compassion to humiliated envoys) and across bonds (military opponents humiliating nations, God humbling the proud). The divine-abasement mode (VCG-03) is universal — God's corrective humiliation of pride crosses all covenantal boundaries. CHAR-2's scope is not covenantally limited.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — The head-covering material (1Cor 11:4-5) operates within the covenant community. Jam 2:6's dishonoring of the poor operates within the community of believers. The dishonoring of Jesus (Joh 8:49) crosses the covenant community's internal boundary. CHAR-3 appears to operate most damagingly within existing relational bonds where worth-recognition is expected and violated.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 operates within community contexts (VCG-01: the shameful conduct of speech in the assembly, the shameful hair practices — all community-embedded evaluations) and within covenantal contexts (the idolatrous shameful-objects of Jer 3:24; 11:13 are specifically about Israel's covenantal infidelity). VCG-02 (disordered passions) crosses community boundaries — Rom 1:26-27 addresses a pattern of moral disorder that is cultural-historical in scope.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — The commands against despising (Rom 14:3; 14:10; 1Cor 16:11; 1Th 5:20) operate within the covenant community. The Boaz-Ruth protection (Rut 2:15, vc=38516) operates across covenantal difference: Boaz protects Ruth, an outsider, from the contempt she would normally receive. The 1Sa 25:7/15 (vc=38530/38531) protection of Nabal's shepherds operates within a social context of armed men restraining themselves. CHAR-5's scope is not covenantally limited — contempt can cross any relational boundary; what is covenantally specific is the community's obligation to protect against contempt within its own relational field.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 operates specifically within the covenant relationship between the person and God: the approach to God's altar (Psa 26:6) is a covenantal act; the divine confirmation of innocence (Gen 20:6) is a covenantal response; the incapacity for innocence (Hos 8:5) is a covenantal failure condition. CHAR-6's scope is specifically covenantal-relational: it is the inner moral condition that the covenant relationship with God requires of the person.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's relational scope shows a consistent pattern: the destructive characteristics (unjust shame, contempt, dishonour) cross covenantal boundaries freely — they can fall on anyone. The constructive characteristics (corrective shame, conscience-activated moral evaluation, innocence-enabled approach) are more covenantally specific. Exceptions: Char 2's God-abasing act crosses all covenantal boundaries (God humbles all pride); Char 5's divine reversal is explicitly extended universally (1Cor 1:28 — God choosing the world's despised). Within the covenant community, specific obligations apply: protect the vulnerable from contempt (Char 5 — Rut 2:15; 1Cor 16:11), honour the worth of all members (Char 3 — Jam 2:6), exercise corrective shame with proper moral grounding (Char 1's entrepō; Char 4). These community-internal obligations are the cluster's most directly applicable finding for relational ethics.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The relational scope of CHAR-1 is universal — no person, people, or period is evidenced as exempt from either possessing CHAR-1 or being subject to God's opposition to it. Pro 16:5 (vc=12083, M08-A1-VCG-03): "everyone who is arrogant in heart" — scope is universal by definition. Isa 2:12 (vc=33957, M08-A3-VCG-04): "the Lord of hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty" — the eschatological judgment encompasses all, without national, ethnic, or covenantal qualification. The day-of-the-Lord corpus (M08-A3-VCG-04) — Deu 32:27 (vc=65750), Isa 2:11–12, 2:17, 10:33, 25:11 — addresses collective humanity as the subject of CHAR-1's universal expression and universal judgment. Job 41:34 (vc=12089, vc=34614, M08-A4-VCG-04): "he is king over all the sons of pride" — the category "sons of pride" encompasses creatures universally.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The relational scope is comprehensive: CHAR-2 is evidenced in individuals (Deu 18:20: the false prophet), communities (Neh 9:16: the ancestors collectively), nations (Jer 50:29: Babylon), and in every historical period from the Exodus to the NT. Pro 11:2 (vc=34109, M08-B-VCG-02): "when arrogance comes, disgrace follows" — stated as a universal pattern without covenantal or situational limitation.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Universal scope. VCG-01 applies to wise, mighty, and rich without qualification (Jer 9:23, vc=33342), to Gentiles (Rom 1:30, vc=33867), and to law-keepers (Rom 2:23, vc=33883). VCG-03 applies within the Christian community specifically (Rom 5:2; Phili 3:3; 1Th 2:19). VCG-02 is specifically Pauline-apostolic but evidences principles of legitimate self-commendation with broader applicability (Gal 6:4, vc=33908: "each one test his own work" — universally addressed).

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4's evidenced relational scope is the NT Christian community in multiple locations. Rom 12:3 (vc=60866, M08-D-VCG-02): the universal address ("to everyone among you") applies CHAR-4's correction universally within the believing community. 2Ti 3:4 (vc=33926, M08-D-VCG-02): tufoō in the end-times character list — universal eschatological scope without community limitation. CHAR-4's scope is broad within the human community, though the 12-verse corpus addresses it specifically through NT community contexts.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The relational scope is universal in the structural-power domain: any nation, community, or individual with real structural power (military, economic, positional, geographical) is evidenced as a potential site of CHAR-5. The ga.on proud-might corpus covers Israel and Judah, Egypt, Sodom, Tyre, Edom, and Babylon — the full historical range of ancient Near Eastern power-holders. 1Ti 6:17 (vc=60878, M08-E-VCG-02) extends the scope to individual wealth-holders in NT communities. CHAR-5's scope is wherever structural power exists.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Universal scope across all five characteristics. The cluster comparison confirms that M08's relational scope is unlimited — individuals, communities, and nations across all periods and covenants are within the scope of M08's characteristics. CHAR-5 has the most extensive cross-national evidence (Egypt, Israel, Sodom, Tyre, Edom, Babylon). CHAR-4 is the most community-specific (Pauline communities). The cluster-synthesis: M08 is the programme's most universally-scoped cluster — no human context is evidenced as exempt from its characteristics.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The scope is broad. The gospel-obedience register (Rom1:5; 16:26; Act6:7) includes all who receive the gospel without restriction. The household register (Eph6:1; Col3:20; Pro30:17) includes all within family structures. The eschatological register (Gen49:10 — all peoples; Heb5:9 — all who obey him) has universal scope. The Gal2:5 instance (submission withheld from false teachers) establishes the one exclusion: submission to illegitimate authority that would compromise truth is explicitly excluded. The scope is thus: all who encounter legitimate authority; none who would be required to submit to what is illegitimate or gospel-distorting.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Both verses use inclusive, non-restrictive language: "the brokenhearted," "the crushed in spirit" (Psa34:18) — any person in that inner state; "him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit" (Isa57:15) — any person of that character. The relational scope appears to be constituted by the inner state itself rather than by external markers (covenant membership, ethnicity, status). God's nearness and dwelling are responsive to the inner condition, not to external identity markers.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Heb5:2 — the "ignorant and wayward" (agnooumenois kai planōmenois) — describes the scope as those who err through ignorance or waywardness, without specifying covenant membership. The relational scope of metriopatheō appears to be constituted by the erring person's condition rather than their covenantal status. Act9:38's scope is the community in need. Together: the characteristic's scope extends to anyone in the condition (wayward, in need) that occasions the response.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The relational scope of semnotēs spans the civic, household, and pedagogical spheres — broad rather than narrow. The characteristic is required "in every way" (1Ti2:2) — the comprehensive scope implies it should characterise the believer's presence in all relational contexts rather than being confined to specific situations.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Exo35:5 — "whoever is of a willing heart" — within the covenant community, the scope includes all whose hearts are genuinely willing regardless of gender (Exo35:22 — "both men and women") or specific role (1Ch28:21 — craftsmen of all skills). Within the covenantal community, willing-heartedness is inclusive of all who genuinely have the inner disposition rather than confined to a priestly or leadership class.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The characteristic's relational scope is extensive. Vertically: the humble before God includes all who take the posture (2Ch7:14 — "my people who are called by my name"; Jam4:6 — "to the humble" without restriction within the community). Horizontally: Phili2:3 and Eph4:2 address believers toward one another; Col3:12 extends to "God's chosen ones." The evidence does not restrict the horizontal scope to any particular subgroup within the community — "one another" is the inclusive relational scope. There is no verse evidencing humility as appropriately withheld from any person.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's relational scopes range from the most universally extensive to the most covenantally restricted. Submission (CHAR-2) has the widest scope — the obedience of faith among all nations (Rom1:5; 16:26), the eschatological gathering of all peoples (Gen49:10), and the judgment of all who do not obey (2Th1:8) give CHAR-2 universal-human scope. Humility (CHAR-1) has the next widest — the wisdom-principle (Pro11:2) and the Christological universality of its paradigm extend its scope beyond the covenant community. Meekness and Gentleness (CHAR-4) and Dignity (CHAR-5) have broad community scopes without explicit restriction to covenant insiders (the "ignorant and wayward" of Heb5:2; the civic sphere of 1Ti2:2). Contrition (CHAR-3) and Willing-heartedness (CHAR-6) have the most restricted scope — primarily within the covenant community or within the individual's Godward relation. The inclusive criterion for CHAR-3's scope is the inner state itself (Psa34:18 — "the brokenhearted" — any person in that inner state); for CHAR-6, the inclusive criterion is the genuine willing orientation (Exo35:5 — "whoever is of a willing heart").

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The relational scope is comprehensive: VCG-01 encompasses the human-God relation; VCG-02 encompasses all human-human bonds (family, king-servant, community, neighbour); VCG-05 adds the self-relation (1Cor 6:18 — sinning against one's own body) and the Christ-relation (1Cor 8:12 — sinning against a brother reaches Christ). The scope thus encompasses the full relational map of the human person: God, other humans, self, and mediately Christ. No relational category is excluded from the scope of wilful sinning.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The relational scope covers: (1) *Universal individual scope*: Jam 1:14 — "each person" — enticement through desire applies to all moral subjects; (2) *Community scope*: Gal 2:13 — the entire community at Antioch is drawn into collective hypocrisy; (3) *Covenantal-communal scope*: Act 21:21 — the Jewish diaspora community as the scope of the apostasy accusation; (4) *Teacher-student relational scope*: 2Pe 2:18 — specific teaching relationships as the enticement channel.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The relational scope of sin as universal condition is the widest possible: every human person without exception (Rom 3:23 — "all"), in every relational and covenantal context (Rom 3:9 — Jews and Greeks), from the beginning of humanity's existence (Rom 5:12 — through one man) to the present. The scope encompasses: individual moral subjects (Joh 9:34 — "born in utter sin"), communities (Mat 3:6 — "all the country of Judea"), nations (Luk 24:47 — "all nations"), and corporate humanity (Rom 5:12 — "all men"). No human relationship exists outside the scope of the condition.

**[CHAR-12]** E — The relational scope is universal and individually specific simultaneously. Universal: Gal 3:22 — "everything under sin" — the imprisoning scope encompasses all. Individually specific: Joh 8:34 — "everyone who practices sin" — the enslavement is individual (each person who practices becomes a slave). Community-relational: 1Jo 5:16 — the enslaving grip on a brother is visible within the community and addressable through intercessory prayer within the relational bond. The scope thus spans: universal structural (all imprisoned — Gal 3:22), individual-personal (each practitioner enslaved — Joh 8:34), and community-relational (the sinning brother within the community — 1Jo 5:16).

**[CHAR-13]** E — The relational scope is universal: Joh 1:29 — "the sin of the world" — the Lamb takes away the sin-record of the entire world, not merely the covenant community. The 205-verse corpus spans individual (Psa 51:5 — "my sin"), communal (Neh 9:2 — "their sins and the iniquities of their fathers"), national (Isa 40:2 — "she has received from the Lord's hand double for all her sins"), and universal (Joh 1:29 — "of the world") scopes. The relational scope is thus comprehensive: no person, community, or nation stands outside the divine record's reach.

**[CHAR-14]** E — The relational scope expands across the canonical arc. OT: the kip.pu.rim system covers the covenant community — "for all Israel" (2Ch 29:24); Exo 30:16 — "the people of Israel." NT: Mat 26:28 — "for many" (the new covenant's scope); Mar 3:28 — "the children of man" (universal human scope); 2Cor 5:19 — "the world" (cosmic scope); Act 10:43 — "everyone who believes" (faith-scope crossing ethnic and covenantal boundaries). The scope moves from Israel → many → world → everyone who believes.

**[CHAR-15]** E — The relational scope is communal-national within the covenant framework: Isa 43:27 — the condition encompasses the entire lineage from the first father through the mediators to the present community; Psa 78:17/32 — the wilderness community as a whole; 1Ki 8:47 — all the exiles; Eze 37:23 — the restoration encompasses "them" as a communal whole. The scope is not individual (each person's personal accumulation) but communal — the whole community stands in the inherited condition together.

**[CHAR-16]** E — The relational scope is universal. Rom 5:8 — "while we were still sinners" — the "we" encompasses all humanity in its pre-redemption state; Rom 5:19 — "the many were made sinners" through Adam — the scope is humanity-as-whole through federal imputation. 1Ti 1:15 — "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners" — "sinners" names the entire target of the salvific mission, not a subset. The sinner-as-moral-character category has universal human scope, not limited to any specific community, covenant, or ethnicity.

**[CHAR-17]** E — The relational scope spans God-to-person (Ezr 9:15 — standing before God in guilt), person-to-God (Hos 5:15 — seeking God's face under guilt), person-to-person (Gen 42:21 — guilt concerning a brother; 2Sa 19:19 — guilt owed to the king), community-to-God (Ezr 9:7 — communal generational guilt), and person-to-community (Lev 4:3 — priest's sin bringing guilt on the people). The guilt-state operates across every relational dimension present in the corpus: no relational context is exempt from the possibility of guilt-bearing.

**[CHAR-18]** E — The relational scope is universal and includes the non-human realm. Lev 18:25 — "the land became unclean, so that I punished its iniquity, and the land vomited out its inhabitants" — the land itself carries and is punished for the iniquity of its inhabitants; Isa 24:6 — "inhabitants suffer for their guilt; therefore the inhabitants of the earth are scorched" — universal human scope; Gen 15:16 — all nations accumulate iniquity before God. The relational scope extends from the individual soul (Eze 18:20 — "the soul who sins"), through the family (Exo 20:5), community (Amo 3:2), nation (Jer 25:12), and creation (Lev 18:25).

**[CHAR-19]** E — The relational scope is universal. Rom 5:15/16/17/18 — "one man's trespass led to condemnation for all men" — the Adamic trespass's scope is humanity-as-whole; Psa 130:3 (CHAR-18 adjacent) — "if you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?" implies universal human transgression-liability. The Amos oracle-series (eight nations) confirms that transgression is a cross-cultural, cross-covenant universal moral reality. The relational scope spans God-to-individual, individual-to-individual, leader-to-community, and Adam-to-all-humanity.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The relational scope covers: (1) *Individual-to-God*: Lev 4:2; Num 15:27/28 (individual's inadvertent violation of divine command). (2) *Representative-to-community*: Lev 4:3 (priest's sinning implicating the people). (3) *Individual-to-neighbor*: Lev 6:2/3 (interpersonal sinning through deception, misappropriation). (4) *Community-to-God*: Lev 9:15 (communal sin offering). (5) *Sacred-space*: VCG-02 (altar, sanctuary defilement). The relational scope is broad — the characteristic does not operate in one relational domain but across the full range of human-God and human-human bonds. The common thread is that inadvertent violation creates real liability in every relational domain it touches.

**[CHAR-20]** E — The relational scope spans: the divine-human covenant (VCG-01 — 57V), the marriage covenant (Num 5:12; Mal 2:14-16), the family bond (Jer 12:6 — family members), the civic-political bond (Judg 9:23 — Shechem leaders), and the friendship bond (Lam 1:2 — friends become enemies). The characteristic's scope is wherever covenant-loyalty was owed and has been broken. The primary and densest scope is the divine-Israel covenant (VCG-01); the secondary scope is the human relational bonds (VCG-02); the tertiary scope is the constitutional inner character (VCG-03).

**[CHAR-21]** E — The relational scope is comprehensive: divine-human (Deu 32:20 — God hiding face; Isa 29:16 — creator-creature inversion), individual-personal (Pro 6:14 — perverted heart; Eph 4:22 — old self corruption), interpersonal-social (Pro 16:28 — close friends separated; 1Cor 15:33 — bad company), cosmic (Rev 19:2 — earth corrupted; Rom 8:21 — creation in bondage to corruption). CHAR-21 is M10's most cosmically-scoped characteristic: corruption extends from the individual inner faculty all the way to the whole earth and creation's bondage.

**[CHAR-22]** E — The relational scope is comprehensive: divine (Jer 2:5 — what wrong in God?), judicial-positional (Psa 82:2), commercial (Lev 19:35), interpersonal-violent (2Sa 7:10; Psa 58:2), civic-structural (Mic 3:10), and cosmic (Rev 18:5; Rom 3:5). CHAR-22 is M10's most institutionally comprehensive characteristic: injustice operates across every human institution (judicial, commercial, civic, political) and every relational scale (individual, community, nation, cosmic).

**[CHAR-3]** E — The relational scope covers: (1) *Individual-to-God* (VCG-01 primary — 2Sa 24:10; Mic 7:9; Luk 15:21); (2) *Corporate-to-God* (VCG-02 — Judg 10:10; 1Sa 7:6; Dan 9:5; Psa 106:6); (3) *Individual-to-person* (Exo 10:16; 2Sa 19:20; Mat 27:4); (4) *Representative individual confessing for a community* (Neh 1:6; Dan 9:5 — Daniel including himself in the community's confession). The relational scope is comprehensive and matches the scope of sin: wherever sin creates a relational breach, confession is the appropriate naming of that breach. The dominant scope is vertical (God-directed); the secondary scope is horizontal (person-directed).

**[CHAR-4]** E — The relational scope covers: (1) *Individual-to-God* (primary — Jer 2:35; Ecc 8:12): conscience suppression most fully manifests in the person's false moral standing before God. (2) *Corporate-to-God* (Jer 16:10): communal conscience suppression manifesting as collective moral blindness before the Lord. (3) *Within-community* (1Cor 15:34; Tit 3:11): conscience suppression operating within the community of faith, producing ongoing sinning and divisive character. The relational scope is primarily vertical (God-directed) with secondary horizontal (community) dimensions.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The relational scope is: (1) *Individual-to-God* (Eze 18:24 — the formerly righteous person's personal refusal; Heb 10:26 — individual deliberate sinning); (2) *Leadership-to-community* (the Kings pattern — the leader's refusal transmitted to the people); (3) *Community-to-God* (Neh 9:29; 2Ki 13:6 — communal non-departure from the sinful course). The relational scope is wide: the characteristic operates in every relational configuration, from the most individual (Eze 18:24) to the most communal (the whole nation refusing to depart — 2Ki 13:6).

**[CHAR-6]** E — The relational scope covers: (1) *Individual-to-God* (1Jo 3:6 — never seen or known him; 2Ki 17:7 — sinning against the Lord); (2) *Communal-to-God* (Heb 3:17 — wilderness generation over forty years; 2Ki 17:7 — "the people of Israel"); (3) *Individual-to-community* (Ecc 9:18 — one sinner destroying much good; 1Sa 2:25 — priestly sinning against the Lord affecting the community); (4) *General human* (1Ki 8:46; Ecc 7:20 — universal scope). The relational scope is the widest of any characteristic studied: habitual defection applies across every relational configuration from the individual's God-relationship to the universal human moral condition.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The relational scope covers: (1) *National scale*: "Israel" (1Ki 14:16; 2Ki 17:21) and "Judah" (2Ki 21:11) as entire national communities receiving the transmitted sinning; (2) *Multi-generational*: 1Ki 22:52 — three generations receiving successively; (3) *Cross-cultural*: Exo 23:33; Deu 20:18 — foreign nations transmitting to Israel across cultural-ethnic boundaries; (4) *Structural-institutional*: 2Ki 23:15 — the altar at Bethel as the physical-structural scope of the transmission outlasting any individual. The relational scope of contagious sin is the widest of any M10 characteristic: it operates at national, multi-generational, cross-cultural, and structural-institutional levels simultaneously.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The relational scope covers: (1) *Vassal-nation level*: Moab against Israel; Edom and Libnah against Judah — nation-to-nation governing relationships; (2) *Intra-covenant political level*: northern Israel against the house of David — internal covenant-community governing relationships; (3) *Spiritual-political level*: 2Ch 21:10 — the ruler's relationship with God as the ultimate ground of political authority. The scope ranges from the immediately political (vassal-nation) to the covenantally grounded (Davidic) to the theologically foundational (ruler-to-God).

**[CHAR-9]** E — The relational scope covers: (1) *Horizontal person-to-person*: VCG-01 — slander directed at community members; (2) *Judicial-social*: Act 6:11 — false witness in a formal juridical context; (3) *Christological*: VCG-02 — blasphemy charge directed at the Son of God; (4) *Spirit-level*: Mat 12:31 — blasphemy against the Spirit; (5) *Cosmic-eschatological*: VCG-03 — beast's blasphemy against God's name, dwelling, and heavenly community. The relational scope spans from the interpersonal-communal to the eschatological-cosmic — the widest relational range of any single characteristic in the M10 cluster.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The relational scope is universal — the characteristic applies to any human being, within or outside the covenant community. The evidence spans Sodom (Gen 18:23-25 — VCG-04), Egypt (Exo 9:27 — VCG-04 — Pharaoh's moment of conscience), Korah's community (Num 16:26 — VCG-04), kings and nations (Psa 9:5 — VCG-05 — "you have made the wicked perish"), Job's contemporaries (VCG-10 — the theodicy discussion), and the eschatological humanity (Dan 12:10 — VCG-05). The characteristic describes a human inner-being orientation that the entire 190-verse corpus treats as a universal moral category rather than a culturally specific or covenantally bounded one.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The relational scope is universal — the characteristic is the constitutional baseline of human inner nature as such (Mat 7:11; Luk 11:13 — VCG-02). Within that universal scope, the NT evidence particularly addresses the ecclesial-communal context: the letters to churches consistently name and address the characteristic (Eph 4:31; Col 3:8; 1Pe 2:1; Jam 1:21 — VCG-05; 1Cor 5:8 — VCG-05). This shows the characteristic's relational scope spans all humanity at the constitutional level while its most intense practical address in the NT is within the covenant-community context, where its presence among believers is a pastoral emergency requiring active response.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The relational scope is broad: the characteristic applies wherever there is a moral-relational framework in which inner character can be assessed. It spans: (1) the personal divine-human relationship (VCG-02 and VCG-03 — individual heart before God); (2) the covenantal community relationship (VCG-04 — Israel's communal abominations); (3) the human-social community (Pro 24:9 — VCG-01: scoffer abominable to mankind; Pro 29:27 — vc=65959: unjust person abominable to the righteous); (4) the cosmic-eschatological scope (Rev 21:27 — VCG-05 — nothing abominable enters the holy city). The relational scope is thus from the intimately personal to the universally eschatological, confirming the characteristic as operating across all levels of moral-relational reality.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The relational scope spans: (1) the intimate individual-divine relationship — the heart that goes after idols departs from the personal covenant relationship with God (Eze 6:9 — VCG-05); (2) the royal-institutional dimension — kings who install or purge abominations shape the entire national community (VCG-03); (3) the national-covenant community — the abominations fill the land (Jer 16:18 — VCG-04) and drive the divine presence from the sanctuary (Eze 8:6 — VCG-05); (4) the eschatological — the abomination of desolation is a cosmic-eschatological event (VCG-06). The scope moves from the personal heart to the cosmic event.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The relational scope spans: (1) the personal divine-human relationship — Psa 66:18 (VCG-04): cherished iniquity closes the divine ear; (2) the intimate neighbour relationship — Psa 28:3 (VCG-03): evil hidden beneath peace-speech toward neighbours; (3) the communal-civic level — Isa 10:1 (VCG-02): iniquitous decrees affecting the community; (4) the communal-embedded level — Psa 55:10 (VCG-01): "iniquity and trouble are within it" (the city); (5) the enemy-relational level — Psa 55:3 (VCG-01): trouble dropped upon the psalmist by personal enemies; (6) the generational level — Job 21:19 (VCG-04): iniquity stored up for children. The scope covers every level from the intimate individual to the transgenerational communal.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The relational scope is maximally wide: (1) vertical divine-human (VCG-01 — the human person against God); (2) horizontal community-level (VCG-03 — 1Pe 2:12: believers accused by Gentile opponents; 1Pe 3:16: slandered by those who revile); (3) individual person-to-person (VCG-02 — 1Cor 4:13: apostle slandered; Rom 3:8: false attribution to Paul); (4) institutional-legal (VCG-03 — Joh 18:30: formal legal charge; Act 25:5: official charge process); (5) eschatological-cosmic (VCG-01 — Rev 13:6; 16:9/11/21: cosmic-scale blasphemy under eschatological judgment). The characteristic operates at every level of the relational hierarchy from the intimately personal to the cosmic-eschatological.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's relational scope is maximal — all six characteristics operate across every level of relational reality from the intimately personal to the cosmic-eschatological. The cluster's scope hierarchy: personal individual (Char 3 — the devious person in divine confidence or exclusion), intimate relational bonds (Char 4 — spousal influence in idolatrous attachment), community level (Chars 1 and 5 — evildoers as a defined community class), national-institutional level (Char 4 VCG-03 — royal institutionalisation of abominations), global-communal level (Char 5 — communal iniquity saturating cities), cosmic-eschatological (Chars 2 VCG-01 — "whole world in the evil one"; Char 6 VCG-01 — Rev 13:6 beast's cosmic blasphemy; Char 3 — Rev 17:5 Babylon as mother of abominations). The cluster addresses inner evil from the personal to the cosmic.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The primary scope is the covenant people Israel and sojourners within Israel's camp. The laws govern the person's standing before God (access to the tabernacle), within the covenant community (camp/camp exclusion), and in relation to other persons (transmission duties). The NT categorical revision extends the scope: the clean/unclean categories are applied to the question of persons from all nations (Act 10:28) and to the relational status of mixed households (1Cor 7:14, M10c-B-VCG-05). The scope expands from Israel-only to all who stand in relation to the covenant community.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The relational scope is universal but with specific covenant-community applications. At the broadest scope: Job 14:4 (VCG-01) — no one can bring a clean thing from an unclean — this is about the human being as such. At the specific application scope: the NT epistolary evidence addresses communities of believers in whom the characteristic should not be present but is found (2Cor 12:21, VCG-02 — Corinthian community; Eph 4:19, VCG-02 — the Gentile world from which the Ephesian believers have been called out). The characteristic is universal in scope (all humanity) and especially pressing within the covenant community (believers called to holiness but susceptible to the characteristic's persistence).

**[CHAR-3]** E — The relational scope is primarily the covenant community (Israel/the house of Israel/Jerusalem as subjects throughout the corpus), but extends to: all relational bonds within the community (marriage — VCG-01; priesthood — VCG-05), the community's relationship with sacred space (sanctuary — VCG-03, land — VCG-04), God's relationship with the community (VCG-02 — divine withdrawal; VCG-05 — cleansing promise), and the community's relationship with surrounding nations (Lam 1:17/4:15, VCG-05 — as perceived by nations). The scope is comprehensive within the covenantal relational network.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The relational scope is universal — the characteristic affects persons across all covenantal, ethnic, and social boundaries evidenced in the corpus. The commissioning at Mat 10:1 and Mar 6:7 (VCG-03) gives authority over unclean spirits without limiting scope to Israel. Act 5:16 — people from "towns around Jerusalem"; Act 8:7 — Philip's ministry in Samaria. The characteristic's scope is co-extensive with the domain of adversarial spiritual powers in the fallen world.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The four relational-scope profiles together reveal the cluster's comprehensive relational reach. Characteristic 1: primarily Israel and sojourners within Israel's sacral space, expanding at the NT to include all persons and households in relation to the covenant community (Act 10:28; 1Cor 7:14). Characteristic 2: universal in scope (Job 14:4 — no one exempt; Rom 1:24 — universal human moral condition) with specific covenant-community urgency (NT epistolary evidence). Characteristic 3: comprehensive within the covenantal relational network (marital, communal, divine-covenantal, land, sanctuary, nations) — the most comprehensively relational defilement in the cluster. Characteristic 4: universal in scope — the adversarial spiritual powers do not observe covenantal or ethnic boundaries (Jewish synagogue, Gentile territory, Samaritan cities). The cluster's relational scope: most bounded (Char 1) → universal-human (Char 2) → comprehensive-covenantal (Char 3) → universal-spiritual (Char 4). Together the four characteristics cover the full relational scope of the defilement domain.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-004: T4 reveals the most structurally developed relational architecture for compassion's scope. God's compassion operates simultaneously on three bases: sovereignly free (Rom 9:15 — "I will have compassion…
findings.finding_value: T4 reveals the most structurally developed relational architecture for compassion's scope. God's compassion operates simultaneously on three bases: sovereignly free (Rom 9:15 — "I will have compassion on whom I have compassion"), covenantally grounded (chesed as the bond-loyalty that grounds the characteristic), and situationally responsive (splanchnizō — triggered by the specific sight of suffering). These three bases are not in tension but in integration: divine compassion is free, covenanted, and responsive simultaneously. The scope finding is among the most analytically significant in the registry: compassion explicitly and repeatedly crosses covenantal boundaries (Nineveh, the Samaritan/Jew axis, the power-asymmetric relationship). Scope is defined by perceived need, not moral standing or covenantal membership — this is formally confirmed in the data and distinguishes compassion from many other relational characteristics. The chesed/splanchnizō distinction maps onto distinct relational registers: chesed sustains within established bonds; splanchnizō extends across distance and difference. T4.4 (receiver's inner-being experience) is the most significant gap — four P-rated prompts, entirely absent from the data. T4.6 (spiritual beings interface) is entirely silent across all four prompts.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-010: T1's scope finding (compassion requires a suffering other; scope is determined by perceived need, not moral standing) is precisely confirmed in T4's relational analysis. The explicit crossing of coven…
findings.finding_value: T1's scope finding (compassion requires a suffering other; scope is determined by perceived need, not moral standing) is precisely confirmed in T4's relational analysis. The explicit crossing of covenantal boundaries (Nineveh, Samaritan/Jew) evidenced in T4 is the relational expression of T1's boundary-definition: compassion ends where the condition (pitiable need) is absent, not where covenantal membership ends. T1's four modes of operation (T1.4) — intra-covenantal, cross-boundary, anticipatory, Christological — map onto T4's chesed/splanchnizō distinction (within-bond sustaining vs across-distance extending) and the scope analysis (covenantal and transcovenantal registers). Definition and relational scope are structurally co-determining.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-015: T2's constitutional origin analysis (somatic-relational-covenantal triple ground) and T4's relational direction analysis are structurally aligned. The somatic origin (womb, gut) grounds the cross-boun…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional origin analysis (somatic-relational-covenantal triple ground) and T4's relational direction analysis are structurally aligned. The somatic origin (womb, gut) grounds the cross-boundary relational direction in T4: splanchnizō's somatic immediacy is precisely what enables it to cross covenantal boundaries — the gut-movement toward the suffering other precedes any covenantal assessment of the relationship. The covenantal origin (chesed) grounds the within-bond sustaining direction in T4. The constitutional origin therefore predicts the relational direction: somatic = cross-boundary; covenantal = within-bond. T2's soul-body interface classification explains T4's scope-by-need finding: because compassion originates at the soul-body interface (before covenantal-rational assessment), its scope is determined by the pre-rational recognition of need rather than the post-rational assessment of covenantal standing.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-019: T3's perceptive-trigger finding (compassion is activated by sight — splanchnizō is perceptively dependent) and T4's scope-by-need finding (scope is determined by perceived need, not covenantal standin…
findings.finding_value: T3's perceptive-trigger finding (compassion is activated by sight — splanchnizō is perceptively dependent) and T4's scope-by-need finding (scope is determined by perceived need, not covenantal standing) are the same finding from two analytical perspectives. T3 names the faculty (perception) and its function (triggering compassion by seeing the pitiable condition); T4 names the relational consequence (scope defined by what is seen). The cross-boundary extension in T4 (Nineveh, Samaritan/Jew) is the relational expression of T3's merit-independence: compassion is perceptively dependent (it must see the need) but merit-independent (it does not assess the moral standing of the one seen). The three relational modes in T3.11 (building/sustaining, restoring/repairing, extending across difference) correspond precisely to T4's chesed/splanchnizō/cross-boundary structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-023: T4's finding that divine compassion operates on three simultaneous bases (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, cove…
findings.finding_value: T4's finding that divine compassion operates on three simultaneous bases (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological) are structurally isomorphic. The sovereignly-free basis corresponds to the encounter/sudden mechanism: divine compassion operating freely produces the sudden compassion-event (splanchnizō). The covenantally-grounded basis corresponds to the covenantal-sustaining mechanism: chesed as the sustaining relational ground operates gradually and consistently. The situationally-responsive basis opens toward the participatory-ontological mechanism: formation at the deepest constitutional level produces a person who is dispositionally responsive to every situation of need. T4's relational architecture and T5's formation mechanisms are the same structural reality described from relational and developmental perspectives respectively.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-024: T4's scope-by-need finding (compassion crosses covenantal boundaries) and T6's co-occurrence landscape (the human-response cluster — peace, faith, will, surrender — co-occurring with compassion) revea…
findings.finding_value: T4's scope-by-need finding (compassion crosses covenantal boundaries) and T6's co-occurrence landscape (the human-response cluster — peace, faith, will, surrender — co-occurring with compassion) reveal a structural pattern: divine compassion reaching across boundaries generates a characteristic cluster of human inner-being responses regardless of the covenantal position of the recipient. The Nineveh response (repentance and turning) and the pattern of peace/faith/will/surrender co-occurring with compassion both confirm this: compassion-received generates a recognisable inner-being response cluster that is structurally consistent across relational positions. T6's mapping of the human-response cluster is the co-occurrence evidence for T4's structural finding about scope and response.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-025: T4's three bases of divine compassion (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) are each grounded in specific textual evidence from T7. The sovereignly-free basis is evidence…
findings.finding_value: T4's three bases of divine compassion (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) are each grounded in specific textual evidence from T7. The sovereignly-free basis is evidenced in Rom 9:15 (T7's argument structure analysis — divine compassion as sovereign determination). The covenantally-grounded basis is evidenced in Exod 34:6 (T7's most multiply-anchored verse — the divine self-declaration in the covenant context). The situationally-responsive basis is evidenced in the Synoptic splanchnizō pattern (T7.2 — the sight-event structure of the Gospels). T7's framework divergences (sovereignty vs automaticity) map directly onto T4's relational analysis: the framework correctly identifies that divine compassion's sovereign freedom (T4.1) is what exceeds the natural empathic automaticity that human science frameworks describe.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-004: T4 establishes the most precisely articulated relational architecture of any characteristic in the review set. The God-to-human direction is primary and dominant (groups 888-001, 889-001, 5471-001 — a…
findings.finding_value: T4 establishes the most precisely articulated relational architecture of any characteristic in the review set. The God-to-human direction is primary and dominant (groups 888-001, 889-001, 5471-001 — all God-as-subject). The basis of divine extension is the giver's character and prior knowing (Exo 33:17 — "I know you by name"), not the receiver's merit — neither merit-based nor arbitrary. The human-to-God direction is specifically supplication: tachanum (H8469) is the receiving side's corresponding vocabulary built into the same root family as the giving side (chen/chanan) — the vocabulary embeds the two-directional circuit in a single root. The human-giving direction extends grace horizontally through three modes: forgiving (charizō — Eph 4:32), gracious conduct (chen as character quality — 889-003), and gracious speech (SD022). The receiving direction is the most underexamined (T4.4 — P-rated throughout); the scope analysis (T4.5) reveals grace crossing covenantal and social boundaries (Ruth narrative — grace in the context of foreign status and vulnerability). T4.6 (spiritual beings) is evidenced at one point: Luk 1:28 (kecharitōmenē — the angel's announcement), which implies angelic ministry as a vehicle of grace rather than grace operating independently in the spiritual-beings register. T4 synthesis: the relational architecture of grace is unique in the programme — it is the only characteristic where the giving-side vocabulary and the receiving-side vocabulary are built from the same root (chen/tachanum), encoding the grace-circuit's two-sidedness at the lexical level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-010: T1's four modes of operation map onto T4's four relational directions. The sovereign-bestowal mode corresponds to the God-to-human direction (T4.1 — primary and dominant). The covenantal-relational-su…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes of operation map onto T4's four relational directions. The sovereign-bestowal mode corresponds to the God-to-human direction (T4.1 — primary and dominant). The covenantal-relational-sustaining mode corresponds to the relational scope (T4.5 — grace operating within and across covenantal boundaries). The capacity-conferring mode corresponds to the human-to-God direction in its supplication register (T4.2 — SD026: grace giving even the capacity to appeal). The character-forming mode corresponds to the human-giving direction (T4.3 — gracious conduct and speech as the horizontal expression of received grace-character). The vocabulary's structural insight (T4 synthesis: giving-side and receiving-side built from the same root, chen/tachanum) explains T1's finding that grace requires the receptor's inner engagement to complete its operation — the vocabulary encodes the two-sidedness because grace is constitutively a two-sided circuit.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-024: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 vers…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T4.2 (the human-to-God supplication direction): seeking is the relational posture, and R140 is the registry that names it. The sequential relationship confirmed in T6.2 (grace precedes and enables faith, repentance, supplication, mourning — SD003, SD006, SD026, SD038) is the causal expression of T4's architectural finding: grace is the enabling condition for every positive human-to-God relational posture. The boundary questions in T6.5 (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-chesed) correspond to T4.5's scope analysis: the characteristics that share grace's scope (particularly love and mercy) are the same characteristics whose relational scope overlaps with grace's at T4.5.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence is not entirely silent on relational boundaries but is thin. Luke 6:35 — "love your enemies and do good... and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil" — explicitly extends kindness beyond the deserving and beyond the covenant partner to include enemies and the ungrateful [OBS-099-078]. This is the most direct boundary-crossing statement in the evidence: kindness is not restricted to those who merit it or belong to the covenant community. The chesed evidence (Exo 20:6 — showing chesed to those who love God and keep his commandments) suggests covenantal conditionality in its sustained manifestation, but Luke 6:35 shows it reaching across that boundary in its initiating mode. The precise scope — how far the boundary extends and what distinguishes sustained chesed from initiating kindness — is not fully resolved from the evidence and requires Session D cross-registry examination.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The commands against despising (Rom 14:3; 14:10; 1Cor 16:11; 1Th 5:20) operate within the covenant community. The Boaz-Ruth protection (Rut 2:15, vc=38516) operates across covenantal difference: Boaz protects Ruth, an outsider, from the contempt she would normally receive. The 1Sa 25:7/15 (vc=38530/38531) protection of Nabal's shepherds operates within a social context of armed men restraining themselves. CHAR-5's scope is not covenantally limited — contempt can cross any relational boundary; what is covenantally specific is the community's obligation to protect against contempt within its own relational field.

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 operates specifically within the covenant relationship between the person and God: the approach to God's altar (Psa 26:6) is a covenantal act; the divine confirmation of innocence (Gen 20:6) is a covenantal response; the incapacity for innocence (Hos 8:5) is a covenantal failure condition. The constructive characteristics (corrective shame, conscience-activated moral evaluation, innocence-enabled approach) are more covenantally specific. Exceptions: Char 2's God-abasing act crosses all covenantal boundaries (God humbles all pride); Char 5's divine reversal is explicitly extended universally (1Cor 1:28 — God choosing the world's despised). findings.finding_value: T4 as a whole reveals contrition's relational structure is strongly asymmetric: the God-to-human and human-to-God directions are richly evidenced; the human-to-human and spiritual-beings directions are thin or silent. The asymmetry is analytically significant — contrition is primarily a vertical characteristic. What the tier establishes collectively is that contrition constitutes the condition for divine-human relational proximity. The key T4 synthesis: the God-to-human direction (God draws near, dwells with, looks to the contrite) and the human-to-God direction (the contrite person approaches God in lowliness) together create the relational event that contrition is. Neither direction alone describes contrition — it is the convergence of the two movements: divine movement toward the contrite, and creaturely movement toward God through brokenness. The substitutionary group (Isa 53:5) is the only instance of contrition vocabulary operating horizontally — and it is unique to the Servant, not a general pattern.

findings.finding_value: T4 reveals fellowship as the most relationally comprehensive characteristic in the registry: it operates in all four primary directions (God-to-human, human-to-God, human-giving, human-receiving) and partially in the spiritual-beings direction. The key T4 synthesis: 1Jo 1:3's structural claim — horizontal fellowship is derived from and grounded in vertical fellowship — means the relational architecture of fellowship is hierarchical: the divine-human fellowship is primary; human-human fellowship is its extension and expression. The scope analysis (Q&A-119) reveals that fellowship scope narrows as its depth increases: all-the-living (widest) → God-fearers → covenant partner → ecclesial body → divine nature participants (deepest-narrowest). Depth and breadth are inversely proportional in fellowship's relational structure.

findings.finding_value: T4 establishes the most structurally developed relational architecture of any characteristic reviewed in this series. All four primary directions are fully evidenced: God-to-human (the dominant vertical direction — exclusively divine in the OT salach domain), human-to-God (seeking-forgiveness — intercession and confession), human-giving (commanded horizontal), human-receiving (implied in the horizontal transaction). The spiritual-beings direction adds the Holy Spirit as the enabling mediator (Joh 20:22-23) and the unforgivable sin as the outer limit (Mar 3:29). The vertical-horizontal interdependence (Mat 18:35; Mat 6:14-15) is the most structurally developed relational feature: the human-giving direction is structurally conditioned on the human-receiving direction (one who genuinely received divine forgiveness can genuinely extend human forgiveness). The scope analysis shows: universal access through faith (Act 10:43) with an absolute outer limit (Mar 3:29). T4's synthesis: forgiveness has the fullest relational architecture of the characteristics reviewed — every direction is evidenced, and the vertical-horizontal interdependence is a structural claim unique to forgiveness.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-004: T4 reveals the most structurally developed relational architecture for compassion's scope. God's compassion operates simultaneously on three bases: sovereignly free (Rom 9:15 — "I will have compassion…
findings.finding_value: T4 reveals the most structurally developed relational architecture for compassion's scope. God's compassion operates simultaneously on three bases: sovereignly free (Rom 9:15 — "I will have compassion on whom I have compassion"), covenantally grounded (chesed as the bond-loyalty that grounds the characteristic), and situationally responsive (splanchnizō — triggered by the specific sight of suffering). These three bases are not in tension but in integration: divine compassion is free, covenanted, and responsive simultaneously. The scope finding is among the most analytically significant in the registry: compassion explicitly and repeatedly crosses covenantal boundaries (Nineveh, the Samaritan/Jew axis, the power-asymmetric relationship). Scope is defined by perceived need, not moral standing or covenantal membership — this is formally confirmed in the data and distinguishes compassion from many other relational characteristics. The chesed/splanchnizō distinction maps onto distinct relational registers: chesed sustains within established bonds; splanchnizō extends across distance and difference. T4.4 (receiver's inner-being experience) is the most significant gap — four P-rated prompts, entirely absent from the data. T4.6 (spiritual beings interface) is entirely silent across all four prompts.

findings.finding_value: T4 establishes the most precisely articulated relational architecture of any characteristic in the review set. The God-to-human direction is primary and dominant (groups 888-001, 889-001, 5471-001 — all God-as-subject). The basis of divine extension is the giver's character and prior knowing (Exo 33:17 — "I know you by name"), not the receiver's merit — neither merit-based nor arbitrary. The human-to-God direction is specifically supplication: tachanum (H8469) is the receiving side's corresponding vocabulary built into the same root family as the giving side (chen/chanan) — the vocabulary embeds the two-directional circuit in a single root. The human-giving direction extends grace horizontally through three modes: forgiving (charizō — Eph 4:32), gracious conduct (chen as character quality — 889-003), and gracious speech (SD022). The receiving direction is the most underexamined (T4.4 — P-rated throughout); the scope analysis (T4.5) reveals grace crossing covenantal and social boundaries (Ruth narrative — grace in the context of foreign status and vulnerability). T4.6 (spiritual beings) is evidenced at one point: Luk 1:28 (kecharitōmenē — the angel's announcement), which implies angelic ministry as a vehicle of grace rather than grace operating independently in the spiritual-beings register. T4 synthesis: the relational architecture of grace is unique in the programme — it is the only characteristic where the giving-side vocabulary and the receiving-side vocabulary are built from the same root (chen/tachanum), encoding the grace-circuit's two-sidedness at the lexical level.

findings.finding_value: T4 establishes two key relational findings: (1) Peace's scope expands progressively — covenant-primary (to Israel, Num 6:26) → covenant-expansive (to nations in the prophets, Isa 57:19) → universally offered through Christ (Eph 2:14, Col 1:20) — with the only sustained exclusion being moral ("no peace for the wicked"). Peace is not only a private inner condition but a publicly contested reality across the cosmic order.

findings.finding_value: M01-A shows fear of God operating in the angelic realm: Psa 89:7 (God is "greatly to be feared among the holy ones in the divine council — his awesomeness surpasses all heavenly beings, making reverential fear the only fitting inner response **even in heaven**"). Fear of God is not merely a human posture but the appropriate posture of the divine council before God. Gen 22:12 (the angel of the Lord affirming Abraham's fear of God as evidenced by his willingness to sacrifice — the fear tested and confirmed through angelic mediation).

M01-B shows angelic mediation of fear extensively: the angelic appearances throughout the NT that produce fear in human persons (Luk 1:12-13; Luk 2:9-10; Mat 28:4-5; Luk 24:5; Act 10:4; Rev 1:17) are the most concentrated evidence. Angels both produce acute fear and command its release ("do not be afraid" from angels across the corpus). Angels operate as the interface through which divine holiness makes itself felt in the human inner life.

M01-B-VCG-01 (fear before supernatural encounters) shows specific instances of adversarial encounter producing fear: Dan 7:7 (the fourth beast — terrifying in appearance, producing fear — in the visionary realm); Mar 14:33 (Jesus in Gethsemane, ekthambeo — though this is the suffering Son before the Father's judgment rather than adversarial encounter). The adversarial spiritual dimension is present but not dominant in the evidenced material.

M01-F-VCG-04's fearful expectation of judgment (Heb 10:27) operates in the context of divine judgment as the eschatological reality — a spiritual-being interface in the sense that it anticipates encountering God as judge.

Angelic beings are prominent mediators of M01-B fear (appearances producing fear, commands releasing fear). The divine council evidences reverential fear of God (Psa 89:7 — M01-A). Adversarial spiritual operations are less prominent in the evidenced material: the beasts of Daniel's visions (M01-B-VCG-01) and the general spiritual-resistance context of M01-G (Rev 21:8's apostasy-under-pressure) are the nearest instances.

Rev 11:18 (M02-A-VCG-02): "God's wrath arrives as a decisive, timed response to the nations' own raging" — the nations' rage (which may include demonic spiritual influence, per the Revelation context) is the occasion for divine wrath's arrival. The characteristic operates across the spiritual-beings interface as both a spiritual-beings state (dragon's fury) and a response to spiritual-beings activity (God's wrath responding to collective human-spiritual rage).

(1) **Heavenly/angelic Joy** — Luk 15:7 ("joy in heaven over one sinner who repents"); Luk 15:10 ("joy before the angels of God") — Joy is an active reality in the heavenly realm, responsive to human repentance; (2) **The Holy Spirit as Joy-agent** — Gal 5:22; 1Th 1:6; Rom 14:17; Act 13:52 — the Spirit is the agent of Joy in the NT's Spirit-mediated register; Luk 10:21 (Jesus rejoices "in the Holy Spirit") — the Spirit is the medium of Christ's own Joy; (3) **Eschatological angelic context** — Jude 24 ("with great joy" before God's presence — at the final presentation); Rev 4:9; 7:12 (heavenly creatures giving thanks — the joy-adjacent thanksgiving of heavenly worship).

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes: (1) **The Holy Spirit as producer** — Luk 10:21; 1Th 1:6; Act 13:52 — the Spirit is the primary agent of Suffering-Joy's most intense form; the characteristic is directly Spirit-mediated; (2) **Angelic context** — Luk 1:44 (the baby leaping at Mary's Spirit-anointed greeting — the Spirit who has overshadowed Mary transmits through the incarnation-announcement context); Mat 5:12's "reward in heaven" implies the angelic-heavenly realm as the context within which the reward awaits.

He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god" — CHAR-1 explicitly directed against the divine order, extending beyond any single deity to claim supremacy over "every god." ## T5 — Transformation and Formation

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. 2Pe 2:4 provides direct evidence: "God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment." Angels committed wilful sinning — the same characteristic (cha.ta/hamartanō) that the human corpus addresses. Their sinning resulted in immediate divine judgment and permanent imprisonment. The angels are thus participants in wilful sinning, not merely observers or tempters. Additionally, the Eze 28:16 cherub passage ("you sinned; so I cast you as a profane thing from the mountain of God") evidences a guardian cherub's sinning — a spiritual being of high standing whose sinning produced expulsion from God's presence.

**[CHAR-10]** S — The 5-verse corpus contains no direct evidence of these mechanisms operating in relation to angelic or adversarial spiritual beings. The mechanisms operate in human relational contexts (enticers and the enticed, hypocritical community, accusers of Paul).

**[CHAR-11]** E — Yes. Act 26:18 — "from the power of Satan to God" — the condition places the person within Satan's power-domain; the condition's location is in the domain of the adversarial spiritual power. Gal 1:4 — "deliver us from the present evil age" — the condition is part of the "present evil age" that has a spiritual-power dimension. Eph 2:1 — "dead in trespasses and sins" is followed (in the broader Eph 2:2 context — not in the 5-verse corpus but structurally implied) by the reference to the prince of the power of the air; the condition's domain involves the adversarial spiritual power.

**[CHAR-12]** E — Yes — the adversarial spiritual dimension is explicitly named. 1Jo 3:8 — "whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning" — the devil is the originary sinning-power whose domain the enslaved person enters through practice; sin's enslaving power is directly connected to the devil's primordial sinning identity. 1Jo 5:18 — "the evil one does not touch him" — the evil one is the specific spiritual agent through whom sin's enslaving power seeks to regain the born-of-God person; the liberation is specifically described as protection from the evil one's touch.

**[CHAR-13]** S — The 205-verse corpus does not explicitly connect the divine record to spiritual beings (angels or adversarial powers). The record operates between the human person and God directly; no angelic or adversarial spiritual agent is explicitly named as a mediator of the record in this corpus. The characteristic is constitutively a human-divine transaction.

**[CHAR-14]** S — The 34-verse corpus does not explicitly name spiritual beings (angelic or adversarial) in connection with forgiveness sought and received. The characteristic operates directly between the human person and God through the priestly or Christological mechanism.

**[CHAR-15]** S — The 8-verse corpus does not explicitly name spiritual beings (angelic or adversarial) in connection with generational sin. The condition operates within the human-God covenant relationship without named spiritual-beings mediation.

**[CHAR-16]** E — Yes — through the angelic joy dimension. Luk 15:10 — "there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents" — the angels are the witnesses of the sinner's repentance; their joy is the spiritual-beings' response to the sinner-identity's reversal. The angels' rejoicing names the sinner-repentance as a spiritually cosmic event, not merely a human-scale moral turning.

**[CHAR-17]** S — The 97-verse corpus does not explicitly name spiritual beings (angelic or adversarial) in connection with guilt as inner-being state. The one near-exception is Isa 6:7 — the seraph touches Isaiah's lips and removes his guilt — but this is divine agent (seraph as God's messenger) acting on God's behalf, not an independent spiritual being mediating guilt.

**[CHAR-18]** S — The 162-verse corpus does not explicitly name angelic or adversarial spiritual beings in connection with iniquity-as-accumulated-moral-crime as its primary agent. The characteristic operates within the direct human-God moral relationship. The seraph in Isa 6:7 (touching Isaiah's lips to remove guilt) is the nearest instance, but this falls in CHAR-17's removal dimension; the CHAR-18 iniquity-accumulation corpus does not feature named spiritual beings mediating its accumulation or maintenance.

**[CHAR-19]** E — Yes — through the Isa 53:12 servant-intercession passage and the Heb 2:2 angelic-law passage. Isa 53:12 — "he was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors" — the servant (who is both human and divine agent) intercedes among the transgressors; this intercession is directed toward God on behalf of human transgressors. Heb 2:2 — "the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution" — angels are named as the mediators of the law whose reliability undergirds the transgression-retribution principle.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. Num 22:34 is the primary spiritual-beings evidence: Balaam's inadvertent sinning occurred in the context of the angel of the Lord standing in the road against him — a fact hidden from Balaam until the angel was made visible. The spiritual being (angel of the Lord) was the morally relevant fact that Balaam's perception did not register, producing the inadvertent violation. The angel's disclosure is what transforms Balaam's uninformed violation into a consciously acknowledged sin requiring confession and offered reversal. The spiritual being operates as the *disclosure agent* — the one who surfaces the morally relevant truth that the inadvertent sinner did not perceive.

**[CHAR-20]** S — The 101-verse corpus does not explicitly name angelic or adversarial spiritual beings in connection with faithlessness as covenant-breaking sin. The characteristic operates within the direct human-God and human-human covenantal relationship without named spiritual-being mediation.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Yes — through the serpent-type passage. 2Cor 11:3 — "as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray" — the serpent is named as the archetypal external corrupting agent; the serpent's deceptive cunning is the model for the false teachers' thought-corrupting strategy. The serpent-type names an adversarial spiritual agency as the paradigmatic external source of the perversion of thought.

**[CHAR-22]** S — The 72-verse corpus does not explicitly name angelic or adversarial spiritual beings in connection with injustice as moral failure of right conduct. The idolatrous direction transmitted through contagious sin points toward spiritual beings behind the false gods. 1Ki 16:13 — "provoking the Lord God of Israel to anger with their idols" — the idols are the objects of the diverted worship; the spiritual dimension behind the idol-worship is implied by the divine jealousy response (jealousy presupposes a relational competitor). Jer 32:35 — "Molech" — the specific false deity to whom children are offered names a spiritual-being referent for the contagious sin's worship direction. The community's transmitted sinning is directed toward these spiritual objects.

**[CHAR-8]** S — The 9-verse corpus contains no direct evidence of political revolt operating in relation to angelic or adversarial spiritual beings. The characteristic operates through human political-authority relationships.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Yes — the most direct spiritual-being interface in the corpus. Jude 9 — Michael the archangel withholds a blasphemous judgment *against the devil* — the confrontation is between angelic and demonic spiritual beings, and the sinful speech in question is the potential blasphemous verdict against a spiritual being. 2Pe 2:11 — "angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord" — "them" refers to spiritual beings. The characteristic thus operates at the interface of angelic-demonic confrontation, where the restraint of sinful speech is a marker of creaturely limit.

**[CHAR-1]** S — The verse evidence in the 190-verse corpus does not directly address the operation of wickedness-as-settled-person-identity in relation to angelic or adversarial spiritual beings. The characteristic is framed throughout as a human inner-being phenomenon in relation to God and other humans. No verse in the corpus directly implicates angelic or demonic mediation in the settling of this characteristic.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes — and this is the INTEGRATION_NOTE carry-forward. VCG-01 (13V) directly addresses the characteristic's operation in relation to cosmic-adversarial spiritual powers. Mat 6:13 (vc=14415 — VCG-01): "deliver us from evil" — evil as a power or domain from which divine deliverance is needed. Mat 13:19 (vc=14435 — VCG-01): the evil one as a supra-personal agent targeting the heart. Eph 6:12 (vc=14413 — VCG-05): "spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places" — supra-human wickedness in the cosmic realm. 1Jo 5:19 (vc=14433 — VCG-01): "the whole world lies in the power of the evil one" — the cosmic-adversarial dimension is integral to understanding the scope of constitutional inner evil. The VCG-01 cosmic-evil sub-corpus is the M27 cross-register signal: these verses address a dimension of evil that is supra-personal and cosmic, not merely constitutional-individual.
